articles.title: New Research Helps Show How Depth Affects Fish Distribution
articles.body:
[ Disponible en español ]

How do the bodies and lifestyles of fishes change as you dive deeper into the ocean? That question is the subject of a new study analyzing footage from waters near Puerto Rico, which is helping scientists understand how fishes at different depths interact with their environment.

Understanding where different kinds of fish live and how they behave is critical for managing ocean resources responsibly. Research on fish distributions is often done by collecting samples with tools like trawl nets. Those physical collections are essential to marine science, but they don’t tell us how a fish interacts with its underwater ecosystem. For this paper, researchers relied on video recorded by remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and submersibles to study fish species in their natural habitats.

The paper’s authors, who included undergraduate students at the State University of New York (SUNY) College at Geneseo, reviewed footage from 30 exploration dives recorded by teams operating NOAA Ocean Exploration’s ROV Deep Discoverer, ROV Global Explorer, and the National Deep Submergence Facility’s submersible Alvin, operated by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The results tell a clear story that supports the findings of other deep-sea experts. Abundance and biodiversity of all fishes decreased with depth, showing that life in the deep requires specialized adaptations. Deeper waters correlated with a higher percentage of bottom-dwelling fish living as ambush predators. Perhaps most interesting, though, is that fish species found swimming in deeper and colder waters tended to have long, eel-like bodies, while those in shallower waters appeared more “normal.”

Experts have suggested a few reasons for this trend over the past several years. It could be that longer bodies help deep-sea fishes swim long distances to find food, making them “endurance runners” compared to shallow-water “sprinters.” A longer body could also help deep-sea fishes sense their low-light environment by adding more sensors to their lateral line, an organ that helps fish detect movement in the water. It will take more research to learn for sure what’s behind the eel-like forms, but confirming that the trend is the same in different parts of the ocean is an important step.

The researchers’ strategy of observing deep-sea fishes where they lived led to other interesting findings, too. Some fishes usually thought of as pelagic (swimming in the water column without touching the ocean floor) were seen interacting with the seafloor or narrowly escaping bottom-dwelling predators like anemones. Fish were also filmed living in and around trash, which was observed frequently during the expeditions that provided the recordings. Discoveries like these would not have been possible without deep-sea footage.

“Opportunities to observe deep-sea organisms in their environment are critical to our understanding,” said Mackenzie Gerringer, the lead author of the new study.

“We learn so much from seeing how some fishes position themselves vertically instead of swimming horizontally, or how some cusk eels regularly forage near deep-sea corals. A species is its DNA sequence and its body shape and characteristics from a collected specimen, but it is also much more. We need multiple ways of looking at deep-sea species to truly understand their lives.”

Use of the newly refitted Alvin submersible was especially helpful for observing the deepest-dwelling fish of the study. Researchers saw multiple cusk eels in the Puerto Rico Trench, which appear to be a very important and understudied group of fish in extremely deep waters. Alvin’s new depth limit of 6500 meters (21,300 feet) opens up new opportunities for exploring extreme ocean environments.

“This is exactly what Alvin was made for—and why the National Science Foundation and Office of Naval Research put so much effort into the upgrades that allow it to dive deeper than ever before,” said Anna Michel, the Chief Scientist of the National Deep Submergence Facility at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution that manages and operates the sub. “Scientists come away from dives in Alvin transformed, and their firsthand observations have revolutionized understanding of the physical, chemical, and biological processes that govern the deep ocean and that help shape life here on the surface.”

This study was conducted as part of a Course-Based Research Experience (CURE) for Undergraduates in a Marine Biology lab course at SUNY Geneseo. Open-access data such as those provided by NOAA Ocean Exploration support meaningful opportunities for undergraduates to engage in deep-sea research. A study supported by NOAA and the National Marine Sanctuary Foundation’s Ocean Exploration Education grant program (#22-01-B-417 to M.E. Gerringer) shows that deep-sea CUREs enhance students’ understanding of the scientific process and engagement with their biology education. The study details how programs like the deep-sea CURE leading to the paper featured in this article can be implemented in biology courses.

This new study was led by Mackenzie Gerringer of the State University of New York (SUNY) at Geneseo. It was co-authored by Chryssanthi Tzetzis, Jacob Calus, Abisage Sekarore, Erin Patton, Julia Cappiello, Emily McMahon, Nikki Fuller, Gabriel Rosado, Allison North, A.J. Petty, Benjamin McPherson, Emily Morgan, Christopher Cook, Cole Janda, Andrew Kareeparampil, Olivia Knudsen, Brooke Licata, Peyton Mackey, Nathan Phillips, Megan Roell, Catie Sawyer, Makena Scarlata, Giovanna Sineo, Evan Weaver, Brett H. Woodworth (SUNY Geneseo), Kasey Cantwell (NOAA Ocean Exploration), Daniel Wagner (NOAA Ocean Exploration, Ocean Exploration Trust), Brian R.C. Kennedy (NOAA Ocean Exploration, Ocean Discovery League, Boston University), Thomas Morrow, Samuel Candio (NOAA Ocean Exploration), S. Adam Soule (University of Rhode Island), Anna P.M. Michel (Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution), Andrea M. Quattrini (Smithsonian Institution), and A. Leitner (Oregon State University).

Gerringer et al. (2026) Observations of deep-sea fishes at depths 250 to 6300 m off Puerto Rico. ICES Journal of Marine Science 83(1). Access the full article online.

articles.title: Silent discipline propels 89th Maintenance Group executive airlift
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md. – A duck floats in the stillness of a lake. Above the water, it appears calm, still and controlled. Underneath, it is constantly moving, kicking its legs and working tirelessly to stay perfectly balanced. Maintaining that level of concentration and effortless appearance takes discipline, time and experience.

When asked how he embodies the concept of the "Silent Professional," U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Putthinan Thongmak, 89th Maintenance Group C-40B executive crew chief, related his work to that duck. He worked hard to reach this point in his career, taking pride in his unit’s motto, "Perfection is Our Standard"—a standard met through rigorous effort that often happens when no one is watching.

The 89th Airlift Wing executes Special Air Missions, operating as a direct instrument of U.S. national power and diplomacy. On his lightweight jacket, Thongmak wears the wing's distinctive embroidered SAM Fox emblem, symbolizing the high expectations placed on those entrusted with executive airlift for the nation's senior leaders. The C-40 aircraft he maintains, a specialized military variant of the Boeing 737, serves as an "office in the sky" for senior leaders like combatant commanders and cabinet secretaries traveling globally.

Thongmak approaches every task head-on with calm, soft-spoken and constant professionalism. "Thongmak is someone I can depend on," said Master Sgt. Alex Trillana, 89th Maintenance Group C-40 aircraft maintenance section chief. "If I need something done, no questions asked, he'd be the first person I would go to."

Trillana noted that Thongmak works thoroughly until every detail is complete without seeking external approval.

"Our mission in the 89th Wing is all about diplomacy," Trillana said. "When it comes to training and hiring, Thongmak makes sure that we have the most qualified, respected crew chiefs to work with our aircrew and the accompanying party, ensuring everyone is comfortable and able to work effectively."

Thongmak's daily dedication directly elevates unit readiness and strengthens mission assurance across the fleet. As an evaluator and hiring manager for flying crew chiefs, he actively selects and mentors the Airmen who uphold the wing's standard of excellence.

To sustain this high-tempo operational pace, maintaining balance at home is essential. His wife, Shelby Thongmak, offered insight into how they manage the unique demands of executive airlift.

"I’d say my husband is a bit more introverted and quieter than me, but he’s very motivated, kind, and compassionate," Shelby Thongmak said. "When he comes home from work, he knows how to leave work at the door."

Adjusting to the wing required adaptation. Flying crew chiefs can be away from home between 80 to 200 days out of the year supporting global diplomatic missions. For the Thongmak family, spending quality time together helps them recharge.

"We spend a lot of time together at home," Shelby Thongmak said. "When he comes home after a mission, he needs his rest, and we get to do that together. We do a lot of at-home projects together like painting, assembling furniture, and watching movies."

Their home is filled with personal touches like the magnets from global deployments that decorate the refrigerator, family photos line the walls, and a cat named Pumpkin roams the rooms. The couple is also preparing for another major milestone: growing their family.

"We are both really excited to have a child together," she said. "I know my husband, and he is going to be a great dad."

For Putthinan Thongmak, navigating mission requirements and family life requires deliberate focus.

"Some people may think a work-life balance is 50-50, but in reality, it can be closer to 90-10," Putthinan Thongmak said. "It’s all about aligning yourself with that part of your life that is more demanding at the time. There are times when the mission must come first, and there are other times when we need to recognize when to take a knee and recuperate."

That levelheaded demeanor keeps him grounded regardless of the mission's complexity. "At the end of the day, I want to be known as the guy that was willing to put in the work," Putthinan Thongmak said. "No matter the task or the mission, you can count on me to get it done to the best of my ability."

Like the duck calm on the surface, Thongmak continues to work behind the scenes, ensuring the wing seamlessly delivers executive airlift and diplomacy around the globe.

articles.title: Communications readiness exercise links Spangdahlem and Büchel Air Base teams
articles.body:
Airmen from the 702nd Munitions Support Squadron and 52nd Logistics Readiness Squadron took part in a cross-base exercise June 30, 2026, to improve communications support in a simulated remote operating environment. During the exercise, the integrated team moved a Transportable Global Aircrew Strategic Network Terminal from Büchel Air Base, Germany, to Spangdahlem Air Base, where they established a communications node designed to support units in remote operating environments. T-GASNT provides around-the-clock communications, enabling command and control nodes to reliably receive and transmit messages in alternate and austere locations. “The 702nd MUNSS is paving the way with the newly integrated TTPs,” said Staff Sgt. Tyler Hermes, 702nd MUNSS non-commissioned officer in charge of command, control and communications maintenance. “These new TTPs allow us to set up the system in less time and move it anywhere on the continent by land.” The training tested the team’s ability to coordinate across communications, operations and logistics functions while moving, setting up, maintaining and later dismantling the system. Once the training objectives were complete, the team tore down the equipment and returned it, validating each phase of the process from movement to employment and recovery.
“Complex, multi-domain operations require diverse, cross-functional expertise,” said Maj. Amanda Schuyler, 702nd MUNSS command and control operations flight chief. “This exercise integrated Airmen from multiple career fields to leverage specialized skills, encourage cross-functional support outside of primary specialties, improve collaboration, and proactively identify operational blind spots.” By training together in the field, participants strengthened working relationships and refined procedures that support contingency operations. “Lethality is built on collective proficiency,” Schuyler said. “The more competent we are in our individual duties and the better we understand our supporting partners, the more lethal and resilient we become as a unified combat force.”

articles.title: EOD Airmen train for the full spectrum of explosive threats
articles.body:
LIMESTONE HILLS TRAINING AREA, Mont. — The call comes in from headquarters.

“EOD, this is Godfather, be advised, hostiles approaching your location. How copy?” Inside the mask, every breath feels like drinking air through a straw. Airman 1st Class Levi Womack keys the radio. “Godfather, this is EOD. Good copy.”

Further up the ridgeline, Senior Airman Mitchell Massa hears the radio chatter and knows time is running out. He is working against the clock to disarm and decontaminate a chemical explosive device found in the woods near a forward operating base. With the seconds slipping by, his entire world narrows down to the problem in front of him, visible only through the fogged lenses of his gas mask.

“EOD, this is Godfather, leave the area. How copy?”

“Good copy, Godfather.”

Massa works his way down the ridge, moving slowly in his chemical protective gear, and drops the device in a decontamination tub.

“End of scenario,” yells the instructor at Field Training Exercise Big Trouble, a week-long exercise at Limestone Hills Training Area near Townsend, Montana. It’s only the morning of the first day, and already Massa and Womack are drenched in sweat as they peel off their protective gear, hot and thirsty under the August sun. Massa has come from the 366th Civil Engineer Squadron at Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho; Womack is assigned to the 341st CES at Malmstrom Air Force Base, and they are here to hone their craft on simulated chemicals and explosive devices.

This is their second problem of the day, and they gather around the instructor for a debrief.

He tells them that the purpose of this specific problem is to teach junior explosive ordnance disposal technicians what to do when external constraints make it too dangerous to continue conducting disposal operations. Knowing when to break off a mission rather than push past the point of safety was exactly the lesson Staff Sgt. Lucky Widjaja wanted every technician to carry off the range.

"The end goal is for them to realize their limitations and capabilities — the miles they're able to travel, and how they function under less-than-ideal conditions," said Widjaja, a 341st CES EOD technician and the exercise's main organizer. "So that if that were to ever happen in a deployed environment, they have that experience to fall back on."

Now in its fourth iteration and its second year drawing EOD shops from around the country, Big Trouble brought six Air Force EOD teams to Limestone Hills to train in a simulated deployed environment. Over the week, technicians worked scenarios spanning the threats they could meet downrange, such as improvised explosive devices, unexploded ordnance, weapons caches, route denial and chemical agents like Massa and Womack confronted that first morning.

The week’s training plan was built for Airmen early in their careers, many of them working through these high-pressure decision-making processes for the first time. The aim was to develop technicians who understood what team leadership demanded and could transfer their skills to real-world deployed environments.

If judgment, leadership, and technical skill were the lessons, communication between shops was the method. Planners paired technicians with counterparts from other shops to trade tactics, techniques and procedures, with the Airmen being expected to sharpen not just their own units but the shops they trained alongside.

"My favorite part is getting EOD members from different shops out here to train," Widjaja said. "It allows us to communicate and exchange learning points so that we are, as a whole EOD enterprise, more ready and capable to face our next emerging threat."

Throughout the week, teams gained experience with the career field's full toolkit. Massa traded his chemical protective gear for the controls of a unmanned ground vehicle, sending the robot to examine a suspected device while the operator stayed outside the blast radius.

At a different problem, careful prior planning made success possible. Staff Sgt. Hartvig Homberg, a 341st CES EOD technician, and Airman 1st Class Jacob Miller-Lujan, a 28th CES EOD technician from Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota, mapped out a plan before tackling a problem seeded with multiple devices, settling who did what and in what order. After each scenario, teams circled up to debrief, learning new lessons before moving to the next problem.

The week’s training tempo left technicians with limited recovery time. Teams woke up early to prep their gear and were on the range by 8 a.m. Once there, they rotated through problems, trading team-leader and team-member roles and switching between mounted and dismounted work. After a short rest at the end of the afternoon, they started a night mission brief around 9 p.m. and conducted training while using night-vision devices until at least midnight.

For Widjaja, he’s also been learning what it takes to organize such a large project.

"This is my first time planning this entire FTX, and I've had a lot of help from the guys at my shop,” he said. “That's been really rewarding."

For the Airmen learning at Big Trouble, the purposeful grind of the exercise teaches not just explosives, but teamwork and endurance.

"The hardest part is being tired, and keeping a good attitude and staying motivated throughout," he said. "But by the end of it, we see teams and players coming together, learning from other shops and exchanging knowledge.”

articles.title: Cyber airman serves local community fighting Little Giant Fire
articles.body:
Over 100 Washington National Guard members arrived at the Little Giant Fire base camp in Plain, WA, on August 2. When they arrived, the fire was around 27k acres and 0% contained. At the end of the Washington National Guard's first two weeks, the fire was over 129k acres and 10% contained. Fourteen members from the 194th Wing were activated to support wildland firefighting on hand crews.

Tech Sgt. Shauna Bonham, a traditional guard cybersecurity intelligence airman from the 256th Intelligence Squadron, was one of the first boots on the ground for the Washington National Guard. She put her life on pause, including her husband, child, and full time job as a network engineer, to come out and assist on the wildland firefighting hand crews. “I like traditional Guard activations because you get to serve your community,” she said.

Hand crew work involves using hand tools to dig containment lines through thick brush and trees to mitigate the spread of fire. After a fire burns through an area and the ground begins to cool, crews mop up the area by using their hand tools to mix cold dirt with residual heat or burning ground cover.

“It was really invigorating. It tested me in different ways that I hadn't anticipated. I got to get involved with a different group of people that I wouldn't normally be able to see,” said Bonham.

Every crew member carries everything they need all day, including food and water, for challenging shifts that often extend over 10 hours. Crews work every day for 14 days and then switch out with fresh crews for rest and recuperation. “I have mad respect for people who do this as a full-time job or even as a part-time job,” she said.

Hand crews can be tasked to support other agencies or crews, depending on the needs as determined by the task force commander. Bonham's crew supported the Tahoe Hotshots during her 14-day orders. “Watching the Tahoe Hotshots shoot off the canisters up into the trees and seeing how dramatically the fire activity can change… considering we live in an area that has fire hazards all the time, it was really neat to be able to learn how all of that works,” she said.

Washington National Guard members are certified to work on hand crews by completing a four-day training course from the Washington Department of Natural Resources. “I thought it would be a really neat opportunity to do something different,” Bonham said about volunteering for hand crew training.

articles.title: From practice to patient care 944th ASTS Airmen support Honduras MEDRETE
articles.body:
SAN PEDRO SULA, Honduras — U.S. Airmen from the 944th Aeromedical Staging Squadron completed a two-week Medical Readiness Training Exercise in Honduras in June 2026, gaining hands-on experience providing patient care in resource-limited environments alongside U.S. and Honduran medical professionals.

The U.S. Southern Command managed MEDRETE, brought together Airmen from multiple Reserve units, Joint Task Force-Bravo, the Honduran Ministry of Health and local healthcare professionals. Teams rotated between community outreach medical locations and local hospitals, where Airmen applied their training to real patients while adapting to unfamiliar conditions and limited resources.

“This mission reinforced exactly why we train,” said Maj. Erika Oquendo, 944th ASTS mental health nurse and mission officer in charge. “Our Airmen delivered compassionate care while operating in an austere environment, enhanced partnerships with our Honduran colleagues, and returned home better prepared to support future contingency operations.”

944th ASTS Airmen supported 1,398 patient encounters, including 1,230 at community outreach medical posts and 168 in hospitals. Their work included trauma, emergency care, operating room support, labor and delivery, intensive care and optometry services.

For Staff Sgt. Jezarae Van Zile, a 944th ASTS aerospace medical service specialist, the mission provided an opportunity to apply skills normally practiced through simulated scenarios. Van Zile supported community outreach before rotating to a local emergency room, where she checked blood sugar levels, provided wound care, drew blood, guided patients through care and assisted with surgical procedures.

Van Zile previously trained in austere conditions during Nexus Forge in Hawaii, but Honduras added the challenge of treating real patients with limited equipment and supplies.

“Being prepared allows us to be thrown anything and be able to make it work with what we have,” Van Zile said. “In Honduras, supplies and resources were limited, so we truly had to think and use what we could to make sure patients were being properly cared for.”

Senior Airman Xochitl Sepulveda, 944th ASTS medical administrator, supported the team as both an administrator and translator. She tracked patients during community outreach before moving to the hospital, where she documented patient encounters and translated between medical teams, patients and their families.

“This mission reminded me of the importance of being prepared for any environment,” Sepulveda said. “When we deploy, we may not know what challenges or conditions we will face, so experiences like this help us develop adaptability, resilience and confidence.”

The mission also brought 944th ASTS Airmen together with members of the 302nd ASTS throughout community outreach and hospital operations, allowing Airmen from both units to combine their knowledge and work together to support patient care. The experience provided an opportunity to apply home-station training in an unfamiliar environment while strengthening the adaptability and teamwork required for future operations.

“For the 944th ASTS, MEDRETE 2026 represented more than humanitarian assistance,” Oquendo said. “It demonstrated the Air Force Reserve team’s ability to rapidly deploy highly trained Citizen Airmen capable of providing outstanding medical care while maintaining combat medical readiness.”

articles.title: Dover reservists invent faster engine fix
articles.body:
Two reserve maintainers with the 512th Maintenance Squadron created a new rigging set for the C-5M Super Galaxy aircraft engine system.

Senior Master Sgt. Chad Bryant, isochronal inspection section chief, and Master Sgt. Tyler Dickson aircraft metals technology section chief, worked together for weeks with several civilian propulsion technicians from the 436th Maintenance Squadron to custom build the new set.

The variable stator vane lever linkages rigging set includes six gauges that allow maintainers to ensure the aircraft’s F-138-GE100 engines are performing properly.

Bryant said failure of the system could cause serious issues.

“It could cause a compressor stall that may cause a lot of expensive damage and cause the engine to shut down,” said Bryant. “Most importantly, if this happens in flight, the pilot would have to shut down the corresponding engine. Being short two engines with a fully loaded aircraft is a dangerous situation for aircrew.”

The current process to adjust the VSV system in the technical order takes a team of five maintainers about 40 hours to complete, said Bryant. In addition, it can cause breakage of hardware and parts that are often hard to procure. With the new gauge, the job can be done by two maintainers over an eight-hour shift and the damage to parts and hardware is minimal.

Bryant, who is due to retire in March, said he couldn’t think of a better legacy to leave for his fellow maintainers. “It makes me feel good that I can leave this job in a better place,” he said. “Some of these jobs can make you sore with all of the working in tight spaces and having to constantly work on items located over your head.”

Bryant drew on his 32 years of aircraft maintenance to create the gauge. The current engines are roughly 12 years old and have left their warranty period. In the past, Bryant had worked extensively with the TF-39 engine that was installed on the C-5B Galaxy. There was a similar rigging set on that engine and Bryant decided to create one for the newer engines.

Bryant then collaborated with Dickson to fabricate the gauge in the base machine shop. Dickson said projects like these are one of his favorite parts of his job.

“It’s a personal satisfaction being able to help other shops increase their productivity and their ability to do their jobs,” said Dickson. “Everybody is so busy with the mission right now that any time gained back is so valuable.” The manufacturing of the gauge is a trial-and-error process, and the prototypes are being made with 7075 aluminum.

“We have an abundance of it, and it’s not expensive,” said Dickson. “If after multiple uses, we start to see fatigue, we’ll switch to something more durable and expensive like stainless steel.”

Bryant said he has been in contact with other professionals in the C-5M community, and they are eager to test out the gauge as well. He said if the testing is successful, usage of the rigging set could be implemented into the technical orders maintainers use to work on the aircraft.

Bryant added, the whole process has been fun for him; and, even with all his years of experience, he still gets a thrill from keeping aircraft in the air.

“We don’t want to hold the rest of the aircraft up from getting back out there and tackling the mission, he said. “As much of a pain it is to run into a problem, what gets my blood pumping is being able to find a solution to something that is out of the ordinary.”

articles.title: Joint K-loader training sharpens Reserve readiness
articles.body:
Reserve and active duty Airmen trained side by side on 25K aircraft loaders at Joint Base Lindsey Graham, South Carolina, Aug. 21, sharpening readiness and building the shared skills Reserve Airmen need to integrate with active duty forces during deployed operations.

The initial qualification training put Airmen behind the controls of the 25K aircraft loader, commonly called a K-loader. The vehicle can carry up to 25,000 pounds of cargo and is used to move cargo and baggage pallets to aircraft. Master Sgt. Sean Judice of the 38th Aerial Port Squadron, here, served as the lead instructor.

“I need to make sure that our drivers are confident enough that when they come out here to go up to an actual aircraft, that they can do it safely and be able to follow the directions of spotters out there,” Judice said.

That confidence comes from more than learning the controls. Airmen must safely maneuver the loader around aircraft, communicate with spotters and understand their role in the larger cargo operation.

Training alongside active duty Airmen also gives reservists an opportunity to learn from personnel who operate the equipment routinely. Staff Sgt. Jacobe Putman, a cargo operations specialist with the 38th Aerial Port Squadron, said the difference in day-to-day operating time naturally creates a learning curve.

“Our active duty counterparts operate K-loaders multiple times a day, on an everyday basis, so there is a natural learning curve between reservists and active duty,” Putman said. “Fortunately, the curve is flattened because active duty helps reservists learn tips and tricks on making K-loader operations smoother.”

The benefit goes beyond qualification. Reserve and active duty Airmen who train together may later work alongside one another during deployments, where familiarity with each other’s procedures and communication can make integration easier.

“It is super important that Reserve and active duty work together before operational missions or deployments because both components are expected to operate as one team,” Putman said. “Training together beforehand builds cohesion, chemistry and communication that carry over when they’re working side by side.”

That integration also gives Reserve Airmen an opportunity to demonstrate the capability they bring to the Total Force. Putman said reservists stepping into roles previously filled by active duty Airmen can reinforce confidence in their training and their ability to carry the work forward.

“When a Reserve Airman fills the role previously filled by an active duty Airman, it shows active duty that reservists are just as capable and have received proficient training as active duty Airmen,” Putman said. “This also allows the Reserve Airman to separate themselves and active duty personnel to gain trust and comfort that the mission will be completed with excellence, just as if an active duty Airman was tasked to complete the mission.”

For Judice, that capability comes down to a common standard. When Reserve Airmen deploy, they are expected to arrive ready to perform alongside their active duty counterparts.

“As reservists, when we deploy, we’re expected to operate at the same level of competency that our active duty counterparts operate at,” Judice said.

That standard allows Reserve Airmen to enter an existing operation, work alongside active duty Airmen or assume responsibility for work already underway.

“When we come in and take over for an active duty aerial port that’s already out on the flightline, we can step in and take control,” Judice said. “We’re trained to deliver the same capability and keep the mission moving from the moment we arrive.”

articles.title: 352d SOW Sharpens High North Readiness at Northern Viking '26
articles.body:
Akureyri, Iceland – Air Commandos from the 352d Special Operations Wing are participating in Exercise Northern Viking 2026, a premier multinational training event designed to bolster defense capabilities in the strategically vital High North.

Operating alongside NATO and joint U.S. forces, the 352 SOW is utilizing the exercise to sharpen tactical readiness, test long-range force employment concepts, and ensure seamless air-domain interoperability in austere Arctic environments.

“Our objectives are the same as NATO objectives: to increase interoperability with our Allies and partners and to deter and defend against potential adversaries in the High North,” said the 352 SOW mission commander. “We are specifically exploring opportunities to employ emerging SOF-peculiar technologies, enabling long-range logistical sustainment of the Allied and Joint Force. Basically, we’ll be employing non-standard airdrop platforms to deliver logistical and medical supplies to far-forward troops.”

The training comes at a critical time as coalition forces continue to reinforce collective security and deterrence protocols across the European theater.

“This exercise gives us a unique opportunity to practice like we expect to play, where we expect to play, and alongside the partners we will play with,” continued the 352 SOW mission commander. “Simply by being here in Iceland and working with our Allies, we are strengthening the relationships across the Alliance and identifying key areas where we can improve our ability to project U.S. and Allied combat power.”

Integrating air and maritime components to conduct joint military operations allows the 352 SOW to partner with other U.S. military services and showcase enhanced training and coordination.

“We specifically want to train in long-range resupply in contested environments and intend to airdrop a powered glider to a detachment of fellow U.S. servicemembers,” continued the 352 SOW mission commander. “This glider will be filled with supplies and airdropped to the servicemembers on the ground validating our capability to deliver critical supplies to SOF teams operating far beyond friendly supply lines.”

The tactics and techniques developed at Exercise Northern Viking will be codified as another important tool in the 352 SOW’s toolkit for supporting a wide variety of SOF-peculiar missions across the U.S. European Command theater of operations.

“We want to express our gratitude and deepest thanks to the government and people of Iceland, and the city of Akureyri in particular,” said the 352 SOW mission commander. “Everyone has been extremely welcoming and supportive of our presence here and it’s been a thrill of a lifetime to be a guest and perform operations across their beautiful country.”

articles.title: 178th Wing hosts CCA C2E demonstration, accelerates next-generation capabilities
articles.body:
The Air Force brought five vendors to the 178th Wing in Springfield, Ohio to test rapidly deployable Command and Control Enclave prototypes Aug. 5-7 in an environment similar to those where airmen could eventually use them: within an expeditionary combat situation.

Rather than selecting a single piece of technology and testing it later, Air Force officials used the demonstration to compare multiple prototypes at once and gather feedback from the operators who could ultimately use the technological capabilities of the equipment.

“What we got to do this week is we brought out five vendors and they demonstrated prototypes of their rapidly deployable portable control segment,” said Michael Schneider, lead engineer for the Command and Control Enclave, or C2E. “This is part of our overall acquisition strategy of identifying who the right integration partner is for the C2E program.”

The approach allows the Air Force to evaluate multiple solutions simultaneously before committing to a single technology, helping officials identify the right integration partner on an accelerated timeline.

Capt. Robert Anderson, C2E lead program manager, Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), said the approach allows the Air Force to incorporate promising technology quickly while ensuring the selected capability meets all requirements.

“We left the door open for them to pick what they think is best to meet our requirements as soon as possible,” said Anderson.

The 178th Wing provided more than a location for the demonstration. Its existing infrastructure, proximity to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and partnerships with organizations involved in emerging technology made it a useful environment for testing prototypes.

“When we reached out, we saw that the 178th was uniquely positioned for a few reasons,” said Lt. Col. Gregory Bieler, the materiel leader, CCA. “The first was the Sky Vision partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory and National Advanced Air Mobility Center. Some of the work they’re doing is going to make it really easy to continue to grow the mission autonomy and test space.”

Those partnerships are part of what the 178th Wing can offer as the Air Force looks to develop and field emerging capabilities. Col. Donald Braskett, 178th Wing commander, said the wing’s location and existing expertise give it an advantage in supporting that work.

“The 178th Wing is uniquely positioned to provide Air Force Life Cycle Management Center with an immediate, cost-effective solution for advancing the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program,” Braskett said. “Our strategic location near Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, coupled with our infrastructure and expertise in unmanned operations, creates a powerful combination.”

The demonstration was intentionally conducted in a simulated tactical environment rather than a controlled indoor setting.

“We didn’t want to be sitting behind closed doors or in a vault somewhere, because that’s not how our airmen are going to use this system. We wanted to be out in the open in a relevant environment,” Bieler said.

The outdoor setting also gave vendors and Air Force personnel a more realistic environment in which to evaluate the prototypes.

The demonstration also put operators into the acquisition process, allowing the people who could eventually use the technology to influence how the capability is developed.

“As part of the Secretary of War’s acquisitions transformation initiative, it’s really important that we do a couple things when we make major technological decisions like this,” Bieler said. “The first thing is that we partner with our operational counterparts, such as the experimental operations unit.”

Schneider said bringing different organizations and perspectives together at the 178th helped move the process forward. The Agile Development Office, or ADO, was among the organizations represented during the demonstration, along with the Experimental Operations Unit and Air Combat Command. For the 178th, hosting the demonstration also showcased how its existing infrastructure, expertise and partnerships can support the Air Force’s investment in emerging capabilities.

“The other thing is that just the responsiveness and the willingness to host of the 178th was bar none the best I’ve ever had in my entire Air Force career,” Bieler said. “To me, when I look at getting stuff for the warfighter, the 178th was willing just to make it work and not worry about bureaucracy and everything else to help us get that.”

The demonstration could also serve as the beginning of a longer-term partnership between the 178th Wing and organizations developing future autonomous capabilities.

“We did this here not only because of the responsiveness, but I also think there’s a long-term opportunity from collaboration between the CCA team, the 178th, and hopefully, mission autonomy as a larger enterprise,” Bieler said.

“What we’re building here has a multiplicative effect across the Air Force, and so we’ve got to get it right, and we’ve got to get the right perspective in here,” said Schneider.

The demonstration gave the Air Force an opportunity to evaluate emerging technology before committing to a final solution while giving operators a voice in how that capability could ultimately be used. For the 178th Wing, the event also demonstrated how its infrastructure, expertise and willingness to support emerging missions can contribute to the development of capabilities designed for the future fight.

articles.title: 103rd CES applies engineering skills across Alaska
articles.body:
In June 2026, members of the 103rd Civil Engineer Squadron traveled to Alaska for two weeks to conduct training as part of the National Guard Bureau’s Deployment for Training (DFT) program. More than 30 Airmen worked on the campus of Seward Military Resort in Seward, Alaska, and nine Airmen worked with active-duty counterparts in the 773rd Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage.

Through the DFT program, Air National Guard civil engineer units can travel around the country to gain immersive, hands-on experience completing real-world construction, electrical, infrastructure and building enhancement projects. The 103rd CES routinely participates in this readiness initiative to provide members with as much practical training as possible within a two-week window.

Located 125 miles south of Anchorage, Seward Military Resort is a recreation facility available for rental to members of the U.S. armed forces and their families. As the first of several units in the DFT program to rotate through the resort this year, 103rd CES members began the project by demolishing a lean-to addition that would later be rebuilt. The structure, part of a supply building that housed machinery, was unable to withstand Alaska’s immense winter snow loads.

“We’re able to be really adaptive here,” said Capt. David Pohl, a civil engineer officer and the officer in charge of this year’s training. “With this environment where we aren’t as constrained on time as we might be on a drill weekend, we’re able to give members the opportunity to try new tools and new machinery.”

After completing demolition of the lean-to and clearing the debris, Airmen prepared the site for the delivery of construction materials and the next DFT rotation’s rebuilding efforts. Additionally, CES Airmen assisted with a wide variety of electrical and minor infrastructure projects around the resort, improving the safety and reliability of facilities that serve the resort and the military community it supports.

“I love things like this,” said Airman Margaret Taylor, an electrical systems specialist with the 103rd Civil Engineer Squadron. “When we’re here, it’s awesome; you’re constantly learning new things and you also get the opportunity to do other jobs that aren’t your own. That’s my favorite part.”

Supporting the DFT mission in Seward, Services Airmen assigned to the 103rd Force Support Squadron prepared and served meals from a mobile kitchen trailer throughout the week. Led by Tech. Sgt. Aisha Chang, the team delivered efficient, high-quality meal service that kept Airmen fueled and on-site, maximizing the time available for training and project completion.

Meanwhile, nine 103rd CES Airmen specializing in heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration, and water and fuel systems maintenance worked alongside the 773rd Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. The Airmen completed installation work orders across the installation, ranging from HVAC maintenance to responding to a sewer-line blockage using specialized equipment. Working within Alaska’s challenging climate also exposed the team to the seasonal demands that repeated freezing and thawing can place on underground utility systems.

By troubleshooting real-world maintenance issues alongside their active-duty counterparts, 103rd CES Airmen strengthened their technical skills and gained experience working with infrastructure challenges they may not routinely encounter at their home station. Across both locations, the DFT gave 103rd CES Airmen opportunities to apply their skills, work alongside new teams and build readiness through projects with lasting value.

“This is the heart of what CE does,” said Pohl. “The more hands-on work we can do, and the more we can go out and experience new, unique things … it only expands our capabilities.”

articles.title: SOUTHAM 2026 brings South American air chiefs together to address regional challenges
articles.body:
TUCSON, Ariz. — Air chiefs and senior military leaders from across South America gathered in Tucson, Arizona, Aug. 25 for the South American Air Chiefs Conference (SOUTHAM) 2026, a four-day conference focused on strengthening regional cooperation and developing coordinated approaches to shared security challenges across the Western Hemisphere.

Hosted by 12th Air Force, Air Forces Southern (AFSOUTH), the air component to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), the conference creates a forum for senior leaders to discuss challenges that extend beyond national borders while identifying practical opportunities to improve communication, interoperability and cooperation among regional air forces.

“The challenges we face today do not respect national borders,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. David Mineau, AFSOUTH commander. “Transnational criminal organizations exploit our geography to traffic illicit goods and undermine regional stability. Cyber threats target our critical national infrastructure and communications networks, requiring us to move forward together.”

He also emphasized, “No single nation can meet these challenges alone. We must approach them with a unified posture, leveraging our collective capabilities.”

During the conference, leaders will discuss secure communications and information sharing, air domain awareness and early warning, counter-narcotics operations, illicit air corridors, transnational criminal organizations, emerging technologies, cyber vulnerabilities and aircraft capabilities.

SOUTHCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan reinforced the importance of those discussions during his remarks to the air chiefs, emphasizing that cooperation among nations does not require sacrificing national sovereignty or autonomy.

“The ability for us to come together and bring unique capabilities, respecting each other’s sovereignty, and finding ways that we can work together; that’s really the strength of this conference,” Donovan said.

He pointed to the relationships among senior leaders as an operational advantage, particularly as threats and challenges increasingly cross national borders.

“Close, continuous relationships among senior leaders build the trust needed for rapid information sharing, seamless integration, interoperability and decisive collective action,” Donovan said. “In a time of borderless threats, the relationships forged here are strategic assets for all of us.”

SOUTHAM brings together delegations from Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay, along with U.S. military leaders and State Partnership Program representatives.

For Gen. Hugo Rodríguez González, commander in chief of the Chilean air force, the gathering also provides an opportunity for partner nations to contribute their own experiences and priorities to the broader regional conversation.

“As air forces of the region, the most important thing we have to do is determine how we integrate and collaborate to achieve common objectives,” Rodríguez said.

He said regional air forces need common doctrine, a common language and shared procedures to work together effectively, particularly when responding to threats such as narcotrafficking.

“If we are going to form a coalition, for example, to fight narcotrafficking, we have to think the same way [and] have similar doctrine,” Rodríguez said.

Rodríguez also contributed Chile’s perspective during a briefing on its space program and opportunities for regional cooperation in research, sustainable development and security. The discussion highlighted the expanding role of the space domain and opportunities for regional air forces to share expertise and strengthen cooperation beyond traditional air operations.

He said the focus now is on translating the conference discussions into action by developing shared doctrine and procedures and improving how regional partners alert and share information with one another.

The conference will pair those discussions with practical engagements designed to advance regional partnerships. Air chiefs will engage with industry representatives to examine emerging technologies and potential capability solutions and visit the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base to discuss aircraft sustainment and regeneration.

State Partnership Program representatives will participate throughout the conference, reinforcing relationships between South American air forces, their state partners and AFSOUTH. Leaders will also conduct bilateral meetings to address individual partnership priorities and identify opportunities for future cooperation.

Senior enlisted leaders are also participating throughout SOUTHAM, reflecting their role in turning senior-leader priorities into operational capability.

“Your presence here is not secondary. It is vital,” Mineau told the enlisted leaders. “We recognize that a professionalized, empowered enlisted force is the backbone of any modern air force and the true catalyst for our operational success.”

Mineau told participants that the trust developed through engagements like SOUTHAM becomes particularly important when nations are called upon to operate together.

“Let us use this week to challenge assumptions, exchange best practices and deepen our bilateral and multilateral ties,” Mineau said. “The trust we build in these conference rooms is the very trust we rely on when we are executing real-world missions side-by-side.”

SOUTHAM 2026 continues through Aug. 28 with senior-leader discussions, bilateral engagements and sessions focused on strengthening the relationships and capabilities needed to address shared challenges throughout the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: I am The 908th: Senior Airman Kaitlynn Nash
articles.body:
Senior Airman Kaitlynn Nash has served as a medical logistics technician with the 908th Aeromedical Evacuation Squadron since joining the unit in August 2022.

Growing up as the youngest in a family she affectionately describes as “nonstop achievers,” Nash enlisted in the Air Force Reserve at just 17 years old to challenge herself and build a foundation of professional experience. Her mother previously served in the Navy, and her father suggested the Reserve as a great way to gain experience and dip her feet in before committing to active duty, though Nash makes it clear the choice was entirely her own.

"Do it because you want to do it," Nash said. "Don't do it because someone else is telling you to do it."

As a medical logistics technician, Nash ensures aeromedical evacuation teams have the exact medications, gear, and supplies necessary to care for patients thousands of feet in the air. Her daily tasks include post-flight inventory, inspecting and properly disposing of expired medical supplies, tracking equipment calibrations, and keeping critical kits mission-ready.

Participating in recent deployment exercises brought her vital role into clear focus.

“I recently went on a deployment exercise, and that was an experience... learning my big 'why' and the mission, and definitely seeing how my role is very important in a deployed setting,” Nash said.

For Nash, the people are what make the 908th AES so special, and she credits the unit's strong sense of camaraderie for driving everyone to perform at their best.

“Here in AES, it's a different kind of morale; it's a different kind of camaraderie,” Nash said. “Everyone comes in and kind of puts their best foot forward, and it's hard not to do the same. It's a great environment to be in, and just be around other like-minded people who just want to get the mission done and have a little fun while doing it.”

That positive attitude and work ethic contributed directly to her selection as the 908th Flying Training Wing’s Airman of the Quarter for the 1st Quarter of 2026.

“I do believe that I come in eager and ready to do my job and do it well,” Nash said. “I feel like it's hard to stand out in a unit where everybody's amazing. So for my leadership and for my other wingmen to see or to feel like I'm doing a little bit more than an ordinary Airman... I feel like I'm actually doing something right.”

Outside of uniform, Nash is a full-time college senior pursuing a bachelor’s degree in psychology with an emphasis in sports psychology. A self-described "introverted extrovert," she balances her academic ambition and military service while enjoying sports, reading, baking, working with kids, and spending time with loved ones.

Her personal motto centers on continuous growth and quiet service to others.

“My main goal is to just continue to help others in the best way I know how, just be a blessing to anybody I come across,” Nash said. “Be the best psychologist I can be. Be the best friend. Be the best daughter. Best sister. Best partner, and just continue to grow. Continue to be a learner. Never stop learning.”

Her advice to prospective recruits remains straightforward: enlist for your own reasons and give it your full effort.

“You put a different level of effort into this job because it does take a lot of effort to put this uniform on,” Nash said. “If it's something you genuinely want to do, it would take a lot less out of you.”

articles.title: 163d Civil Engineer Airmen Sharpen Skills During a DFT to Alaska
articles.body:
SEWARD, Alaska — Airmen with the 163d Civil Engineer Squadron, March Air Reserve Base, Calif., refined critical civil engineering skills while improving infrastructure and facilities during a deployment for training (DFT) at Seward Military Resort, August 10-28, 2026.

A DFT provides service members an opportunity to sharpen their occupational skills while operating under conditions different from those at their home station. For the 163d CES, the geographically isolated location provided Airmen an environment designed to replicate some of the challenges they could encounter during a deployment.

“We are in a geographically separated location to put members in a non-threatening environment to give them trade skills, training and leadership training,” said Master Sgt. Lucas Wilkins, 163d CES water, fuels and systems maintenance specialist. “This allows junior supervisors to take on more leadership roles and other junior technicians to train proficiency in their classification.”

During the DFT, five civil engineering shops worked together to complete two primary projects and two secondary projects. The work included construction, concrete work, metal wrapping and electrical installation. The hands-on training allowed Airmen to expand their technical skill sets and gain experience performing tasks outside their primary specialties.

“We're here in Alaska doing two major projects. One is a pole barn, the other is a maintenance shed, as well as a few other miscellaneous projects,” said 1st Lt. Michelle Weston, officer in charge of the 163d CES. “Primarily, this DFT is meant to give operational training to members in their job while improving the infrastructure of Seward Military Resort.”

Airmen at every level received on-the-job and cross-training opportunities that strengthened their technical skills, expanded their ability to perform multiple roles and enhanced the squadron's ability to sustain infrastructure in a deployed environment.

“This DFT has allowed me not only to work on my skill set, but also help out where I'm needed. Right now, I am working on a concrete pad, getting my hands dirty,” said Senior Airman Anthony Perez, 163d CES pavement and construction technician. “Our mission is to finish the construction of different areas and make sure all of the different areas are operational and safe to use.” Thirty-nine CE members representing seven different Air Force Specialty Codes participated in the DFT. Throughout the exercise, Airmen had the opportunity to sharpen skills within their respective career fields while gaining valuable hands-on experience in other areas of civil engineering.

Staff Sgt. Darrell Fleig, a power production craftsman assigned to the 163d Civil Engineer Squadron, typically specializes in generator operations. During the DFT, Fleig expanded his skill set by routing electrical power to buildings under construction, gaining valuable hands-on experience outside his normal duties. This kind of experience increases Airmen’s confidence in their ability to deploy and support the mission in multiple ways.

“I am now confident that not only can I perform on the power production side, but I can definitely perform on the electrical side in a deployed location,” said Fleig.

The 163d CES is the fifth National Guard unit to participate in this exercise. The work accomplished during the DFT would not have been possible without the combined efforts and support of the units involved.

The DFT allowed the 163d CES members to strengthen mission-ready skills while improving Seward Military Resort (SMR). SMR is a morale, welfare and recreation facility designed for supporting veterans, service members and their families. Through the project, Airmen gained valuable hands-on experience while giving back to those who served, enhancing both their readiness and ability to execute the mission.

articles.title: Idaho National Guard members train for wildland fire response
articles.body:
CAMP ORCHARD, Idaho — Idaho Air and Army National Guard members participated in a Red Card certification training at Orchard Fire and Emergency Services at Camp Orchard, Idaho, August 17-21 and August 24-29, 2026, preparing them to support wildland firefighting efforts across the state, if activated.

The training provides Guardsmen with the foundational skills and knowledge needed to safely operate on a wildland fire incident while increasing the number of personnel available to support Idaho during periods of heightened fire activity.

“What we're doing here is creating ready teams to potentially meet our state's needs for wildland fire,” said Army Command Sgt. Maj. Sheldon Stace, senior enlisted leader of the Joint Staff, Idaho National Guard.

According to Stace, approximately 250 Idaho National Guard Soldiers and Airmen have received the qualification, though some would currently require recertification. With refresher training, he said the Guard could have roughly 250 Red Card-qualified personnel prepared to respond within one to two days.

For Guardsmen participating in the course, the training covers more than simply how to fight a fire. Students learn about fire behavior, weather, safety, risk mitigation and the rapidly changing conditions they could encounter on the fire line.

Assistant Fire Chief Jeb Baker, Orchard Fire Department, said understanding those hazards is essential before Guardsmen are sent to support an incident.

“We want to ensure that when we send them away from their home, they're also coming back to their home,” said Baker. “It's important that they have that knowledge and understanding of how it works across the country, because they could get sent anywhere, not just here in our backyard.”

Baker said Guardsmen also bring experience from their military and civilian careers that can make them valuable additions during large-scale incidents. From operating heavy equipment and driving trucks to agricultural backgrounds and experience working in demanding environments, those existing skills can help them quickly integrate with firefighting teams.

For Air Force Airman 1st Class Cole Kanamoto, an munitions system specialist with the Idaho Air National Guard’s 124th Maintenance Squadron, the course offered a new perspective on the complexity and danger of wildland firefighting.

“I didn't know a fire could outrun you,” said Kanamoto. “I didn't know how much it mattered to a fire what the relative humidity is or how fast the wind's blowing. I gained a lot of respect for the people that do this for a living.”

Kanamoto said the course prepared him to step into an entry-level role on a wildland fire response team if called upon. The certification also supports his personal goal of pursuing a civilian career in firefighting. While the training provides Guardsmen with another skill set, Stace said it also reflects a larger part of the National Guard's mission, remaining ready to respond when Idaho communities need support.

“These Soldiers and Airmen are members of the community,” said Stace. “They're doing this as extra training outside of their military training to make sure that they're ready to meet the needs for Idahoans.”

Whether responding to wildfires, floods or other natural disasters, Stace said maintaining trained and ready personnel allows the Idaho National Guard to provide additional capability to state and local agencies when requested.

“I want them to know that the Guard's got their back,” said Stace. “We're going to continue to train to meet the state's needs.”

articles.title: Operation TREK808: PACAF, HING Rapidly Provide Critical Aid to Hawaii Island Recovery
articles.body:
Because of Hawaii’s geographic location, responding to natural disasters requires unique logistical capabilities. To accelerate recovery efforts following Tropical Cyclone Lala, Pacific Air Forces (PACAF), the Hawaii National Guard (HING), and state agencies executed a rapid-response airlift effort, named Operation TREK808, to deliver essential utility equipment from California to Hawaii Island from Aug. 23 - 25.

A total payload of 143,790 pounds — including six commercial power and utility repair trucks and a support trailer — was delivered to Hilo, Hawaii, by C-17 Globemaster III aircraft over the course of two airlift missions. By bypassing traditional, slower maritime transport routes, the joint military effort delivered power restoration capabilities to the community.

What began as a simple text message from a local electric company to Gov. Josh Green evolved into a complex, multi-component defense support of civil authorities mission.

“Operation TREK808 demonstrates what we can accomplish when federal, state and private-sector partners respond with urgency and purpose,” said Gov. Green. “Following my request for federal assistance, the Department of War, Adm. Samuel Paparo and U.S. Pacific Command, Pacific Air Forces, the Hawaii National Guard, Southern California Edison and Hawaiian Electric moved quickly to bring utility crews, trucks and critical equipment to Hawaii Island. This coordinated mission will accelerate repairs, restore power sooner... and I am deeply grateful to everyone who answered the call.”

Mobilizing under a tight timeline, total force Airmen from Team Hickam and March Air Reserve Base turned a mission concept to a full-blown rapid response in a matter of hours.

The emergency airlift began in California, where the 452nd Air Mobility Wing prepared March Air Reserve Base to serve as a critical continental staging hub. March personnel established the airfield and logistics support to process emergency cargo, working seamlessly alongside Team Hickam to execute a swift delivery across the Pacific.

A critical linchpin in ensuring the commercial vehicles were approved to fly was Hickam's 647th Logistics Readiness Squadron. Given a no-notice tasking on Sunday afternoon, Tech. Sgt. Sable Miller, an Air Transportation specialist, was packed and boarding an aircraft to California within 90 minutes. Working overnight, Miller completed all necessary hazardous material certifications for the civilian trucks, preventing aircraft delays.

Active duty and Hawaii Air National Guard aircrew and loadmasters from the 535th and 204th Airlift Squadrons were among the teams on the ground in California. Collaborating directly with civilian utility experts, the military engineering crews worked tirelessly to overcome the challenges of a massive commercial cargo load by calculating weight balances and securing the heavy electrical equipment, working through multiple days to ensure the final trucks were safely downloaded in Hilo on Tuesday, Aug. 25.

“This mission demonstrates Team Hickam’s ability to respond and deliver aid during dynamic and demanding times,” said Col. Kyle Clinton, 15th Wing commander. “We rise together to support our neighbors in their time of need, alongside our Guard and state partners. That’s what being part of this community is all about.” For state and local utility leaders, the Air Force's presence, total force integration, and heavy-lift capability on the island were irreplaceable factors in the recovery efforts.

"Military crews worked tirelessly to incorporate civilian equipment specifications into transportability by the nation's premier Globemaster," stated Maj. Gen. Stephen Logan, Hawaii Adjutant General. “The total force integration relationship between Pacific Air Forces and the Hawaii Air National Guard accelerated execution, an absolute necessity given the state’s archipelagic construct and geographic separation from the continental United States."

The Operation TREK808 flights ran parallel to extensive ground operations by the HING, which currently has 222 personnel deployed across the islands. On the Big Island alone, Guard members are assisting with wide-area search operations, debris clearance and hundreds of community wellness checks in the wake of the storm. Imagery and video of Operation TREK808, including the C-17 uploads in California and downloads in Hilo, are available on the official DVIDS feature page: https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.dvidshub.net%2Ffeature%2FTREK808.

articles.title: 125th Security Forces Squadron Trains on Active Shooter Response Exercise
articles.body:
JACKSONVILLE, FL – Members of the 125th Security Forces Squadron, part of the Florida Air National Guard’s 125th Fighter Wing, completed active shooter training at the on-base alert building, on April 9, 2026.

The exercise simulated a real-world active shooter event involving a lone gunman, a wing member acting as the shooter’s victim, and the security forces team that responded to the incident. Security forces leadership observed the team’s reaction to the call.

The training is designed to be as realistic as possible to generate stress and create an environment that will resemble a real-world active shooter event.

“There are not many ways you can induce high stress that will be what you experience during a real-world event,” said U.S. Air Force Senior Master Sgt. Thomas Evenson, the Senior Enlisted Leader of the 125th Security Forces Squadron.

The exercise’s realism was enhanced by having the shooter use an air compression type weapon to replicate the sound of gunfire and a role player to act as a victim. The scenario is further intensified by using data provided by the FBI to model active shooter tactics. These effects are intended to prepare Defenders for the physiological effects of a real gunfight, such as tunnel vision and auditory exclusion.

By simulating these diverse variables, the exercise prepares service members to manage their physical and mental stress responses during a real-world crisis, said Evenson.

The core of the exercise is to sharpen the fundamental skills required to neutralize a threat quickly.

This exercise included mission partners, such as members of the base fire department who serve as part of the rescue task force.

“The integration of mission partners, it all begins well before an actual incident,” said Evenson.

Having the ability to communicate with mission partners in a training environment provides the repetitions needed to understand each group’s roles, tactics, techniques, and procedures prior to the actual event occurring.

Through repetition leadership gets to practice their command and control and their utilization of the forces available, said Evenson.

The commitment to constant improvement reflects the professional mindset of the leaders at the 125th Security Forces Squadron. This type of exercise is rooted in the 125th Fighter Wing’s mission to protect and serve the community and its service members.

“Everything that we do matters,” said Evenson. “It matters whether or not someone makes it home at the end of the day.”

articles.title: From surfer to savior: Training makes the difference
articles.body:
MISAWA AIR BASE, Japan – White-capped Pacific Ocean waves crashed onto the shores of northern Japan. Wind roared over an empty stretch of beach as two surfers rode the waves just offshore with precision.

They effortlessly transitioned from belly to feet in a split second, finding their balance on a wavering surface and standing tall over the ocean with only a board between their feet and the icy water. Ocean spray pelted their wetsuits, faces and pruny fingers.

Water dripped from the tips of their short hair. Exhilaration tore whoops of joy from their throats.

The wave collapsed and dragged the surfers back inland. After a high-five and another cheer, they paddled back out to repeat it all over again. The frigid ocean embraced their burning muscles.

“We’d been out there for one hour already,” said Nick Pallett, American Red Cross Lifesaving Award recipient and spouse of a member assigned to the 35th Fighter Wing. “We both surf a lot so we were just having a good time. But bad things can happen at any moment.”

Nick had taken lifesaving courses through the American Red Cross, a decision that proved critical when a routine day in the water turned into an emergency with no one else around to help.

Nick watched from a little further out as his friend, Craig Hale, prepared for a wave, straddling his own surfboard in the rolling currents. Salty air chapped his lips. He swiped water from his scruffy beard.

Craig approached the wave. At the crucial moment between balance and failure, the ocean consumed the front of his board.

The board shot out from under Craig, tossing him into the churning surf. Emerging from the torrent, he clutched his board, struggling for air.

“I remember calling out to him and only getting a shake of the head back,” Nick said. “When I asked again, he didn’t respond.”

Nick’s stomach dropped as he paddled up to Craig.

Nick helped his friend get back on the board, tugging limbs out of the water one at a time. Craig groaned in pain as his right leg came up with blood mixing in the water. A three inch gash spurted blood onto the surfboard.

“It was gross,” Nick recalled. “The surfboard shot out of the water and somehow the fin on it sliced his leg through his wetsuit. I knew I had to get him out of the water. I was worried about infection.”

Nick pushed his friend to the shore, jumping off his own when the swell carried him into the shallows. He fought through the surging tide towards the safety of the beach, kicking water in every direction.

“I told him to keep his wetsuit on and tied a surf leash just below the knee to act as a tourniquet,” Pallett said. “The bleeding stopped but we were still soaking wet.”

He gritted his teeth tugging the improvised tourniquet as tight as he could and heaved Craig into his car, ignoring the sand and saltwater contaminating the interior.

Nick tried calling Craig’s wife at the 35th Medical Group, but got no answer. Then he called his own wife and told her everything.

“I could hear the concern in his voice,” said Dr. Alicia Pallett, 35th MDG chief of medical staff. “Given his estimated time of arrival, I dropped what I was doing and helped to coordinate receipt of the inbound patient at the medical group.”

They were fifteen minutes away from the base clinic.

His heart pumped with adrenaline, his leg bouncing at every stoplight and red sign as the seconds ticked by. Every minute felt too long.

“I kept checking on him,” Nick said. “He was already pale and pretty nauseous by that point. I wasn’t sure how much blood he had lost before the tourniquet, so I just kept talking to him, trying to keep him calm but conscious.”

He sped to the urgent care center. He pulled up to the curb and emergency medical services met him at the door.

Nick helped get his friend out of the car before medical personnel took him in a wheelchair.

He followed inside, his wetsuit barely dripping water by that point. Bright, sterile lights, white tile floors, short corridors and closed doors surrounded him. His bare, sandy feet were incongruous.

“I was honestly just so impressed at his ability to act swiftly and resolutely,” said Alicia. “It takes years of practice for some to be comfortable in an emergency like this.”

They took Craig into the trauma bay to suture his wound, and he was released after three hours.

“He would’ve done the same thing for me,” Nick said. “I just thought, ‘Thank goodness I’d went through that lifesaving training.’”

His record of lifesaving skills didn’t stop there.

A few months later, Nick responded to another emergency off base when a strong gust of wind knocked an older Japanese woman to the ground in a parking lot of a grocery store. Blood pooled around her head. He applied pressure with a padded crib mattress cover from his car and helped coordinate the emergency response through a translation app.

“While he has completed CPR and First Aid training through the American Red Cross, he has no formal medical training and was never a lifeguard,” said Alicia Pallett. “Recognition on a job well done is most definitely deserved.”

These rescues eventually led to Nick’s recognition at a wing awards ceremony. His wife led him to believe that she was getting an award, so he brought along his children.

Then the master of ceremonies called his name, and his wife urged him forward in the dark room. Pallett said he just shook his head at his wife, catching on to her white lie, but was still surprised.

“They called my name last,” Nick said. “I wasn’t expecting to go up there. Everyone else did their handshakes and salutes, and I went to stand beside the 35th Fighter Wing commander for this award.”

The American Red Cross Lifesaving Awards Program recognizes individuals trained in courses such as CPR, First Aid and AED who use those skills to respond during emergencies. For Nick, that was two emergencies he responded to with exceptional skill.

“He has received tons of thanks and congratulations from the community, and, of course, his family is beaming with pride,” Alicia said. “Our spouses deserve as much, if not more, recognition for the ways in which they contribute to our Misawa community. For Nick, he’s a lifesaver!”

Nick’s lesson was simple.

“I’m always going to maintain my lifesaving training, no matter what job I get in the future,” he said. “Training like that matters, especially when there’s no one else around to help.”

articles.title: RED FLAG-Alaska 26-3: Battling in (cyber) space
articles.body:
EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE, Alaska – RED FLAG-Alaska 26-3 will draw to a close on Friday, August 28, after two weeks of coordinated air combat training conducted within the Joint Pacific Alaska Range Complex, the Department of War’s largest overland airspace.

But not all battles take place in the air, on land–or even in the physical realm.

This year marks the second iteration in which cyberspace capabilities have been integrated into the RF-A exercise.

“I believe it is important to have cyber in these exercises to demonstrate the types of capabilities we are available to employ, to assist in a matter of layered effects,” said U.S. Air Force Chief Warrant Officer 2 Alexander Childs, 835th Cyberspace Operations Squadron chief operations advisor, and red team lead for RF-A 26-3. “Layered effects allowing a person or group of people to maneuver safely into contested areas is what we’re attempting to portray throughout the exercise.”

Layered effects, says Childs, are multiple types of capabilities that are being employed simultaneously to allow an action to happen. For example, in a Hollywood-esque action film, one might have an adversary controlling traffic lights while the other jams radio communications, which causes their opponent to be more confused and have to expend more effort and energy into attempting to correlate or communicate their movements to their partners.

Scenario development for the exercise began in January, during which cyber experts were tapped to weigh in.

“We created a scenario where we could have a realistic impact on the scenario that they were coming up with, and how we can play a role into that going forward,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Dennis Cracraft, 837th COS chief operations advisor, and blue team lead for RF-A 26-3.

In a traditional exercise, cyber teams do not integrate on such a tactical level. RF-A 26-3 is the first total force exercise these cyber protection teams have participated in, interacting with a wide range of careers and military branches to execute both kinetic and non-kinetic effects on the day’s mission objective. As the 353rd Combat Training Squadron further develops these unique opportunities for the Air Force’s cyber Airmen, they are opening a whole new pathway of what can be achieved for training across the board.

“The scenario [for RF-A 26-3] is that the red team has already compromised the network, and now the blue team has to go in there and solve the puzzle of what occurred,” Cracraft. “Then they have to develop action to kick them out of the network as soon as possible while also maintaining dominance. The way to do that is by teaching them certain hunt tactics, good practices on what they should do as operators, and what to look for.”

While defensive network operations are somewhat routine for cyber Airmen, the red team gets to have a bit more leeway with their work.

“For the offensive side, we are using a little more of the creativity that we don't typically get an opportunity to use,” said Childs. “With three of our four operators on the offensive side, they are traditionally defensive operators that have experience either doing red teaming or have experience doing threat emulation. We are utilizing that experience to build out what the threat looks like. That gives them a little bit of flex that way, a little bit of experience and more practice in developing those threats, so they can then document them and we can work to train our defensive cyber operators.”

At the end of the day, exercises are all about learning for everyone involved.

“It's been a unique experience,” said Childs. “With the inclusion of [cyber], we have been able to spark questions, ideas, theories and more questions amongst the flyers. So as they go through their non-kinetic effects planning processes, they reach out to us and say, ‘Hey, are you able to?’ That's what we want out of this. Additionally through that, if we're not able to in the real world, then we can go back and say, ‘Hey, these are effects that they want to generate. How do we get to that?’ Then that can spark more conversation internally.”

Homeland defense requires layered, integrated operations extending beyond U.S. borders–physically and through the web of networks spanning the globe. Exercises such as RF-A provide the training to sustain the capability and readiness required to support power projection and prepare for the full range of contingencies.
