articles.title: No Runway Required: Joint service members perform contingency airfield operations
articles.body:
LEJIMA, Okinawa, Japan — U.S. joint service members and participating airlift units performed airpower operations from austere environments during the Pacific Air Forces Landing Zone Operations Course at Lejima, Okinawa, Japan, Aug. 19, 2026.

The course is a two-week course designed to build mission-ready Airmen who can establish, secure, and operate in contested environments. This iteration served as the official course validation from the Air Force Special Operations Command, authorizing multiple installations across PACAF to host and scale contingent airlift capabilities throughout the theater.

"We aren’t just teaching technical skills," said Master Sgt. Benjamin Stewart, 374th Operations Support Squadron PACAF LZ Operations Course instructor. "We are building joint relationships and empowering our non-commissioned officers to make command-level decisions on the ground. The validation of this course means we can now scale this combat capability across the Indo-Pacific theater, ensuring our forces remain agile, lethal, and ready."

The course integrated several flying commands, including the 36th Airlift Squadron, the 374th OSS, the 353rd Special Operations Wing, and the U.S. Marine Corps’ III Marine Expeditionary Force and Marine Aerial Refueler Transport Squadron 153.

The training balanced classroom instruction with realistic, hands-on field applications while encouraging creative problem-solving and team building needed for operating outside of traditional air base environments.

The training culminated with a C-130J Super Hercules assigned to the 36th AS, Yokota Air Base, Japan, successfully executing tactical landings on the island’s undeveloped landing strip.

"The job requires much more than knowing how to assess and operate a landing zone," said Tech. Sgt. Gabriel Garcia, 374th OSS landing zone safety officer and instructor. "It requires making informed, real-time decisions when conditions change. Our instructor team is confident these students are prepared to do exactly that and safely enable airpower wherever the mission requires it."

articles.title: 163d RTS hosts Bivouac training, bolsters readiness
articles.body:
MARCH AIR RESERVE BASE, Calif. — Forty-four Airmen from the 146th Civil Engineer Squadron traveled to the 163d Regional Training Site for a five-day bivouac exercise designed to move their technical training from the classroom into a realistic field environment.

A bivouac is a field training exercise in which Airmen simulate living and working in forward operating conditions, often establishing temporary facilities and operating with limited infrastructure and resources. The training tests their ability to apply technical skills in austere environments while preparing for the challenges of deployed operations.

The 163d RTS serves as a centralized training location for Civil Engineer Airmen across the Total Force, providing specialized equipment, instructor expertise, and a field environment many units do not have at their home stations. RTS instructors train more than 1,000 Airmen annually in Rapid Damage Repair and other Civil Engineer specialty courses, building the skills and confidence needed to operate in demanding environments.

“We have a lot of new Airmen in our squadron, so we can go through things on a discussion level, but they can’t get their hands-on portion until we come here,” said Senior Master Sgt. Marc Trujillo, a 146th Civil Engineer Squadron superintendent.

During the exercise, Airmen trained on forklifts, water purification systems, heavy equipment, aircraft arresting systems, power production and other equipment and systems used across Civil Engineer career fields.

“Whatever the team needs to focus on, I can adjust my training. This group is newly out of technical school and junior Airmen, so my focus is getting them trained on the basics,” said Tech. Sgt. Rafael Jaime, a 163d Regional Training Site instructor for heating, ventilation and air conditioning.

The training also emphasized troubleshooting and restoring essential services in demanding conditions, requiring Airmen to draw on their technical knowledge and adapt as problems arise.

“We don’t have a technical order like other career fields, so I have to teach and mentor them how to troubleshoot on the spot to restore these services,” Jaime said. “You have people doing shift work and sleeping during the day a lot of times, and these HVAC units will go down when it’s over 100 degrees. We have to troubleshoot and get it working quickly.”

The field environment at the RTS added another layer to the training, exposing Airmen to conditions more representative of what they may encounter during an exercise or deployment.

“We’re moving people from the theoretical to practical, and the climate here also adds to the training,” Trujillo said. “We’re practicing with our combat gear on too, and simulating the stressors we may face elsewhere to build that muscle memory for a warrior mindset and to execute our mission at the top of our game.”

Staff Sgt. Joseph Navarro, 146th Civil Engineer Squadron HVAC team lead, said the training environment allowed his team to focus on troubleshooting skills that are difficult to replicate in a classroom.

“I like seeing my guys get the hands-on training with equipment we don’t have at home station,” Navarro said. “It’s great here because there are no distractions and we can get straight to work and focus on training.”

At the 163d Regional Training Site, the 146th Civil Engineer Squadron is turning technical knowledge into hands-on capability, building the agile combat support needed to project decisive airpower. Through realistic training, Airmen strengthen their confidence, readiness and warrior mindset, preparing them to execute the mission with excellence wherever they are called.

articles.title: Beyond the runway: 37 AS tests C-130J versatility in Iceland during NV26
articles.body:
KEFLAVIK AIR BASE, ICELAND -- As the Arctic becomes more accessible and complex, a 75-year defense partnership between the United States and Iceland remains vital to North Atlantic stability. Meeting modern security challenges head-on at the “Gateway to the Arctic”, the 37th Airlift Squadron is playing a vital role in exercise Northern Viking 26, Aug. 22-Sept. 3, 2026.

Iceland sits at the crossroads of increasingly accessible maritime corridors with new transit routes and resources in the Arctic and High North setting the stage for increased activity and competition.

Northern Viking is a biennial military exercise hosted by Iceland and led by the U.S. Navy’s Sixth Fleet. Eleven NATO nations have joined this iteration, which includes training events taking place across Iceland.

The 37th AS, based out of Ramstein Air Base, Germany, arrived Aug. 21 to support NV26 and test their training in the north’s austere environment. They brought two U.S. Air Force C-130J Super Hercules aircraft to engage in specialized operations alongside NATO Allies.

U.S. Air Force Capt. Jill Ruane, 37th AS pilot, explained how critical operating in new environments is to sharpening unit readiness.

“Our participation in Northern Viking this year is super important because we’re working with other countries, other branches, other air platforms, and it’s really great training for us,” Ruane said.

The goal of Northern Viking 26 is to bring together U.S., Icelandic and NATO Allied activities in the Arctic into one overarching operational approach to the region to maintain a stable and prosperous Arctic region. Exercise missions hone partner nations’ ability to seamlessly operate together.

The nine-day exercise includes a wide variety of missions, testing force readiness for everything from rapid power projection to humanitarian aid. The objective for the 37th AS is to train in extreme conditions that pose unique challenges, testing crew readiness as well as the limits of the C-130J aircraft.

“This airplane is very versatile; it can do a lot so it’s really fun when we get to go out and actually put those types of things to practice,” said U.S. Air Force Senior Airman Lydia Knight, 37th AS loadmaster. “Especially here in the higher regions where it’s colder, we have procedures that we get to do, so it’s really fun to actually implement those. That way if circumstances arise where we have to do them, we know we have the skills and the wherewithal to execute.” U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Tessa Townsend, 37th AS loadmaster, described the various missions they were called on to perform during Northern Viking such as cargo drop, aeromedical evacuation, search and rescue, and formation flights.

The 37th AS uses the slick variant of the C-130J, meaning it is highly adaptable. “We’re not modified for any specific mission set, so we can configure to a lot of other things,” Townsend said. “We move people, cargo, pretty much anything, that needs to be tactically moved. We’re your guys.”

The crew are trained experts on their diverse mission sets, but training in the High North opens the door to an even broader array of conditions. Ruane spoke about the tactical flying she looked forward to throughout the exercise, to include her favorite low-altitude flying permitted by the exercise’s Icelandic hosts.

“We had the opportunity to practice at landing zones which are different than your typical airport,” Ruane said, “We landed on a beach for example and a grass field. This airplane can really do it all.”

This ability to operate independent of infrastructure matters for combat and personnel recovery missions alike. Training on unimproved surfaces expands operational access and reduces dependence on permanent runways, increasing the resilience and mobility of Allied airlift forces and giving commanders additional options to disperse, position and sustain forces.

“We’re working with a special platform of airdrop where we can guide it exactly where we want it to go. That really gives us versatility in being able to resupply people in various situations,” Knight said. “If anything happens with this inclement weather, someone’s stuck somewhere they need food or water, we’re able to get that directly to them. Especially in places like Iceland where weather can be a challenge for a lot of different aircraft.”

NV26 is not only vital to training for the conditions normally found in the High North, but to building cohesion betweenU.S. and the 11 participating NATO Allies. Ruane spoke about the 37th AS having the opportunity to interact with Allies at Ramstein Air Base where they’re located, but noted how the exercise had brought that collaboration to another level.

“We’re getting to stretch our cultural competency muscles that allow us to interact with different people from all over the world who have different ways of doing things,” Ruane said. “It’s really important to understand that every person is different, every country is different, but we still have to be able to work as a team to be able to provide security in the High North region and all over the globe.”

articles.title: Lightweight, baby!: 53rd TSS rack supports electronic warfare testing
articles.body:
TYNDALL AIR FORCE BASE, Fla. — Two hundred pounds can take many forms.

On a weight bench? “Ain’t nothin’ but a peanut,” as bodybuilding legend Ronnie Coleman would say.

In an electronic warfare work center, though, where every pound of it costs roughly $1,000, asking for an extra set of hands—or several—might be the best course of action.

Or, if you’re a member of the 53rd Test Support Squadron at Tyndall Air Force Base, Florida, you could bring the rack.

A newly developed electronic warfare pod rack from the squadron’s Advanced Threat Replication flight is turning what once required a two-person carry into something personnel can more easily move, store and maintain.

The solution may never leave the shop, but the equipment it holds helps create the threat environments Air Force aircraft and weapons are tested against, said 1st Lt. Maxine Bresnaider, 53rd TSS lead engineer of special devices.

“Moving that equipment in a way that safely secures them and allows for testing without additional alterations to the electronic warfare pods is highly desired,” Bresnaider said.

Moving the weight, though, was only part of the problem.

EW payloads contain sensitive equipment that requires proper handling and storage. Any solution therefore had to do more than get a pod from one side of the shop to another. It also had to keep it secure once it got there. For equipment this sensitive—and potentially expensive—that support is crucial.

“If a part or asset were to fall off during storage or maintenance, it could break critical assets or cause up to hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage,” said Senior Airman Daniel Dehart, 53rd TSS metals technology journeyman.

Unlike equipment designed for flight, however, the pod rack doesn’t have to satisfy aircraft airworthiness requirements.

It never leaves the shop.

Instead, engineers focused on making sure the materials and structure could support the loads placed on them during storage and maintenance.

The simplicity is intentional.

By making the pods easier to access, maintain and move, the rack reduces handling required between storage and use while allowing the flight to accommodate additional payloads.

That can translate into less time preparing the equipment and more time having it ready to support the mission. “This capability allows the flight to store additional pods in a way that provides easy calibration and assembly to get them out the door quicker,” Bresnaider said. “The ease of movement is an additional capability that allows our flight to operate more efficiently.”

The rack itself won’t replicate an adversary’s electronic signature. It won’t fly. It won’t even leave the shop.

But when the equipment sitting on it is needed for the next test, the rack helps make sure hundreds of pounds of sensitive electronics are ready to go with it.

articles.title: Red Flag- Alaska 26-3
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – RED FLAG-Alaska’s third and final iteration of 2026 took place Aug. 14-18. RF-A training spans from individual skills to complex, large-scale joint engagements. The exercises can be adapted to integrate various forces into a realistic threat environment using the 120,000 square miles of airspace in the Joint Pacific Alaska Range Complex. RF-A is an annual Pacific Air Forces-sponsored exercise. By utilizing the JPARC, RF-A leverages the expansive area and diverse training environments of Alaska, with primary operations based out of Eielson Air Force Base and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. RF-A 26-3 was a designated Special Technical Operation flag – meaning participants can practice synchronizing multi-domain capabilities across air, space and cyberspace to replicate capabilities of peer or near-peer adversaries to solve complex high-end problem sets. “We focus on integrating STO effects into the battlespace to provide realistic degradations that our forces can expect to see in a peer and near-peer conflict,” said U.S. Air Force Capt. Jason Bentley, 354th Operation Group Detachment 1 Red Flag 26-3 team lead. “For example, we leverage non-kinetic effects, which are military or strategic actions that achieve goals without using physical destruction or traditional explosive force that disrupt and complicate coordination for our forces.” Participating aircraft this year included U.S. Marine Corps F-35C Lightning II assigned to Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 251 from Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina; E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control Systems flown by the 961st Airborne Air Control Squadron from Kadena Air Base, Japan; and F-22 Raptors assigned to the 3rd Wing from JBER, Alaska. Since RF-A 26-3 is an STO exercise, it provided unique challenges to both planners and players. Joint and coalition and participants practiced how to coordinate efforts against complex air defense threats and efficiently integrate a wide spectrum of effects to defeat those same threats, said Bentley. “Working with the Air Force during this exercise has been a great opportunity to learn from each other and see how different teams approach the same challenges,” said U.S. Marine Corps 1st Lt. Phil English, F-35C Lightning II pilot assigned to the VMFA-251. “We’ve been able to talk through different exercise scenarios, share our experiences and learn what works well from one another.”

RF-A has a sustained history of allied and partner participation. Combined training exchanges tactics, techniques and procedures and directly improves interoperability. Homeland defense requires layered, integrated operations extending beyond U.S. borders, coordinated across combatant commands and with allied and partner forces. RF-A provides realistic air combat training to sustain that capability and support power projection.

“Executing an exercise of this scale can be a challenge, and it’s been humbling to see how we coordinate logistics and sustainment over such a vast area,” said Bentley. “Our forces overcome those challenges through rigorous mission planning, execution and successful debriefs from each sortie.”

articles.title: RED FLAG-Alaska 26-3 draws to a close
articles.body:
EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE, Alaska – RED FLAG-Alaska 26-3 wrapped up here on Aug. 28, after two weeks of realistic combat training for joint partners and allied nations at both Eielson Air Force Base and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.

The training brought together 79 aircraft from 10 units within the Joint Pacific Alaska Range Complex, the largest instrumented air, ground and electronic combat training range in the world. This environment was optimal to expand the capabilities of 5th generation aviators in the F-35 Lightning II, which the 13th Fighter Squadron from Misawa Air Base, Japan, flew in the exercise for the first time.

“The training airspace in Alaska is the best in the world,” said U.S. Air Force Col. Jeromy Guinther, 35th Operations Group commander at Misawa AB, and deployed forces commander for RF-A 26-3. “It's the largest overland training airspace that the Department of War has anywhere, and we have the great beauty and terrain which allows for us to do things here in Alaska that we cannot do at other places.”

RF-A distinguishes itself from other similar exercises by providing a realistic opposing force–known as ‘Aggressor’ units–who can replicate real surface-to-air and air-to-air threats, employing enemy tactics during air combat training. The 18th Fighter Interceptor Squadron, assigned to Eielson AB, provides F-16 Fighting Falcons to achieve the most realistic simulated combat environment in the Pacific.

“We love having them, we love putting them to work,” said U.S. Marine Corps Capt. Jacob Decelles, Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 225 F-35B pilot. “It’s important to fight not just the aircraft that you’re in, so having the [F-16] out here was awesome.”

Another major aspect of RF-A is getting to train with and learn from joint partners and allies. Often, sister services and allied nations’ service members study the same material, but there are differences in how it is interpreted, said Decelles. Learning those differences and building on strengths and weaknesses makes those partnerships stronger.

“Anywhere we go in the [Pacific area of responsibility], the United States is not going to go alone,” said Guinther. “We're going to go with our allies. A few of the key ones are here training with us at RF-A 26-3: most notably, the Australians, who do everything with us and are very close allies.”

As the last iteration this year, RF-A 26-3 prepares many of its participating units for future deployments in the Pacific AOR.

“I've told the team to treat 26-3 as their last chance,” said Guinther. “Whether it's the maintainer on the flight line, the support cook at the kitchen, or any of the team that helps get these aircraft into the air and back home safely. I want them to remember that this might be the last chance for a lot of these aviators. This is our last chance to get folks the training they need that will bring them home in combat.”

articles.title: Air University earns 3 of 4 DoW honors in Academic Research Challenge
articles.body:
MAXWELL AIR FORCE BASE, Ala. - Air University researchers took on three very different problems facing the joint force: deterring an amphibious attack in the Indo-Pacific, building expeditionary airfields faster and keeping information moving when communications fail. Their work earned Air University three of the Department of War's four recognitions in the 2025-26 Academic Research Challenge.

The three recognized papers came from different parts of the university. Squadron Officer School's Air University Advanced Research program produced the first-place paper, Air Force Global College produced the second-place paper, and Air War College produced the honorable mention. Air Command and Staff College and the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies also submitted research.

The deputy secretary of war and the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff co-sponsor the Academic Research Challenge, administered by the Joint Staff J-7. Each year, students and faculty at professional military education institutions develop research on strategic and operational issues.

For Margaret Sankey, Air University director of research and electives, the results start with the students willing to take on the work. "The exceptional quality of Air University research stems directly from the intellectual curiosity of our students," Sankey said. "When you have company grade officers volunteering to take on additional, intensive research during a fast-paced, five-week Squadron Officer School course, it shows a relentless dedication to solving the most complex and pressing challenges facing our military."

Five officers in Squadron Officer School's Air University Advanced Research program authored the first-place paper. Air Force Capts. Kurt Clauder, Greg Lee, Youngjun Park, Alex Richard and James Shifflett studied commercially available autonomous technologies and deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. They proposed pairing low-cost loitering munitions with artificial intelligence-enabled target recognition to identify and engage high-value amphibious transport assets during a potential Taiwan contingency. The concept was designed to keep operating through communications disruptions and electronic warfare.

Air Force Maj. Ashley Klase of Air Force Global College earned second place for research on speeding up Agile Combat Employment by changing how expeditionary airfields are built. Her research considered modular infrastructure, additive manufacturing, robotics, deployable microgrids and advanced soil stabilization, with the goal of cutting construction timelines from several weeks to 24 to 72 hours while reducing the logistics needed for dispersed air operations.

Air Force Lt. Col. John Schade of Air War College turned to lessons from Ukraine for the paper that received an honorable mention. He studied how Taiwan could use citizen reporting, crowdsourced intelligence and commercial cloud computing to build a distributed information network. The approach could help maintain situational awareness and battlefield transparency when communications and electronic systems are degraded.

The projects aligned with Joint Staff priorities such as contested logistics, integrated deterrence, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. The first- and second-place researchers briefed the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and senior Joint Staff leaders during a May 2026 virtual briefing. Schade's paper has also been selected for a future Pentagon briefing.

"Our students are capturing true operational relevance that directly informs warfighting and lethality by bringing their real-world experiences to the table," Sankey said.

articles.title: Indianapolis teacher named Thunderbirds Hometown Hero at Grissom Air and Space Expo
articles.body:
For Megan Justice, a math teacher at George Washington High School in Indianapolis, a day with the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds became more than a once-in-a-lifetime flight. It became a lesson in trust, teamwork and inspiration she hopes to carry back to her students.

Justice, the 2026 Indianapolis Public Schools Secondary School Teacher of the Year, was selected as the Thunderbirds Hometown Hero for the Grissom Air and Space Expo. According to Staff Sgt. Sebastian Romawac, the Thunderbirds public affairs representative, the program serves two purposes: honoring the selected Hometown Hero and giving that individual the opportunity to learn the Thunderbirds mission so they can advocate for it.

As part of that experience, Justice spent the day behind the scenes with the team before flying with Maj. Samuel Lawson, Thunderbird 8/Advance Pilot/Narrator.

After seeing the team up close, Justice said her impression of the Thunderbirds was shaped not only by their skill, but by the professionalism and care they showed throughout the day.

“The Thunderbirds consist of a team of people who are genuinely kind, dedicated, and talented,” Justice said. “Their professionalism was prevalent throughout the entire day that I spent with them. I felt extremely supported through each briefing, fitting, and ride! It was amazing to see how much detail goes into their work.”

That support left a lasting mark on Justice, especially after hearing one phrase repeated throughout the day: “blind trust.”

“I noticed the Thunderbirds using the saying ‘blind trust’ throughout the day and it really resonated with me,” Justice said. “As crazy as it was, I didn’t feel scared for my flight. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I believe it was because I had ‘blind trust’ in the Thunderbirds and the rest of the team. I think everyone can apply this into aspects of their lives. Trusting in your team, your people, or your circle is a crucial component on a path towards success!”

“I hope that I show my students that anything is possible if you believe in yourself!” she said.

Justice said a ninth grade math teacher inspired her path into education. “I had a ninth grade math teacher that made me and my peers feel important, capable, and supported every day,” she said. “She inspired me to make others feel the same way in my own classroom.”

When asked what keeps her motivated, Justice pointed to her students. “Without a doubt, my students. Watching them grow and learn every day and every school year brings me so much joy!” she said. Being named the Thunderbirds Hometown Hero, she said, was especially meaningful because it recognized the work she loves most.

“I got here by being an impactful educator,” Justice said. “It means the world to know that the profession I love so much brought me this once in a lifetime opportunity. I would not be the teacher that I am without all my past, present, and future students. I also have an amazing school community in the Indianapolis Public School system where I am a part of an amazingly wonderful team at George Washington High School. Lastly, I’m incredibly thankful for my parents, fiancé, family, and friends who cheered me on every step of the way for this flight and through life!”

For Justice, the day at Grissom was not only about the thrill of flight, but about seeing excellence up close and bringing those lessons back to the classroom. In the end, the experience reflected the same values she works to instill in her students every day: confidence, trust and the belief that anything is possible.

articles.title: Tick prevention begins before stepping outdoors
articles.body:
For Airmen and Guardians, readiness means protecting their health wherever their day takes them, including on wooded trails, grassy training areas, field exercises and during time outdoors with family.

Ticks are typically small in size, but some may transmit diseases that can significantly impact military readiness. These parasitic arachnids are most active as the season warms into spring and summer months, though service members must remain alert to tick exposure, which can occur year-round.

The Department of War closely monitors tick-borne diseases since symptoms can quickly compromise an Airmen or Guardian’s physical readiness, resulting in lost duty days and potential long-term health complications.

“Practicing personal protective measures against ticks is a direct action to preserve force health, maintain operational strength and ensure mission readiness,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Timothy Davis, medical entomology consultant and theater preventive medicine flight commander at Kadena Air Base, Japan.

While Lyme disease is one of the most recognized tick-borne illnesses in the United States, the Department of War and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also monitor cases for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis and babesiosis.

Know about alpha-gal syndrome

Lone star tick bites can also trigger alpha-gal syndrome, an allergic condition that can have lasting implications for those affected. Unlike Lyme disease, which is caused by bacteria, AGS involves an immune response to alpha-gal, a sugar molecule found in most mammals.

AGS reactions can be delayed for several hours after consuming mammalian meat and byproducts or other goods containing alpha-gal. Symptoms can range from hives and gastrointestinal problems to more serious allergic reactions.

For service members, the condition can present unique challenges to nutrition and field operations. Davis noted that an AGS diagnosis may require careful planning around military meals and other deployment considerations.

Build layers of protection

The most effective way to prevent tickborne illness is to reduce the chance of being bitten. Davis shared personal protective measures outlined in Armed Forces Pest Management Board Technical Guide 36, identifying this resource as a primary reference used by public health and preventive medicine personnel to train Airmen and Guardians on personal protection before field exercises and deployments.

Steps to Prevent Tick Bites

Post-outdoor tick check

Davis emphasized that tick prevention does not end when outdoor activity is over.

After spending time outdoors, check your entire body for ticks. Pay particular attention to areas such as behind the knees, under the arms, around the waist, behind the ears and along the scalp. Showering soon after outdoor activity can also help remove unattached ticks.

Despite the risk of tick exposure, Davis said these proactive measures can contribute to increased safety when outdoors.

“Do not let the threat of ticks slow you down or keep you inside,” he said. “Physical fitness, mental resilience, and family bonding are built outdoors. By taking a few proactive minutes to apply repellent and treat your gear, you can safely enjoy the outdoors, stay fit, remain healthy, and be ready to win when the nation calls!”

Got a tick bite?

If an attached tick is found, remove it promptly with fine-tipped tweezers. Service members should also pay attention to changes in their health following potential exposure.

Early symptoms associated with tickborne illnesses can include fever, fatigue, headache, muscle or joint aches and a rash. Davis said that the rash does not always appear in the classic “bull's-eye” pattern and may instead appear as a solid pink-to-red patch.

If symptoms develop after spending time in an area where ticks are present, seek medical evaluation and tell your healthcare provider about the potential exposure. Davis recommended informing providers about recent field training, land navigation or time spent in wooded or grassy areas because that information can help inform the evaluation.

The Defense Health Agency offers free tick testing and pathogen identification, through milTICK, to Department of War personnel and dependents based in the United States. The CAC-enabled dashboard also monitors cases of various tickborne illnesses across statewide installations.

Visit the DHA tick webpage for more information.

articles.title: Virtual Flag 26-4: DMOC Forges Joint and Coalition C2 Readiness for High-End Conflict
articles.body:
To prepare the joint force for high-end conflict, the 705th Combat Training Squadron hosted Virtual Flag 26-4 from August 4-7, 2026. bringing together co-located and distributed players in a large-scale, simulated command and control exercise that successfully integrated tactical and operational-level C2.

The exercise brought together operators from the U.S. Air Force, Space Force, Army, and Marine Corps, alongside key coalition partners from the United Kingdom and Australia, to practice executing war-winning airpower in a realistic, virtual battlespace.

“The foundation of joint warfighting is built in exercises like Virtual Flag,” said U.S. Air Force Col. James Fields II, 505th Command and Control Wing commander. “This event is where we prove that we are the Air Force's premier organization for operational command and control. By bringing together operators from every service and our key allies, we are not just testing systems; we are building the integrated, combat-ready teams required to succeed in any environment.”

Building a Realistic, Multi-Domain Battlespace

A key focus of VF 26-4 was replicating the realistic friction between the tactical and operational levels of C2, a challenge that requires deep integration across the joint force.

“For this exercise,Marine Air Support Squadron 1was instrumental,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. James McCarthy, 705th CTS director of operations. “They provided the critical expertise needed to ensure every single participant, from our pilots in the virtual simulators to our commanders in the AOC, was looking at the exact same, accurate common tactical picture. That shared view of the battlespace is the absolute foundation of joint C2.”

Another major objective was to challenge battle managers with a robust, realistic intelligence picture, requiring the deep integration of the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance enterprise.

“In a peer conflict, identifying tracks and targets is going to require a robust ISR enterprise,” McCarthy explained. “Rather than just white-carding the answers, we had actual operators from theMQ-9 ReaperandRC-135 Rivet Jointcommunities participating. This is extremely valuable because it helps our C2 community understand what the ISR enterprise can and cannot provide in a high-tempo fight.”

The exercise provided a unique training opportunity for the ISR crews as well. The MQ-9 operators were tasked with not only identifying targets but also aiding in personnel recovery efforts for simulated downed pilots. Simultaneously, the RC-135 crews were critical in helping to identify key targets for strike packages.

“It gives these communities an opportunity to participate in a mission set that they may not be able to get after back home,” McCarthy added.

Training the Warfighter at Every Echelon

Serving as the exercise's operational-level C2 hub, the 505th Combat Training Squadron provided a robust and realistic Air Operations Center replication, driving the scenario for the entire joint and coalition team.

“Our team provided realistic AOC replication, serving as the operational-level C2 hub for the joint training audience,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Jason Guest, 505th CTS commander. “This high-fidelity environment was especially critical for our Air Expeditionary Wing participants, as it provided the realistic operational C2 link they needed to validate their distributed command and control training.”

The exercise provided a critical training environment for two Air Expeditionary Wings challenging their C2 Force Elements to execute distributed C2 in a contested, simulated agile combat employment scenario. This forced commanders to make difficult decisions regarding both mission execution and survival under realistic constraints.

“Stepping into a Wing Operations Center to manage six Mission Generation Force Elements across three simulated bases is a massive departure from our Airmen's daily tactical routines, and Virtual Flag 26-4 provided the proving ground,” said a U.S. Air Force major serving as the VF 26-4 exercise deputy offensive director.“What started as an uncomfortable learning curve quickly turned into operational confidence as our team synchronized our offensive and defensive sections from home station. They streamlined our internal reporting, integrated real-time logistics and base defense with sortie generation, and proved our forces are ready to execute distributed command and control under contested conditions.”

A Global, Coalition Effort

Integrating coalition partners from the U.K. and Australia was another key objective.

“There are immense benefits from connecting the Air Battlespace Training Centre at Royal Air Force Waddington and the DMOC’s systems,” said RAF Wing Commander Richard Kinniburgh, 505th Test and Training Group Deputy Commander and RAF Exchange Officer. “With the increasing dependency on virtual training for major exercises, this partnership is more critical than ever for ensuring our forces are ready to operate together.”

Ultimately, the DMOC provides a cost-effective, repeatable, and highly flexible training venue that live-fly exercises cannot match.

“The virtual environment allows us to provide high-quality, high-repetition training in a fiscally responsible manner,” McCarthy concluded. “More importantly, it allows us to present our warfighters with a scale of conflict that would be impossible to replicate in a live-fly exercise. We also remove many of the real-world friction points that can cancel live-fly training, ensuring our warfighters get the maximum training value out of every event.”

articles.title: Ready for BATTLE School
articles.body:
JOINT BASE LINDSEY GRAHAM, S.C. — The sun beat down on the training area as Airmen held their positions around the simulated base. Heavy equipment filled the yard, dust hung in the air and the weight of their protective gear pressed against them as they waited for the next detonation in the stifling heat. Boots shifted against the ground. Voices came through radios. Some Airmen scanned the surrounding area while others watched the people beside them, waiting for the next cue.

No one knew exactly when the next blast would come.

Around them, the exercise continued. Radios crackled as Airmen moved through the simulated environment, communicating with one another and responding to problems designed to test how they would react when familiar conditions disappeared.

U.S. Air Force Senior Airman Miguel Dee, 628th Air Base Wing plans and programs battlefield, assessment, and tactical training learning environment school cadre, watched from the edge of the training area. He helps prepare Airmen for the realities of operating in contested and deployed environments.

But tactical training had not always felt relevant to him.

From where he stood, Dee was reminded of the uncertainty he once felt himself. As an aerial port Airman, he was accustomed to a mission centered on cargo. He worked with the movement and handling of equipment and supplies, making sure cargo reached where it needed to go to support the mission.

For Dee, the question was simple.

Why would an aerial port Airman need tactical training?

“I’m a port dawg by trade, so I always wondered, ‘What do I need this for? When am I going to be in this situation?’” Dee said.

Tactical training felt different.

Now, he teaches it.

On the training ground, Dee moved between the groups, watching the Airmen as they worked through the scenario without immediately intervening. When one team struggled, he waited. The Airmen talked through the problem, adjusted their approach and tried again. Only when they needed direction did Dee step forward.

“I never thought I would be an instructor,” Dee said. “Teaching isn’t really in my nature. Being in front of a lot of people sometimes makes me nervous.”

The role pushed Dee outside his comfort zone, but those who worked with him saw potential in the Airman standing in front of the class.

Staff Sgt. Barbara Brun, Dee’s former supervisor in the 437th Aerial Port Squadron Cargo Services section, saw something in him that Dee didn’t necessarily see in himself.

“I recommended SrA Dee to become a BATTLE school instructor because he's a dedicated, hard-working Airman who naturally stands out as a leader among his peers,” Brun said.

Dee’s experience in the role has required more than simply learning how to teach. It has required him to make decisions, communicate clearly and recognize when to lead from the front and when to let others take over.

“During deployment, SrA Dee demonstrated elite potential by training his shift and leading critical missions,” Brun said. “Back home, he seamlessly assumed the Cargo Handling Supervisor role during my absence, keeping the team focused and mission-ready.”

Those experiences helped shape how Dee approaches instruction.

“It’s more than just knowing how to do the job,” Dee said. “You have to be able to make decisions, adapt and support the people around you.”

As Airmen move through the training scenarios, he focuses on more than whether they complete each task correctly. He wants them to understand what they are doing well enough to make decisions when the situation changes.

“We’re teaching them to build a foundation and from there go to the next step,” he said. “Once they have that foundation in place, they can act independently.”

For Dee, the goal is not simply another requirement checked off. He wants Airmen to understand why they are learning a skill and have the confidence to use it when circumstances change.

But preparing Airmen means more than teaching them how to respond to a threat.

Some of the most important lessons happen in the relationships Dee builds with the people he teaches.

Not every Airman arrives at training worried only about the next scenario. Dee has also interacted with Airmen preparing to leave home for the first time, facing the uncertainty of a new environment and the possibility of being separated from the people they love.

For some, the unknown can be just as intimidating as the training itself.

Dee drew from his own experiences and offered reassurance to the Airmen.

“For me, it’s more about the people you’re with rather than the job,” he told the interviewer. “Be there for them and have their backs.”

The advice reflects the same approach Dee brings to BATTLE school. Skills provide the foundation, but people provide the strength to operate when conditions are unfamiliar.

“It’s a great opportunity for me to meet a lot of people, share those experiences with them, and also be the one who helps them or gets them prepared for their upcoming expedition,” Dee said.

Brun said Dee's ability to build those relationships is central to his leadership.

“His defining strength is his ability to build a cohesive, trust-based environment where Airmen support one another and execute the mission with confidence,” Brun said.

The Airman who once wondered why he needed tactical training now helps others understand why they might.

Around him, Airmen continue moving through the training area, working through problems they may one day face somewhere far from home. The questions may be different, the environments may be unfamiliar and the circumstances may change, but Dee wants them to leave with something that can carry into any situation: the confidence to rely on their training and the people beside them.

What once felt like a question about his own job has become another way for Dee to prepare the people around him.

“You’re not alone,” Dee said. “I’m always here for my Airmen.”

articles.title: Refueling the Rescue Mission
articles.body:
MOODY AIR FORCE BASE, Ga. -- Crews from the 41st and 71st Rescue Squadrons took part in a Combat Search and Rescue Task Force (CSARTF) exercise over the Gulf of Mexico, Aug. 26, 2026.

The exercise brought together the three components of the rescue triad—the HC-130J Combat King II, HH-60W Jolly Green II and Guardian Angel weapon system—to practice the tactics, techniques and procedures used during real-world combat search and rescue missions.

“This exercise and CSARTF sorties as a whole give all the players of the rescue triad a chance to work together and practice the tactics, techniques and procedures we will use in combat in a structured and permissive environment,” said Capt. Steven Griffin III, 71st Rescue Squadron pilot.

The training was designed to simulate the complicated and demanding conditions rescue crews could face in combat, including multiple isolated personnel, threats, long-range flight and aerial refueling. The mission began long before the aircraft left the runway. Crews spent approximately 10 to 12 hours in the Mission Planning Cell preparing for the sortie, reviewing intelligence, identifying threats, gathering survivor information and planning routes. In the end the sortie included one aerial refueling, the recovery of two survivors and responses to multiple simulated threats.

“As the pilot these scenarios mean long missions, low-level over-the-water flying and a big mental load,” Maj. Kayla Pipe, 41st Rescue Squadron pilot said. “While we all work together in the aircraft, the pilots are the ones on the controls. We are ultimately responsible for keeping everyone safe.”

Once airborne, the training scenario continued to evolve. One of the most demanding portions of the mission was helicopter air-to-air refueling, or HAAR. The HH-60W crews practiced receiving fuel from the HC-130J while operating at low altitude over the water.

The narrow margin for error makes HAAR a skill that requires consistent practice. Weather, turbulence, aircraft weight, altitude and experience can all affect the refueling process. One of the best ways to become proficient is simple: practice.

“The more you do HAAR the better and more comfortable you become,” Pipe said.

While the aircraft crews focused on maintaining precise flight and communication during refueling, the larger CSARTF continued operating around them.

“The main issue with aerial refueling in exercises is the larger battle does not stop while we are giving gas,” Griffin said.

The crews must continue monitoring the tactical situation, communicating with other aircraft and maintaining awareness of potential threats while temporarily dedicating personnel to the refueling operation. That integration is central to the CSARTF mission.

“Internal to the CSARTF there is an assumption that all other participants are doing their job,” Griffin said. “This frees up brain bytes and mitigates risk by ensuring the crucial information is heard.”

Trust is built through repeated integration between the 41st and 71st RQS, as well as the Guardian Angel teams which is comprised of Combat Rescue Officers, Pararescuemen and Survival, Evasion, Resistance and Escape (SERE) Specialists. Training together helps crews understand one another beyond simply knowing their roles.

“Relationships play a huge part of learning to build trust,” Pipe said. “When you personally know the A-10 pilot overhead, live next-door to someone in the HC-130 flying with you to pass fuel or play ping-pong with the PJs sitting in the back of your helicopter, things become more personal.”

The exercise also introduced unexpected challenges. Simulated pop-up survivors required crews to reassess their plans, calculate fuel requirements and determine whether additional recoveries were possible while continuing to account for the existing threat picture.

Weather added another real-world variable. Thunderstorms forced Pipe's crew to alter its route to the Gulf and added approximately 20 minutes to the flight. Those complications are intentional. CSARTF training is designed to force crews to adapt when a carefully planned mission no longer goes according to plan.

“We do an excellent job training and do our best to simulate real world dangers and threats, but there are some things you cannot simulate, and the enemy always gets a say,” Pipe said.

For Griffin, the lessons learned during these exercises can influence how future crews approach similar missions.

“From these iterations we develop lessons learned that can be applied so that when the next crews are faced with a similar scenario they can prevent the mistakes we made and ultimately pick up JACK in a more timely and safer manner,” Griffin said.

But beneath the aircraft, communications systems and tactical scenarios is the reason the rescue mission exists in the first place: the person waiting to be rescued. Training becomes more personal when crews consider that the person they may someday be sent to recover could be someone they know.

“When you know that you are going to rescue fellow Americans—ones you might have worked with previously, are friends with, went to college or pilot training with—things become personal and sometimes emotional,” Pipe said.

That connection is part of what drives the crews to take training seriously. Every exercise provides an opportunity to practice the procedures, build trust and learn from mistakes before those lessons are needed in combat. For the 41st and 71st Rescue Squadrons, the goal is not simply to complete the next training sortie, it is to be ready for the day when the scenario becomes real.

articles.title: Cox assumes command of Training and Education Center
articles.body:
Cox assumes command of Training and Education Center

MCGHEE TYSON AIR NATIONAL GUARD BASE, Tenn. — Leadership of the I.G. Brown Training and Education Center changed hands during a change of command ceremony Thursday.

The traditional passing of the colors symbolized the change of leadership as Col. William J. Cox Jr.assumed command of the TEC from Col. Angela M. Tapia. Maj. Gen.Troy D. Havener, commander of the Air National Guard Readiness Center, presided over the ceremony.

“To the Total Force Airmen of the TEC, thank you for allowing me to lead,” Cox said. “I believe leading is serving and serving is leading, so please know that I am here to serve you.”

As TEC commander, Cox will oversee training and development across the Total Force and with partner nations. He will lead a team of more than 80 Airmen and civilian employees across three divisions focused on providing shared education and meeting the demands of current and innovative teaching techniques.

Before assuming command of the TEC, Cox served as senior executive officer to the acting director of the Air National Guard at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

“Col. Tapia, I thank you for your selfless duty to our nation and the outstanding leadership and mentorship you have provided this organization over the past few years,” Cox said. “I am deeply grateful for your hospitality these last few weeks as you talked me through the details.”

After relinquishing command of the TEC, Tapia will retire after 33 years of military service.

“Col. Cox, I believe you are the right leader at the right time for the TEC,” Tapia said. “What excites me is your strategic mindset. General Brown founded this institution because he could see beyond what the Air National Guard was at the moment and envision what it needed to become. I believe the TEC is at another one of those moments.”

The I.G. Brown Training and Education Center includes three divisions: the Chief Master Sgt.Paul H. Lankford Enlisted Professional Military Education Center, the TEC-University Video Production and Learning Development Division, and the Mission Support Division. Together, the divisions represent the Regular Air Force, Air National Guard, Air Force Reserve Command and civilian workforce, working side by side to develop today’s Airmen for tomorrow’s fight.

articles.title: Alaska Airman Builds Partnerships, Expands Leadership Perspective Through Indo-Pacific Forum
articles.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii — Staff Sgt. Eva Dennison arrived at the Inter-Pacific Junior Enlisted Leadership Forum expecting a professional military education opportunity. She left with a broader understanding of leadership, new relationships with international partners and a renewed interest in supporting future State Partnership Program engagements.

Dennison, a financial operations technician serving in the 168th Wing Comptroller Flight, Alaska Air National Guard, participated in IPJELF 26-1, July 21-27, at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.

The seven-day forum brought together 18 junior enlisted leaders from the United States and 11 allied and partner nations, including Australia, Canada, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Japan, Thailand, the United Kingdom and Taiwan. The cohort also included members of the Alaska and Hawaii Air National Guards, active-duty military, U.S. Space Force and the Mongolian Air Force Component through the State Partnership Program.

IPJELF is designed to strengthen leadership competence, broaden regional perspectives, enhance strategic awareness and foster international partnerships for national and regional security.

For Dennison, the course description immediately caught her attention.

“I read the course description and thought it sounded right up my alley,” Dennison said. “My degree is in cross-cultural communication, and the summary sounded just like what I like to nerd out about. It absolutely was. It sounded like exactly what I studied.”

On the first day, in the first minute, participants were placed in a practical search-and-rescue scenario. Sitting in an auditorium receiving a mission briefing, the students had to organize themselves into teams and work together despite differences in language, culture, and experience.

“Apart from a little chatting in the halls, none of us knew each other,” Dennison said. “English skills were their second or third language for some of them. We had some barriers.”

Those initial challenges became part of the learning experience. Throughout the week, participants returned to lessons from the exercise while discussing leadership, resilience, mission intent, command and control and multinational operations.

Dennison said one of her biggest takeaways was learning how to apply mission intent and command and control at the junior NCO level.

“It’s stepping back and taking a look at the bigger picture and figuring out what the intent is and how I can help execute that intent amongst my peer-level cohort,” she said.

The course also provided an opportunity to examine leadership during crisis situations. Participants visited Pearl Harbor and worked in breakout groups on a capstone project focused on resilience and leadership. The course culminated in an analysis of how different cultures, economies and militaries could combine their strengths and weaknesses to successfully execute a multinational exercise.

While the classroom instruction provided valuable lessons, Dennison said the relationships formed throughout the week were equally important.

“The people just made the course,” she said. “We were all on the same wavelength professionally and personally. It was nice to connect with peers from a different culture and have so many similarities rather than differences.” Those similarities extended to military humor, family life and the challenges of working with people.

“It was incredibly surprising to me that we all had the same jokes or the same perspectives on a peculiar situation,” Dennison said. “Having that military camaraderie and military humor, it felt the same as banter with an American counterpart.”

Dennison said the experience challenged some of her assumptions about cultural differences.

“You hear about more cultures being more reserved or that sort of thing. No, they were cutting it up,” she said. While language differences can sometimes create challenges during multinational engagements, Dennison said the group quickly found common ground through shared experiences.

“That wasn’t necessarily the case here,” Dennison said. “We bonded a lot over how to navigate difficult people or coworkers. Someone would say, ‘I do it like this,’ and I’d be like, ‘No, no, no — you’ve got to be like that.”

Despite long days in the classroom and limited free time, Dennison also found opportunities to share her familiarity with Oahu culture with members of the cohort. Having visited the island several times, she drove fellow participants to local restaurants, shopping areas and beaches away from the typical tourist destinations.

“It was fun to show them local culture,” Dennison said, adding that the informal experiences helped strengthen the relationships developed in the classroom.

For Dennison, the experience also reinforced the value of her background in cross-cultural communication.

“When you study a specific topic like cross-cultural, it makes you more aware of your own situational awareness,” she said. “My degree helps me to be more mindful in that aspect. It helps me generate ideas on how to approach people with respect.”

That awareness can be especially important when working with international partners, she said. Understanding that different cultures may have different customs, communication styles and expectations can help leaders establish trust.

“When you don’t necessarily know, just learning a quick phrase or gesture can really go a long way when you are working with a team other than yours,” Dennison said

The experience also strengthened Dennison’s connection to the Alaska National Guard’s partnership with Mongolia.

The Alaska National Guard’s State Partnership Program provides opportunities for Alaska and Mongolian military members to develop professional relationships and exchange knowledge through engagements and training. Dennison said she initially did not realize IPJELF was connected to SPP.

“At first, I didn’t realize it was part of SPP,” she said. “I thought it was a cool PME, TDY and some knowledge learning. Getting involved with SPP has been really fun.”

The Alaska-Mongolia State Partnership Program, established in 2003, connects the Alaska National Guard with Mongolia’s armed forces through military-to-military engagements, professional development and training opportunities designed to strengthen relationships, interoperability and regional security.

Working alongside Mongolian military members in a classroom setting offered a different type of engagement than a traditional exercise.

“This is a wonderful way to engage with our state partner equivalents and to get to know them and their military a little bit better for future engagements with our state partner,” Dennison said.

The participants also discovered a shared connection through their environments. Mongolia’s cold, dry climate gave Dennison an opportunity to compare experiences with people who understood what it was like to operate in an Arctic environment.

“A lot of people can’t relate to having such a dry climate that’s so cold,” she said. “I was like, ‘Finally, someone gets it.’”

Dennison hopes to build on those relationships during future engagements and potentially bring some of the leadership concepts from IPJELF to Alaska-Mongolia partnership activities.

“Work toward bringing this course material to SPP engagements in Mongolia would be my end goal,” she said. “It would be incredible to do.”

She also plans to bring the lessons back to the 168th Wing.

“I can talk about experiences working with other partners, whether it is mission command and control or mission intent, and take back some of those scenarios and disseminate that in my job and in my office,” she said. “I can supplement with different topics and new topics.”

For Dennison, the value of IPJELF extended beyond learning how to become a better leader. It demonstrated how relationships, cultural understanding and shared experiences can help build the trust necessary for multinational teams to accomplish a common mission.

“When you don’t necessarily know, just learning a quick phrase or gesture can really go a long way when you are working with a team other than yours,” Dennison said.

After eight years of service in the Alaska Air National Guard, Dennison returned to Alaska with a new perspective on her role as an NCO and a desire to continue building the partnerships that help strengthen security across the Indo-Pacific.

For her, the forum was just the beginning.

“It was great,” Dennison said. “This was just a little scratch of the surface of the State Partnership Program.”

For the Alaska Air National Guard, those relationships are more than professional connections. They are part of building the trust and shared understanding necessary to operate alongside allies and partners in an increasingly interconnected Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: DAF Accelerates Joint C2 with AI, Space Force Integration in Latest DASH Experiment
articles.body:
In a fast-paced, two-week experiment, the Department of the Air Force continued to demonstrate that human-machine teaming, integrating artificial intelligence to handle heavy data processing so human operators can make faster and smarter decisions, can significantly accelerate the joint kill chain.

The latest Decision Advantage Sprint for Human-Machine Teaming, or DASH, further advanced the Department of the Air Force’s command and control modernization efforts. During the two-week event, an integrated operational crew led by a U.S. Space Force Guardian worked alongside U.S. Air Force battle managers and industry software developers to validate an agile acquisitions model designed to deliver capabilities to the warfighter at speed.

“Our goal is to get the most advanced capabilities into the hands of the joint force at speed,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Corey Ellsworth, Advanced Battle Management System Cross-Functional Team integration lead. “This entire framework was built from the ground up to ensure that once a capability is validated here, we can securely and efficiently transition it to the classified networks where our Airmen and Guardians will actually use it in a high-end fight.” Hosted at the 805th Combat Training Squadron’s Shadow Operations Center-Nellis, the event was a “whole of lab” effort, co-led by the ABMS CFT and the Air Force Research Laboratory.

Driving Multi-Domain Integration

The integrated operational crew, led by a Space Force Guardian, exemplified the joint collaboration required across the services.This leadership, combined with scientific analysis from the711th Human Performance Wing, validated a core hypothesis: that the fundamental challenges of C2 are the same across all domains.

“As a joint force, we operate as a single, cohesive team focused on the exact same objective. It isn't about the 'Air Force way' or the 'Space Force way'; it is about the 'warfighting way,'”said U.S. Space Force Maj. Erik Murdock, 57th Space Aggressor Squadron Operations Division chief.“Because while our domains are different, our decision-making challenges are identical. This experiment demonstrated that when you give a joint team common objectives and a shared set of tools, the integration happens naturally.”

Dr. Elizabeth Frost, the AFRL DASH lead, echoed that sentiment, explaining that the quantitative data and human-factors analysis supported the operators' conclusions.

“Our data and direct observations confirm that the fundamental cognitive challenges for a battle manager are domain-agnostic,” said Frost. “Both Airmen and Guardians are tasked with synthesizing vast amounts of complex data and prioritizing actions under intense time pressure. This event demonstrated that a well-designed human-machine team can effectively free up an operator's cognitive resources.”

A Realistic Battlespace and an Agile Architecture

To ensure the highest degree of combat realism, the experiment's scenarios were designed by the ShOC-N's own team of veteran operators, leveraging their more than 50 years of collective experience in tactical and operational C2.

“This isn’t a scenario from a video game; it is one crafted to challenge operators and engineers alike,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Wesley Schultz, 805th CTS commander. “We reflect the real-world challenges of geography and logistics, and even real-time changes in the rules of engagement, because that reflects the reality of modern warfare.”

The technical backbone of the experiment was an AFRL-developed "orchestrator," a government-owned software interface that allowed multiple, competing industry applications to be tested in a modular ecosystem.

“Successfully demonstrating this 'plug-and-play' ecosystem was a critical milestone,” said Kevin McFarland, AFRL Advanced Capabilities Directorate project management lead. “Government ownership of the orchestrator significantly decreases integration bottlenecks. We are no longer locked into a single vendor's closed architecture.”

By bringing operators and developers together on the operations floor, the experiment facilitated an immediate and highly effective feedback loop.

“The AFRL Information and Spectrum Warfare Directorate developed software providedreal-time assessment of the baseline experimental runs and the baseline runs with vendor solutions,”said Ryan Hilliard, AFRL Information and Spectrum Warfare Directorate C2 Research Area Lead. “This real-time assessment allowed vendors and operators to see process execution metrics associated with each trial to give immediate feedback on the benefits of introducing technology solutions into battle manager’s decision-making process.”

From Experiment to Enterprise: An Agile Model for Acquisitions

This collaborative development process is a key component of a rapid acquisitions model championed by the Command, Control, Communications, and Battle Management enterprise.

“The DASH series is a textbook example of what we are trying to accomplish,” said Jeffrey Palumbo, AFRL C3BM Capability Area lead. “This approach of user-producer co-creation allows for proof of concept, energizes the industrial base, and allows for early operator feedback to shape development. It sets us up to deliver chunks of warfighting capability to the operational force in a rapid and repeatable cycle.”

This coordination between technical developers and the operational requirements community is designed to rapidly and securely transition unclassified laboratory trials to classified warfighting networks.

“The integration with AFRL at these experiments has enabled the C3BM Operational Response Team to project transition opportunities with the broader Department of the Air Force Battle Network,” said U.S. Air Force Col. Rowland Cardoni, C3BM ORT chief.

Cognitive Superiority: The Future of Battle Management

For the operators on the floor, the impact of this collaborative approach was undeniable. “These sprints represent the biggest shift in battle management in my career,” said Schultz. “We’re taking what technology allows for and shaping it in a way that magnifies the skills and training of warfighters to ensure we maintain decisive advantage in conflict.”

With the DASH sprints demonstrating continuous advancements in capability development, the ABMS CFT, the Portfolio Acquisition Executives C3BM, and AFRL are working closely together, looking ahead to the next evolution of battle management.

“The future of battle management isn't just about accelerating our reaction time; it's about fundamentally changinghowwe make decisions. The experimentation focused on game theory and will continue in future experiments, too,” said U.S. Air Force Col. John Ohlund, ABMS CFT director. “We are moving beyond simple, reactive scenarios and presenting our warfighters with complex, ambiguous problems where they must be proactive, weigh trade-offs, and make decisions when there is no perfect answer. This approach is essential for developing the cognitive superiority our joint force needs to out-think and outmaneuver a peer adversary in a high-end conflict.”

articles.title: Hawaii Guard, partners build toward expanded HADR exercise during Super Garuda Shield 26
articles.body:
Military members, civilian agencies and international partners came together Aug. 31 to Sept. 4 for a Humanitarian Assistance Disaster Relief Table Top Exercise, or HADR TTX, at the Indonesian Armed Forces Staff and Command School during Super Garuda Shield 26.

The five-day engagement focused on strengthening coordination among organizations involved in disaster response and establishing a common understanding of their respective roles, responsibilities and capabilities.

“The exercise was designed to begin at the local and provincial response level and build to how the respective regional, national, and international response frameworks support current plans,” said U.S. Army Lt. Col. Earl Tsuneyoshi, Hawaii Army National Guard 1st Battalion, 298th Multifunctional Training Regiment commander and planner for the HADR TTX. “This week in particular was to establish that baseline understanding of roles and responsibilities throughout the different phases of a response, but also understanding how each of the different countries do things so that we can collaborate better.”

Super Garuda Shield is an annual exercise between the Indonesian National Armed Forces and U.S. military designed to strengthen bilateral interoperability, capabilities and cooperation.

For the HADR TTX, that concept of interoperability extended beyond military-to-military cooperation. Organizers emphasized a whole-of-society approach designed to improve coordination among military forces, civilian agencies, law enforcement, emergency responders and other organizations that may be called upon during a natural or man-made disaster.

“Whole-of-society government response is necessary to ensure that we have a unified and effective response,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. Maria Ercira Guisadioabis, Hawaii Air National Guard medical plans officer and HADR TTX planner. “Every stakeholder from the national, regional and local levels needs to know what their roles and responsibilities are and how to synchronize their efforts.”

The exercise was structured to move from broad national-level disaster response frameworks toward increasingly regional, provincial and tactical perspectives.

During the early portion of the HADR TTX, participants examined national response frameworks from Indonesia, the United States and partner nations. Later sessions brought in additional organizations and response stakeholders to discuss capabilities, responsibilities and how those organizations interact during disaster operations.

By the final portion of the engagement, discussions had moved toward organizations operating closer to the tactical level, including search-and-rescue and other response assets.

“This first iteration was really about education,” Guisadioabis said. “It was about making sure everyone understood where the different agencies fit and what capabilities they bring.”

The HADR TTX is the first step in a multi-year training approach planners described as “educate, train and demonstrate,” similar to a crawl-walk-run model.

While this first year focused on educating participants and developing a common understanding of disaster-response systems. Future iterations are expected to move into more practical training before culminating in an event where participants demonstrate their ability to coordinate across organizations during a more complex disaster-response scenario.

Part of the long-term intent is to evolve the HADR engagement beyond a tabletop format and into an operational exercise within the broader Super Garuda Shield portfolio, progressively building toward an event that requires participating organizations to apply what they have learned and demonstrate an integrated disaster response.

Planners said the model is also intended to create a repeatable framework that can eventually be adapted to different disaster scenarios and locations throughout Indonesia.

Indonesia already has extensive disaster-response experience and established response systems, but organizers said the engagement provides an opportunity to continually evaluate and improve those systems as conditions, organizations and capabilities change.

“There’s always a feedback loop,” said Guisadioabis. “There are changes in the environment, changes in training and changes in manpower. Even when there’s already an effective system, there are always lessons learned and opportunities to improve.”

Recent disaster-response operations in Indonesia underscored the need for continued coordination among military, civilian and emergency-response agencies. A deadly West Bandung landslide in January 2026, which affected communities in the mountainous region surrounding Bandung and the current wildfires in Kalimantan and Sumatra, also provided real-world examples of the challenges responders face during large-scale disasters.

The HADR TTX also builds upon long-standing cooperation between the Hawaii National Guard and Indonesia through the U.S. Department of War State Partnership Program.

Hawaii and Indonesia have engaged through the program for 20 years, conducting engagements and subject-matter exchanges designed to strengthen relationships, share expertise and improve partner capabilities. Officials said State Partnership Program engagements conducted throughout the year can help sustain momentum between annual Super Garuda Shield exercises and support development of future HADR training.

“What we’re trying to do is synchronize and integrate those efforts,” said Tsuneyoshi. “We don’t want all of these exercises and engagements going in different directions. We want them to be unified and mutually supporting.”

Under that approach, State Partnership Program engagements can provide additional opportunities for Indonesian and Hawaii National Guard personnel to address specific disaster-response topics, exchange lessons learned and prepare for the larger HADR exercise held during Super Garuda Shield.

“It augments the touch points that we have,” Tsuneyoshi said. “Instead of engaging only once a year, the State Partnership Program provides additional opportunities for continuous planning and engagement.”

By creating those relationships and establishing a shared understanding before a disaster occurs, planners said participating organizations can be better positioned to respond collectively when resources, communications and infrastructure may be strained.

articles.title: 60th LRS delivers excellence, earns six logistics awards
articles.body:
TRAVIS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. — The 60th Logistics Readiness Squadron earned six 2025 Director of Logistics Annual Awards, recognizing Travis Air Force Base, California Airmen and teams at the Air Mobility Command and Headquarters Air Force levels.

The awards span multiple areas of the logistics mission, including vehicle management, ground transportation, plans and integration and materiel management.

U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Kyle Branham, 60th LRS vehicle management superintendent, earned the Headquarters Air Force-level Vehicle Management Chief Master Sgt. Tim Stern Senior Noncommissioned Officer of the Year Award.

“Winning this award is a true testament to what the Airmen of the Travis Vehicle Management team bring to the fight,” Branham said. “I am incredibly proud to serve alongside a team that lives by our creed — discipline, execute, do your job.”

Branham’s individual recognition accompanied an AMC-level win for the 60th LRS vehicle management team. The team maintains a fleet of 721 vehicles supporting the Travis mission and global contingency operations. The squadron’s Installation Deployment Readiness Cell also earned AMC’s Plans and Integration Team of the Year Award after managing a significant surge in deployment operations.

“With a team of just 20 members, we compressed 91% of the wing’s annual taskings into a grueling three-week window,” said Capt. Alexa Poveromo, 60th LRS installation deployment officer. “We are a small team, but we carry a massive scope of responsibility that directly enables global rapid reach.”

Additionally, the 60th LRS Ground Transportation Element was named AMC’s Ground Transportation Wheeled Warriors Team of the Year.

"Being named team of the year validates the quiet, heavy lifting our team does behind the scenes," said Master Sgt. Jessica Arlyn Mitchum, 60th LRS ground transportation section chief. "Whether expediting aircrew or executing cargo drops, our daily hustle directly translates to the wing's ability to project power. We own the ground so the wing can own the skies."

Rounding out the AMC-level honors, the 60th LRS earned the Daedalian Maj. Gen. Warren R. Carter Logistics Effectiveness Award, and Senior Airman Victoria May Littlejohn was named the 2S Airman of the Year.

Senior Master Sgt. Diego Veliz, 60th Logistics Readiness Squadron deployment and distribution flight superintendent, said the six awards reflect the collective efforts of Airmen and civilians across the squadron.

“Attaining recognition at this level is never the result of a single, individual action,” Veliz said. “Instead, it’s the accumulation of every team member’s unwavering commitment to operational excellence, mutual support and a shared sense of purpose.”
