articles.title: 31st LRS wins 2025 Daedalian Logistics Effectiveness Award
articles.body:
AVIANO AIR BASE, Italy — The 31st Logistics Readiness Squadron received multiple awards for their achievements and contributions throughout 2025, exemplifying that mission success starts with the Airmen behind the scenes.

“Nothing moves on Aviano, or really South of the Alps or on the Eastern Flank, without the 31 LRS.” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Teresa Crampton, 31 LRS outgoing commander.

Most recently, the 31 LRS earned the 2025 Daedalian Maj. Gen. Warren R. Carter Logistics Effectiveness Award, recognizing excellent logistics performance and the ability to support mission aircraft, weapons and operations in a demanding environment.

The award acknowledges the collective efforts of Airmen across the squadron’s flights, including cargo movement, materiel management, fuels and ground transportation.

“Our Airmen’s ability to innovate under operational tempo is what makes the 31 LRS stand out,” said U.S. Air Force Senior Master Sgt. Brendan Victory, 31 LRS senior enlisted leader. “Across every flight, our team streamlined processes, supported NATO Allies and delivered results while competing against units across the Air Force.”

Throughout the year, the 31 LRS not only maintained daily mission requirements but went above and beyond, delivering increased support to NATO Allies and operations across USAFE-AFAFRICA.

“Our synchronized response during peak NATO support operations, which consisted of managing surge cargo across Europe while overhauling customs protocols and securing 14 new innovation-driven contracts, proved our team's resilience under real-world pressure,” said Victory.

Logistics operations often go unnoticed outside the career field, yet they are imperative to every successful mission. Before aircraft can launch, equipment must be delivered, fuel must be stored, vehicles must be available, and cargo must reach its destination.

“People see aircraft generate and take off, but they don't always see the logistics chain that enables every sortie,” Victory explained. “Every pallet built, customs clearance expedited, fuel transfer completed, and vehicle dispatched represents an LRS Airman's direct fingerprint on mission execution across Europe.”

The 31 LRS culture of teamwork and excellence were also highlighted by U.S. Air Force Maj. Chase Barnes, 31 LRS director of operations, who was named ‘2025 Outstanding Logistic Readiness Field Grade Officer of the Year’.

“My win at the USAFE level is built solely on the incredible work of this squadron,” said Barnes. “None of this is possible without the squadron’s dedication and tireless efforts around the clock to our mission South of the Alps.”

Additionally, U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Derek Wilson from Fuels and Staff Sgt. Matthew Martinez from Ground Transportation were both named ‘2025 noncommissioned Officer of the Year’.

“Wilson and Martinez demonstrated proactive mentorship, mission ownership, and the ability to turn complex logistics requirements into seamless operational results,” said Victory. “Their recognition demonstrates that the 31 LRS develops technically proficient NCOs who lead from the front.”

The combination of the squadron’s inner workings and individual recognition attest to the strong foundation and culture within the 31 LRS, where mission success is built through the collective efforts of the squadron.

“Winning at the MAJCOM and Air Force levels validates that the extra hours and procedural innovations our Airmen implemented truly moved the needle. It demonstrates that base-level execution at Aviano sets the standard for logistics operational readiness across the entire enterprise,” said Victory.

The 31 LRS’s diverse responsibilities establish the logistical backbone that keeps the wing and its partners ready across Europe and NATO. Though much of their work happens behind the scenes, its impact is felt across the flightline and throughout the region, proving that logistics is not simply about moving resources, but keeping the mission moving forward.

articles.title: CONR-1AF (AFNORTH & AFSPACE) Welcomes Lt. Gen. Everman as New Commander
articles.body:
TYNDALL AIR FORCE BASE, Fla. – Continental U.S. North American Aerospace Defense Command Region – First Air Force (Air Forces Northern and Air Forces Space) leadership changed hands during a ceremony at Tyndall Air Force Base, Sept. 2, 2026.

Lt. Gen. Bradford R. Everman officially took the helm from Lt. Gen. M. Luke Ahmann as he received the command guidon, marking a seamless transfer of operational authority and round-the-clock responsibility.

Gen. Adrian Spain, Commander, Air Combat Command, presided over the ceremony, praising the command’s round-the-clock defense posture and joint operational readiness. Total force mission partners, civic leaders and distinguished military guests attended the event.

Prior to assuming command, Everman served as the Special Assistant to the NORAD and USNORTHCOM Commander for Reserve Matters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado.

"Lt. Gen. Ahmann did an amazing job leading this team, and I could not be more excited to step in and continue the vital mission of First Air Force," Everman said. "Our job is to stay one, two, three steps ahead of anything that could threaten our nation. Whether that means unmanned aircraft, inbound ballistic missiles, manned aircraft, or natural disasters like hurricanes and wildfires. We are applying the lessons learned around the globe every day to ensure the nation remains safe and secure across our aerospace warning, aerospace control, maritime warning, and homeland defense missions.

As the commander of CONR-1AF (AFNORTH & AFSPACE), Everman directs three distinct operational missions across the air and space domains. In his CONR role under NORAD, Everman oversees airspace warning, air sovereignty and aerospace defense for the continental United States under Operation Noble Eagle. As the air component commander for USNORTHCOM, he leads air operations focused on homeland defense and defense support of civil authorities during national emergencies and natural disasters. Additionally, as the air component commander to U.S. Space Command, he directs theater air support, contingency rescue operations and worldwide search and recovery support for human space flight missions.

On the service side, First Air Force is one of four numbered air forces assigned to Air Combat Command. The organization trains, equips, and oversees full-time active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve personnel, and the civilian volunteers of the Civil Air Patrol.

About CONR-1AF (AFNORTH & AFSPACE):

Headquartered at Tyndall Air Force Base, Florida, CONR-1AF (AFNORTH & AFSPACE) ensures the aerospace defense of the continental United States, serves as the air component to U.S. Northern Command and U.S. Space Command, and provides rapid response capabilities to support civil authorities and lead human space flight rescue operations. For more information, visithttps://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.1af.acc.af.mil.

articles.title: Nurse with the 144th Medical Group Chases Country Music Dreams
articles.body: FRESNO AIR NATIONAL GUARD BASE, California — U.S. Air National Guard 2nd Lt. Brian Hanes, an officer with the 144th Medical Group, serves his country and community while chasing his dreams of being a country music star in Fresno, California Aug. 20, 2026. Hanes is a full time surgical nurse by day, a medical officer on drill weekends and an aspiring country artist by night. Though Hanes is committed to serving his country at the 144th Fighter Wing, that does not stop him from pursuing his lifelong goals and ambitions, cultivating a spirit of multi-capability within him. From an early age, Hanes knew that he wanted to help people. Having a younger sister who suffered from biliary atresia, a disease affecting the liver, and another who was premature, Hanes spent a lot of time in hospitals. “To be honest, when I was graduating high school, I didn't want to have anything to do with hospitals because I had spent so much time in them,” said Hanes. Though he grew a disdain for hospitals, Hanes’ desire to serve and help others grew stronger. As he was searching for his calling, Hanes discovered his passion. He was only 10 years old when he began to play the drums. Growing up in Fresno, California, Hanes was immersed in rock, R&B, and country, and music became his first love. Playing and performing music gave Hanes a deeply rooted form of expression–one that blossomed into a much-needed outlet. “It was never to be popular,” said Hanes. “But when you play music, you connect with people.” When Hanes was 13, he discovered that music was more than just a passion–it was a way to create something of his own. Unlocking his rhythmic mind through the drums was just the beginning. As he developed his skills, he realized he could do more than play songs–he could write them. “I wanted to have the capability of making something, not necessarily for it to be a tangible product to sell, but to create something,” said Hanes. After high school, Hanes spent several years searching for the right career path. A year-long study-abroad opportunity took him to England, but it was his later experiences working in health care that sparked his interest in nursing. Hanes began working as an EMT in California shortly after his return from England. As a patient transporter, he began to witness the bigger impact that he could have on people. Seeing the nurses in the hospitals operate and interact with patients ignited a spark within him and, for the first time, Hanes’ calling in health care was clear. “Their lifestyle appealed to me,” said Hanes. “Their conversation, their education, that all appealed to me, and I started to think, ‘You know, I think I could be a good nurse.’” After earning a degree in public health and exploring several careers in health care, Hanes decided nursing offered the most opportunities. Hanes applied to a 12-month Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) program and, when he was accepted, moved across the country to Omaha, Nebraska, to attend. “It was really, really hard,” said Hanes. “I mean, there was a lot of blood, sweat and tears for a 12-month BSN, but I did it.” Though Hanes faced hardship, he persevered through adversity and emerged triumphant. Hanes returned to California and began working as a nurse at Fresno Heart Hospital, bringing him full circle to the place he once sought to avoid. His tireless devotion to achieve his goals spilled over into every aspect of his life as he continued to write and perform country music and, soon after, was commissioned into the Air National Guard as a medical officer at the 144th Fighter Wing. Hanes’ father, a retired senior master sergeant, served at the 144th, so serving at his local Air National Guard unit was always something that Hanes was eager to do. “We all want to put that uniform on, so we're all here for a reason,” said Hanes. “I think that being involved in the military is something that inspires me, inspires others, and it's something that I can be proud of.” At his most recent military Innovative Readiness Training (IRT) in Henderson, Kentucky, medical Airmen provided medical, dental, optical and veterinary care to underserved communities. Here, Hanes was presented with an opportunity that brought his military career and music profession into harmony. Hanes was asked to perform country songs for patients during the IRT. The experience brought him full circle, allowing him to fulfill multiple dreams at once. He was making a difference, not just as a nurse, but on stage as a country singer as well. “Being able to sit there and sing for an hour and a half [in] uniform, representing my country, playing a bunch of covers but entertaining all the patients, [did] a lot for me as far as putting the uniform on,” said Hanes. Hanes is now living three lives. At his day job, he is a pediatric surgery nurse at Valley Children’s Hospital, providing healthcare and connection to kids in need. In his free time, Hanes continues to write country songs, connecting with audiences through music and performance. Finally, one weekend a month, Hanes puts on his uniform and serves his country as an officer with the 144th Medical Group, providing medical care to service members. Through his years of dedication to his musical craft, his commitment to completing nursing school, and his burning desire to serve in the military, Hanes shows that strength and readiness is not built overnight. Hanes faced hardship along the way and proved that serving his country with the 144th Fighter Wing does not mean sacrificing his lifelong goals and ambitions. Instead, his journey and experiences as a nurse, Airman and musician have cultivated a spirit of multi-capability and devotion, allowing him to pursue his passions while continuing to serve others. He has been an example to others that personal, professional, and recreational development are all essential in shaping multi-capable Airmen. “Being able to work in this environment and train gives me the confidence to be a nurse in the civilian world, be a nurse in the military and be able to perform [as a] professional entertainer and country artist,” said Hanes. “They are all intertwined. My music reflects all the emotions I feel and the things I see as a nurse, and those experiences are reflected in my music.”

articles.title: Florida and Ohio Guard Units Strengthen Communications Partnership
articles.body:
JACKSONVILLE AIR NATIONAL GUARD BASE, Fla. - The 125th Fighter Wing (125th FW), Florida National Guard, recently joined forces with the 220th Engineering Installation Squadron (220th EIS), Ohio National Guard, to improve communications infrastructure, strengthen mission readiness and provide hands-on training for Airmen.

Airmen from the 220th Engineering Installation Squadron, which specializes in capabilities such as network infrastructure, communications systems installation and maintenance, and spectrum analysis, traveled to the Jacksonville Air National Guard Base, Florida, in July to assess and document its existing communications infrastructure, serving as an opportunity to integrate and provide expert support.

“We are documenting the layout of the communications infrastructure currently in place,” said U.S. Air Force 1st Lt. Grant Warren, a cyberspace operations engineer assigned to the 220th EIS. “We are making sure it’s properly labeled and accurately updated within the digital repository used by communications squadrons and engineering installation units across the service.”

The team’s work includes tracing communications pathways between facilities, confirming cable routes, reviewing labels and updating infrastructure records.

Accurate documentation is critical when communications systems are damaged or disrupted. If a cable is cut or a building experiences an outage, technicians must quickly determine where the problem occurred and how it affects the broader network.

Having keen and accurate insight into the communications infrastructure keeps the base out of the dark, said Warren.

“We may know that it starts in one building and ends in another, but we need to know what happens in between,” Warren said. “Having a better understanding of that infrastructure increases our strategic capabilities when it comes to the mission.”

The assessment also supports long-term planning. By understanding which pathways and resources are currently available, the 125th FW can make informed decisions about future communications requirements, infrastructure upgrades and support for new mission systems.

Reliable communications enable command and control, aircraft operations, maintenance, logistics and coordination with military and civilian partners. According to Warren, that makes communications infrastructure a critical part of mission success.

“Without communications, many operational missions would not be possible,” Warren said. “We provide that capability, and it’s a critical linchpin to have individuals who are capable of meeting the standards, ensuring that missions can go uninterrupted.”

This project also gives junior Airmen new experiences outside their normal day-to-day practice, giving them a greater sense of the capabilities and expectations of the communications squadron’s mission.

“It’s important to do the job right the first time, because that means less work for the Airmen who come after us,” said Airman 1st Class Jacob Brommeland, a radar, airfield and weather system specialist assigned to the 220th EIS.

Brommeland said serving as a multi-capable Airman broadens his experience and gives him opportunities to work with his hands while learning different parts of the mission.

The partnership demonstrates one of the National Guard’s key strengths: the ability to share expertise and resources across states. The 125th FW gained a clearer understanding of its communications network, while the 220th EIS received realistic training in a differing operational landscape.

By working together, both units improved their capabilities and contributed to a force that is always ready and always there.

articles.title: Building the 926th Wing from within: Development and Training Flight shapes future Airmen
articles.body:
For new recruits in the 926th Wing, their journey starts long before basic military training. Before ever setting foot onto the drill pad, these future Airmen are already learning exactly what it takes to succeed in the Air Force Reserve.

Serving as the catalyst for this transition, the wing’s Development and Training Flight bridges the gap between civilian life and operational military service. By coming in regularly alongside current wing members, trainees get a firsthand glimpse into their future. During this time, they are introduced to the core tenets of military life, learning essential customs and courtesies, drill procedures, and rank structure to establish a baseline of knowledge.

However, the 926th Wing program goes one step further with an initiative specifically designed to start building the wing from within. Beyond military fundamentals, trainees also embed with operational squadrons to gain firsthand experience with units they may eventually join.

"The Development and Training Flight is built for newly enlisted reservists that come into our wing," said Tech. Sgt. Bench Riche Lagus, 926th Wing D&TF program coordinator. "It helps them prepare for BMT and tech school, but it also helps them get integrated with the wing that they're about to work for.”

Trainees recently observed the 555th Rapid Engineer Deployable Heavy Operational Repair Squadron Engineers and traveled to Creech Air Force Base to witness security forces field operations.

For trainees like Abril Fonseca, a future vehicle mechanic with the 555th RED HORSE, this early exposure eases the transition into military life and provides a tangible goal.

"It’s cool to see what our day-to-day is going to look like," Fonseca said. "Everybody is just so pumped.”

Establishing a common baseline can be a challenge as trainees enter the flight with different levels of experience, from recent high school graduates to those with established civilian careers. As they move through the program, they rely on one another to learn military expectations and adjust to their new environment.

"The other trainees around me that have been there longer helped me out," Fonseca said. "It's a cycle; the people who have been here the longest help the newbies out, and then we just carry that on.”

Alongside military fundamentals and wing integration, physical readiness remains a cornerstone of the D&TF curriculum. The program incorporates monthly fitness tests, group workouts, and participation in wing fitness events to familiarize trainees with Air Force fitness standards.

This proactive approach ensures recruits arrive at basic training already equipped with the physical resilience required for military service. For many trainees, the group environment provides the exact motivation they need.

"I was not good at working out consistently before I got to the flight," Fonseca said. "But now it feels like I can actually do it. What makes it better for me is that I have my teammates around me supporting and pushing me.”

To learn more about serving with the 926th Wing and opportunities in the Air Force Reserve visit AirForce.com/Reserve. If you are interested in enlisting contact a local Air Force Reserve recruiter or visit www.airforce.com/find-a-recruiter.

articles.title: Total Force, one mission: AFRC and Georgia ANG break new ground at 2026 EO training conference
articles.body:
ROBINS AIR FORCE BASE, Ga. — Nearly 100 Equal Opportunity professionals from around the Total Force gathered at Robins Air Force Base June 22-26 for the 2026 Air Force Reserve Command Equal Opportunity Training Conference, an event that made history by integrating Reserve, Guard and civilian components for the first time.

Hosted by the Headquarters Air Force Reserve Command, the week-long conference brought together leaders ranging from technical sergeants to lieutenant colonels, representing 18 Air Force Reserve wings alongside their Georgia Air National Guard counterparts. The event carried the theme "LOCKED IN: Mission Mindset, with a Culture of Accountability," a deliberate signal that the career field is tying its work directly to warfighting readiness.

While the conference satisfies an annual training requirement, Chief Master Sgt. DeBlair Tate, EO MAJCOM Functional Manager, who served as the host, said the real purpose runs deeper.

"The true why is about taking care of our people," Tate said. "EO professionals operate in the trenches every day dealing with complex human issues. We need to make sure our team is equipped with the right tools, the latest strategies and the confidence to advise our commanders effectively.”

That focus, she said, comes back to the Airmen the career field serves. "At the end of the day, it is about empowering our EO pros so they can ensure every Airman is supported and focused on the mission.”

The career field meets for training every year, usually alternating between a larger worldwide event and a smaller MAJCOM-specific Reserve gathering. In-between years, like 2026, have traditionally followed a familiar script, but this year broke from it.

"The Guard actually reached out to us to see about teaming up, and we thought it was a great opportunity to join forces and work together," she said. "We did not just invite them as guests; we fully integrated.”

As host, Tate welcomed Maj. Luz Delannoy, ANG Readiness Center program manager, Master Sgt. Antoinette Murphy, GA ANG EO specialist and their team, a partnership she said elevated the depth and reality of the week's discussions. Paired with this year's theme, the collaboration changed the tone of the conference.

"The energy was just different this year," Tate said. "We moved past just talking about administrative processes and had real, gritty conversations about how the EO mission directly impacts warfighting readiness, and how we hold ourselves accountable to that standard."

Tate said the career field functions as the pulse of an installation's climate, operating in environments where the right answer is rarely obvious.

"Our folks operate in the gray areas, which are complex environments where there is not always an easy textbook answer," she said. "Getting everyone in one room ensures we are all rowing in the same direction and providing consistent, high-level counsel to our leadership. That is how we get better at dismantling barriers before they ever impact the mission.”

One of the week's defining moments did not happen in a classroom. Midway through the conference, the group came together for a morning physical training session, putting nearly 100 leaders on the track to sweat, encourage one another and bond outside the briefing environment.

"It was an incredible morale booster and really cemented that Total Force feeling," Tate said. "The genuine connections made on the track and in the hallways were just as valuable as the formal training.”

For Tech. Sgt. Chandra O'Bryant, EO director for the 908th Flying Training Wing and one of the career field's newest members, the week delivered exactly the kind of insight she came for. Drawing on experienced professionals from across the Reserve and Guard gave her tools she could carry home.

"I appreciated their different perspectives, engagement, collaboration, leadership tools, and processes that I can implement within my own wing," O'Bryant said.

The PT session tested that lesson in real time.

"At first glance going into the PT session, I thought I wouldn't make it through and survive," she said. "When considering all the individual exercises and reps that were given was overwhelming, but I quickly realized that this was a team effort. It was a reminder that resilience, teamwork, and accountability extend beyond our duty within our career field. Pushing ourselves together to get the mission completed."

For Master Sgt. Lorenzo E. Franklin, 403rd Wing EO superintendent and member of the AFRC EO Executive Team, the conference represented years of investment. He has helped plan the MAJCOM conference twice, and he traces that commitment back to his first conference as a young professional in 2019.

"I saw then what I wanted out of a training conference," Franklin said. "Instead of complaining, I chose to become a part of the solution.”

That decision led him to join the planning effort in 2023 alongside former Program Manager Ms. Renita Duncan and Tate, work that carried into the 2024 conference. By 2026, the scope had expanded to include the ANG.

"We brainstormed, collaborated, agreed, disagreed, laughed, became frustrated and worked hard," Franklin said. "The ideas became a plan, the plan was executed, and the execution produced a successful MAJCOM Training Conference for the AFRC and ANG.”

Franklin also noted there was a clear return on that investment stating, "I took back more confidence and a greater desire to see my EO office at the 403rd Wing and the AFRC EO career field grow in knowledge and increased morale.”

The 2026 conference offered a template for what Total Force integration can look like when components stop working in parallel and start working as one.

"No matter the component, our mission mindset is exactly the same," Tate said.

articles.title: Meet a Deployer: U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Dominique Johnson Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations Religious Affairs Airman
articles.body:
U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Dominique Johnson serves on the Resiliency Team at Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations (AFMAO) as a Religious Affairs Airman. In a mission defined by dignity, honor, and respect; Johnson provides emotional, spiritual and relational support to the Airmen who carry out the solemn responsibility of honoring fallen service members and supporting their families. In this “Meet the Deployer” spotlight, Johnson reflects on the purpose, challenges and lasting impact of serving in this uniquely meaningful environment.

What were your initial thoughts or feelings when you received your assignment to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations?

“When I received notification of my assignment to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations, I was initially nervous. It was unlike any mission I had previously been part of, and I understood the emotional weight and zero-fail nature of the work. I also did not know whether I had what it took to work alongside those in a morgue, given the unique environment and the level of composure it requires.”

“At the same time, I felt a deep sense of responsibility and commitment. I wanted to ensure I was fully prepared to contribute in whatever capacity the mission required.”

Can you describe your role and what a typical day looks like for you and your team?

“As a Religious Affairs Airman assigned to the Resiliency Team, my role centers on providing emotional and relational support to AFMAO members. A typical day may involve facilitating one of our resiliency events, such as morning meditation; teaching or briefing on a specific topic; leading a devotion; offering counseling; or simply being present and building meaningful relationships with the team.”

“Our focus is to ensure members have consistent support and access to resources as they carry out this unique and demanding mission.”

What is the biggest misconception people have about the mission you perform here?

“One of the biggest misconceptions about the AFMAO mission is that the work is strictly procedural or administrative. Every action taken here is deeply intentional, compassionate, and centered on honoring the fallen and supporting their families.”

“People often do not realize the level of emotional resilience, teamwork and care that goes into every step of the process. Our mission is not just about execution, it is about dignity, respect and ensuring no family walks through this experience alone.”

The AFMAO mission is centered on providing ‘Dignity, Honor, and Respect’ to the fallen and ‘Care, Service, and Support’ to the families of the fallen. What does that mantra mean to you personally?

“To me, the mantra of providing dignity, honor and respect to the fallen, as well as care, service and support to their families, carries deeply personal meaning. It reminds me that every individual who comes through AFMAO is someone’s loved one, and every family is facing one of the most difficult moments of their lives.”

“This mission calls us to show up with compassion and intentionality while also caring for ourselves and those around us. It reflects the spirit ofohana, the understanding that family extends beyond blood and that no one should carry their burdens alone.”

What is the most challenging aspect of serving in this unique and emotionally demanding environment?

“The most challenging aspect is balancing the weight of the mission with the need to care for yourself and those around you. Every day requires emotional resilience. You are supporting a mission centered on loss, honoring the fallen, and being present for families during some of the most difficult moments of their lives.”

“That responsibility can be heavy, and it does not always end when the workday does. Finding the right balance between showing up fully for the mission, maintaining your own well-being and supporting your teammates is one of the most significant challenges. At the same time, that is part of what makes this work meaningful. We lean on one another, stay grounded, and make sure we can continue serving with compassion and strength.”

Conversely, what has been the most rewarding or fulfilling moment for you during this deployment?

“The most rewarding part of this deployment has been witnessing the impact of our support on both the families and the team here at AFMAO. There is a profound sense of fulfillment in knowing that even small actions, a conversation, a check-in, or simply being present, can make a meaningful difference for someone carrying a heavy emotional load.”

“Being part of a mission where every effort contributes to honoring the fallen and supporting those who care for them has been incredibly humbling.”

How do you and your fellow Airmen support one another through the difficulties of this sacred duty?

“We support one another both on and off duty. Whether it is leaving encouraging notes on each other’s doors, conducting wellness checks, having dinner or cooking together, volunteering as a group, or even playing bingo, we are intentional about the time we share.”

“These moments help ensure no one carries the weight of the mission alone, while also giving each of us space to recharge and care for ourselves. That balance of connection, care, and personal grounding is what keeps us strong as a team.”

How has this experience changed your perspective on military service, life, or the concept of the ‘Air Force family’?

“Serving at AFMAO shows you just how interconnected we all are, every Airman, every family and every story. The mission reminds you that service goes far beyond the uniform. It is about humanity, compassion and showing up for one another in ways that truly matter.”

“This experience has made me more intentional about appreciating the people around me, valuing time and recognizing the impact we have on each other, both in and out of uniform.”

Is there a particular story or moment from your time here that has had a lasting impact on you?

“A moment that will stay with me forever was my very first dignified transfer. From the sound of the aircraft landing to seeing the precision and care in every detail, the flag perfectly placed over the transfer case, the prayer offered and the carry team moving in complete unity, it was unlike anything I had ever experienced.”

“Standing there and witnessing the reverence of the process, I felt the full weight of the sacrifice represented in that moment. It reminded me of the words on the bridge: ‘All gave some; some gave all.’ That experience changed me. It grounded me in the meaning of this mission and in the responsibility, we carry every time we honor someone who gave everything.”

What is the single most important thing you want the public to know about the fallen service members you care for and the Airmen who serve alongside you?

“The single most important thing I want the public to know is that every fallen service member we care for is honored as someone’s loved one, not simply as a uniform or a name, but as a whole life filled with relationships, memories, and sacrifice.”

“Their service is treated with the utmost dignity from the moment they arrive, and every step of the process reflects the respect they deserve. Behind every dignified transfer, every detail and every moment of care is a team of Airmen showing up with intention, humility and a commitment to give their absolute best in honoring those who gave everything.”

Through work on the AFMAO Resiliency Team, Johnson helps sustain the Airmen behind one of the Air Force’s most solemn missions. The role reflects a simple truth: caring for the fallen and their families also requires caring for those who perform that duty each day. By fostering connection and resilience, the team helps AFMAO personnel continue serving with the compassion and professionalism the mission demands.

articles.title: 62d AW pioneers first sUAS training for C-17 inspections in AMC
articles.body:
JOINT BASE LEWIS-MCCHORD, Wash – 62d Maintenance Group personnel completed a four-day, hands-on training program on the Skydio X10D small unmanned aircraft system at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Sept. 3, 2026. The training, which is the first of its kind in Air Mobility Command, included classroom instruction and practical applications of the system, introducing new, timely and safe capabilities into routine maintenance operations.

The 62d Airlift Wing is the first unit within AMC to fully implement a dedicated sUAS training and qualification program for maintenance inspections on the C-17 Globemaster III aircraft. The program is designed to be a streamlined, standardized course that can be easily replicated throughout AMC, and used as a base for further sUAS implementation.

The 62d MXG employs the Skydio X10D sUAS to conduct exterior and elevated visual inspections on the wing’s fleet of C-17s. The initiative aims to significantly reduce inspection timelines while reducing safety hazards associated with personnel conducting visual assessments.

“As a crew chief, I’m out on the line working on the C-17, which is a huge aircraft,” said Staff Sgt. Marcuscio McCampbell, 62d Aircraft Maintenance Squadron crew chief. “Being able to use the drone to perform duties like upper wing inspections, that normally take much longer, saves us time and helps the maintainers of tomorrow.”

Implementation of the X10D is not a new concept; the sUAS has already been fielded for aircraft maintenance inspections across the Department of the Air Force. Furthermore, Skydio liaisons to the Air Force introduced the system to Team McChord in 2025, demonstrating its ability to complete C-17 inspections in approximately 40 minutes. Now, the 62d MXG has a standardized training program that qualifies maintainers for C-17 inspections with the system.

“Drone technologies are expanding fast,” said Tech. Sgt. Austen Russell, 62d MXG maintenance qualification training program instructor. “I think it’s good for us to learn about them and autonomous operations, that way we’re not sending our people into harm’s way. We’re saving our people time and eliminating risks.”

Decreasing inspection times and removing excess dangers for personnel with the sUAS program increases the wing’s operational agility and accelerates crew readiness, especially in austere or expeditionary environments where specialized ground equipment may be unavailable. By utilizing the high-resolution cameras and thermal sensors equipped on the X10D, maintainers can rapidly assess entire aircraft in detail from safe ground positions.

“Having people that are qualified on using this technology is going to be a steppingstone,” said McCampbell. “We can start using drones for all types of things, it’s not necessarily just going to be aircraft maintenance.”

As the lead unit implementing sUAS maintenance training within AMC, the 62d AW is establishing standardized qualification models, flightline operating procedures, and safety protocol to serve as a scalable model across the larger mobility force. The 62d MXG is setting the standard, utilizing innovative technology to accelerate aircraft turnaround times and project rapid global mobility more efficiently.

articles.title: Turning Virtual Wrenches: Alamo Wing Reimagines Maintenance Training
articles.body:
Inside a quiet, air-conditioned room, Senior Airman Emerson Plewacki slides a black virtual reality headset over his eyes. Instantly, the quiet room vanishes, replaced by the towering, grey fuselage of a C-5M Super Galaxy.

For Plewacki, a 433rd Aircraft Maintenance Squadron aero repair journeyman, this digital flight line is a playground of possibilities. In this virtual world, there is no scorching South Texas heat, no deafening roar of departing aircraft, and critically, no risk of making a million-dollar mistake.

"Going to tech school, you have big classes, so getting everyone reps is very difficult," said Plewacki, who recently transitioned to the Air Force Reserve from active duty. "When you do the VR program, the smaller eight- to 10-person classes really help by letting you get a lot of reps and individual training. You do it as many times as you need to feel comfortable, and then when we get out to the aircraft, it goes a lot smoother."

Plewacki is among the third class of maintainers benefiting from the 433rd Maintenance Group’s virtual reality driven Maintenance Qualification Training Program, an initiative preparing Airmen for high-tempo missions today while transforming training methods for the future. The latest course got underway in mid-August.

"We currently live in a resource-constrained environment," said Col. Michael Egbalic, 433rd MXG commander. "Whether it’s people, planes, parts, or money, anywhere we can save certainly helps us move the football forward, one yard at a time."

The Alamo Wing operates in a uniquely demanding environment, supporting dual-flying operations for both its operational airlift squadron and the formal training unit responsible for training all C-5 crews in the Air Force. This high-tempo schedule places natural constraints on aircraft availability for ground training.

"We’ve got to think of ways to overcome this," Egbalic said. “The VR program allows us to operate virtually without the use of an aircraft. It saves us money, saves us time, and gets qualified maintainers back to the flight line faster to keep our jets flying."

The financial returns are already compounding. Tech. Sgt. Martin Calles, a 433rd Aircraft Maintenance Squadron crew chief and one of the lead instructors in the VR program, tracked the metrics from a recent class of nine students. In just 72 academic days, practicing tasks in the virtual world instead of a running aircraft saved more than $152,000 in fuel and equipment costs.

"If you multiply that across a full year, we’re looking at well over $500,000 in savings," Calles said. "And that doesn’t even account for the wear and tear we’ve prevented on the aircraft or the components we didn't damage through student error."

The program’s dynamic learning pace also allowed the most recent class to graduate two weeks ahead of schedule, returning capable, flight-line-ready maintainers back to their units early to support operations.

Beyond cost savings, 433rd MXG leaders say the program is actively helping to curate a more adaptable Reserve force of the future. In 2027, the Air Force plans to consolidate several maintenance career fields, requiring Airmen to qualify on a broader range of skills.

"With an AFSC merger, you're going to have expanded training requirements," said Chief Master Sgt. Byron Frost, 433rd MXG senior enlisted leader. "The VR program is a huge leap in capability because it allows people to train on their own, get the general lay of the land, and build muscle memory before they do the actual evaluation. It’s like finding a way to get players more practice before a football game without risking them getting hurt."

The technology is also proving highly effective for developing Airmen transitioning to the C-5 from other airframes. Recently, five Alamo Wing Air Reserve Technicians who came from working on fighters used the VR program to study the Super Galaxy’s massive and complex digitized systems, accelerating their qualification training by weeks.

Non-maintenance personnel are also using the system. Under the "multi-capable Airman" concept, Airmen with medical and planning specialties learned basic safety and ground operations, while newly commissioned officers with limited mechanical background used VR to better understand flight line dynamics and lead more effectively.

"This younger generation of Airmen is highly technological," Egbalic said. "They learn from video games, YouTube, and electronic media. This bridges that learning curve in a tactile way."

Egbalic also emphasized how the program helps preserve and protect Reservists’ ability to serve by streamlining training. He noted focused VR training respects their time by reducing administrative flight line delays so they can learn more efficiently during tight training windows.

The success has caught the attention of the wider C-5M Super Galaxy community. Recently, active-duty maintainers from the 515th Air Mobility Operations Wing based out of Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam in Hawaii traveled to San Antonio to train with the Alamo Wing. They leveraged the VR setup to get required training reps they cannot easily get at their home station. Other Air Force Reserve Command C-5 wings have also expressed interest in sending their Airmen to the program.

"We want to be the central hub outside of technical training for C-5M Super Galaxy maintenance," Calles said. "We can help create versatile, capable Airmen at a much faster rate."

Despite the program's massive success, it faces a primary hurdle: manpower. Currently, the instructors managing and running the VR lab are pulled "out of hide," meaning they split their time with primary flight line duties.

"Having authorized, dedicated instructors for this system would be a massive force multiplier," Frost said. "It would allow us to keep software and modules updated, expand our class sizes, and offer this world-class training to the rest of the AFRC enterprise."

Leaders overseeing the program have been clear about one key factor: virtual reality is not a replacement for turning wrenches on a real aircraft. However, it is an accelerant to higher quality, more efficient training on live aircraft.

"The virtual world cuts out the noise, the paperwork, and the prep time so we can focus strictly on the task at hand," Calles said. "It gets our Airmen to a higher level of proficiency before they ever step onto the flight line. In today's Air Force, that's how we stay ready."

articles.title: 934th Civil Engineer Squadron hosts training with U.S. Navy Reservist
articles.body:
There was nothing glamorous about the task.

It involved a high-voltage cable, a specialized tool, and precision.

Airmen from the 934th Civil Engineer Squadron (CES) and 11 Sailors from U.S. Northwest Regional Maintenance Center (NWRMC) Minneapolis worked side by side during the September 2026 unit training assembly. The two services conducted hands-on training on electrical systems used to establish and sustain bare-base operations. For someone inexperienced with the task, preparing the cable by hand can take one to two hours.

They were surprised to learn their instructor was keeping a secret.

The same task, with the right training and a specialized tool, could take about five minutes.

Time is valuable.

At a forward operating location, where engineers may be responsible for building the infrastructure needed to support an operating force, time becomes part of the mission.

Senior Master Sgt. Kyle Sunne, 934th CES, knows that distinction well. The system the Airmen were demonstrating is designed for environments where an established electrical grid may not exist.

The Air Force is not the only service that knows what it means to build in an austere environment. “These guys work on land bases, and we work on bases at sea,” said Senior Chief Andrew McKay, NWRMC Minneapolis.

Despite the difference in typical work environments, the two services came together to strengthen their expeditionary engineering capabilities.

The training opportunity came to light when a retired 934th CES member Master Sgt. Tony Jarosz reached out to Sunne, prompting him to reach out to his Navy Reserve contacts.

“Well, you guys do pipefitting, though, right?” McKay asked.

“Well, and that’s just it. So we have all the other trades,” Sunne replied, before rattling off a list of possibilities.

“Pipefitting, I think, would be great,” McKay said. “Because everybody in the yards eventually gets voluntold to work on piping systems, pulling them apart, putting them back together.”

Sunne immediately jumped back in. “Yeah, and that would be great. Actually, we have quite a few very talented welders over here!”

While Sunne and McKay continued discussing future training opportunities, knives scraped away layers of insulation as Airmen and Sailors worked their way around the cable, carefully exposing the components needed for the connection.

After nearly an hour, they completed the tedious task.

That’s the moment when Tech. Sgt. Colin Western, 934th CES, electrical craftsman, reached for the specialized tool and began his final cable stripping demonstration.

A few minutes. A piece of cable. Ready to connect.

The cable was only one piece of the training. The larger objective was building something that could not be measured in feet of wire or minutes on a clock: the ability to understand, trust and work alongside another service before the mission requires it.

Sunne then stepped in to demonstrate the next step. In a bare-base scenario, he would use the load break elbow to connect the cable to the electrical distribution system.“If we show up to a bare-base site and are completing set up one team will work on laying out cable and making all of these connections. The base doesn’t have sustainable “permanent” power until this process is complete,” Sunne explained.

The Air Force may build bases on land and the Navy may work on them at sea, but the engineers on both sides are preparing for the same fundamental challenge: creating the infrastructure that allows the mission to move forward.

articles.title: Keeping the mission moving, one part at a time
articles.body:
MCCONNELL AIR FORCE BASE, Kan. – The sound of the flight line rolls through the 22nd Logistics Readiness Squadron’s aircraft parts store.

The deep rumble of KC-46A Pegasus and KC-135 Stratotanker engines carries into the building as aircraft come and go. Inside, forklifts move through the aisles while vertical lift modules rise and lower, moving trays of parts much like an industrial vending machine.

The large doors remain open, letting air flow through the facility and bringing in the Kansas heat. Under the warm tint of the overhead lights, personnel work between rows of green storage units, shelves, and equipment. When one of the units is opened, the smell of stored equipment and packaging escapes into the warehouse.

Among the units is one holding parts for the KC-46A Pegasus.

The storage unit contains a High Priority Mission Support Kit, commonly called a HIT-MIS kit. The mobile kits carry parts maintenance personnel are likely to need wherever KC-46 operations take them, allowing maintainers to access what they need without waiting for a part to be ordered and shipped.

That is why personnel are working through the kit.

OneHIT-MIS kit recently returned from an overseas location after supporting operations for approximately six months. Before it can be sent out again, its contents must reflect what maintenance needs.

Each year, supply and maintenance personnel review the parts being used and determine what should change. A part stocked in a quantity of two may only need one, while another may need more based on demand.

Those recommendations then move to Air Mobility Command A4, the staff directorate responsible for Logistics, Engineering, and Force Protection, which considers the needs of the KC-46 fleet as a whole.

“We take what maintenance wants, we give it to AMC A4, and they decide based on the whole fleet what kind of changes they’re going to do to a kit,” said Nadine Wiese, 22nd LRS aircraft parts store supervisor.

The process keeps the kits aligned across KC-46 locations.

“This kit, with the parts that are listed that are allowed to be in here, is the same kit that’s going to be at Fairchild [Air Force Base, Washington] and Pease [Air National Guard Base, New Hampshire] and any other [KC-46] base,” Wiese said.

Once the updated requirements make their way back to the base, the work moves from a conference room to the warehouse floor.

Personnel open the kit and work through its contents, checking parts and quantities against what it is supposed to carry. Items that no longer belong are identified, while other parts are prepared to be added.

The warehouse provides the equipment to do it.

Forklifts move the larger loads. Vertical lift modules bring trays of parts to the operator. Storage units can be moved and positioned for transport.

The work is physical, but what it supports happens somewhere else.

The kit may leave McConnell and spend months supporting operations at another location before returning to the warehouse. When it is gone, the people who prepared it may never know which part will eventually be needed; they only know that one may be. When that happens, the difference between having it in the kit and having to wait for it to arrive can reach beyond the parts store.

“If they don’t have the part here, then we have to wait for it to be ordered and delivered by [a] shipping company,” Wiese said.

Having the part already available means a maintainer can retrieve it, get it to the aircraft and continue the work instead of waiting for a shipment.

That is what the reconciliation is preparing for –not simply a complete inventory, but a kit ready for the next time it is needed.

Outside the open doors, another KC-46 or KC-135 moves along the flight line, its engines carrying through the warehouse.

Inside, the forklifts continue through the aisles, and the vertical lift modules keep moving trays into position as personnel prepare the kit for its next destination.

“It’s an effort to not stop the mission,” Wiese said. “They’re able to get the part from the kit, go install it on the plane, and get back to business.”

The aircraft may be the part of the mission people see and hear, but the work to keep them moving begins long before they leave the flight line.

articles.title: New targeting center strengthens capabilities for joint force deterrence
articles.body:
A new Air Force construction project at Joint Base Langley-Eustis is positioning the 363d Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Group to deliver faster, more integrated targeting intelligence to Air Force and joint warfighters operating in an increasingly contested global environment.

The 363d ISRG marked the opening of the facility during a ribbon-cutting ceremony in June, but the center’s significance extends beyond the event. The 90,470-square-foot facility consolidates targeting analysts, intelligence professionals, communications Airmen, cyber specialists and mission partners into a shared operational environment designed to improve collaboration across the Air Force Targeting Enterprise.

The new facility supports the group’s mission to provide target intelligence, expertise and advocacy to Air Force and joint warfighters. By bringing multiple intelligence disciplines together, the facility is intended to shorten the distance between raw data, target development, combat assessment and decision-making support for combatant commanders.

“I see this facility as a direct investment in the combat readiness and future of our Airmen. By bringing our teams together, we are accelerating our pursuit of the vital targeting outcomes that deliver a decisive advantage to the Joint force,” said Col. Christina Sheets, 363d ISRG commander. “This shared space allows our Airmen to integrate faster and solve complex targeting problems at the speed modern conflict demands. It enables Airmen to build the daily combat readiness that underpins deterrence; and should deterrence fail, deliver decisive results.”

The 363d ISRG directs elements of the Air Force Targeting Enterprise, which includes active-duty, Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard units across eight states. The new facility provides a common space for the 17th Intelligence Squadron, 36th Intelligence Squadron, 42nd Intelligence Squadron and 363d Intelligence Support Squadron, strengthening the group’s ability to support target system analysis, target vulnerability studies, intermediate and advanced target development, Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile support and combat assessment.

The center also enables greater integration of air operations center, Distributed Common Ground System and targeting functions on a common network. That integration is designed to support advanced battle management, ISR-to-targeting processes, kill chain automation and signals intelligence missions.

For Air Combat Command and the joint force, that capability matters because deterrence depends on credible, timely and precise information. Targeting intelligence helps commanders understand adversary systems, identify vulnerabilities and assess effects, giving warfighters the information they need to plan and execute operations with speed and accuracy.

The facility’s design reflects that operational demand. It includes an operations floor, training labs, team rooms, video teleconference suites, conference rooms and resiliency spaces. Those features are intended to give Airmen the environment, connectivity and proximity needed to solve complex targeting problems together rather than through separated work centers. For Senior Airman Kendall Mallory, a 17th IS all-source analyst, consolidating mission partners into one facility will help Airmen understand how their individual roles contribute to the broader targeting enterprise.

“Being spread across different buildings before made cohesion and communication between flights and squadrons more difficult,” Mallory said. “I think all the 363d ISRG being together in one building will create a closer relationship between us, and we will have a better understanding of everyone’s role in the 363d’s targeting enterprise and why what we do is so important.”

The center is also expected to improve Airman development by increasing daily access to subject-matter experts, mission partners and adjacent intelligence disciplines. For junior analysts, that proximity can turn routine coordination into real-time learning, allowing Airmen to see how their products connect to operational planning, command decisions and joint force requirements. As the group continues its transition into the facility, the focus remains on building a more connected targeting enterprise capable of supporting warfighters at the speed of modern conflict.

The ribbon cutting marked the formal opening of the facility, but its broader purpose is operational: giving Airmen the tools, space and integration needed to improve targeting intelligence, strengthen decision advantage and support deterrence across the joint force.

articles.title: Department of War, state agencies airlift support to Kauai after Hurricane Lowell
articles.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii — In the aftermath of Hurricane Lowell, Governor Josh Green requested military assistance to transport specialized utility vehicles from Hawaii Island to Kauai to assist with continued widespread power outages. This airlift was an integrated effort, coordinated between the U.S. Pacific Command, U.S. Air Force, Hawaii National Guard and Hawaii Emergency Management Agency, executed by the 15th Wing on Sept. 12 – 13, 2026.

Power outages began Monday as Hurricane Lowell approached Kauai. By 6:40 a.m. Tuesday, approximately 36,000 residents across the island were without electricity.

"I simply decided that we had to do everything possible to shorten the time to recovery, and partnering with the military and utilizing our National Guard on the ground has been a major addition to our state and county efforts," said Governor Green.

Utility trucks originally relocated from California to Hawaii Island in the wake of Tropical Cyclone Lala were loaded onto two Hickam-based C-17 Globemaster IIIs for transport. The equipment was flown from Hilo to Lihue to be repurposed on Kauai to restore essential services.

On the ground, Department of War Emergency Preparedness Liaison Officers and Hawaii National Guard members received the equipment. The airlift augmented support from the 74 members of the National Guard who are currently providing Kauai ground support in the wake of the storm.

“I feel the State of Hawaii Department of Defense is extremely fortunate to be located in such proximity to U.S. Pacific Command and the Pacific Air Forces which enables a rapid response and unity of effort in times of crisis," said Hawaii Adjutant General, Maj. Gen. Stephen Logan.

Transport of the utility vehicles will aid the approximate 6,800 residents that were still without power as of Sunday evening.

“We are committed to continuing support for our community members without power in whatever way we can,” said Col. Kyle Clinton, 15th Wing commander. “Supporting those that support us in times of emergency is why many of us chose to serve.”

These consolidated partnerships across Department of War and state agencies enable near real-time synergistic response capabilities to natural disasters across the Hawaiian Islands.

Imagery and video of this airlift and additional military support efforts in the wake of Hurricane Lowell are available on the official DVIDS feature page: https://www.dvidshub.net/feature/Hurricane-Lowell

articles.title: 163d RTS strengthens emergency management readiness through Phoenix EMBER
articles.body:
MARCH AIR RESERVE BASE, Calif. — Cadre from the 163d Civil Engineer Squadron sharpened the skills of emergency management Airmen across the Air Force and enhanced their ability to assess, collect and test hazardous materials in austere environments through the Emergency Management Battlefield Expeditionary Readiness course at the Regional Training Site, March Air Reserve Base, California, Aug. 31-Sept. 4, 2026.

Emergency management is a career field within civil engineering focused on preparing for, responding to, and recovering from emergencies and threats that could impact Air Force operations. One of EM’s major responsibilities is chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) defense. However, the career field encompasses much more. Airmen assess hazards, advise leadership, protect personnel, and help ensure missions can continue despite those threats.

According to cadre at the 163d RTS the emergency management career field is evolving from a static response force to toward a lighter, leaner expeditionary force, focused on addressing modern threats while enhancing its lethality. The 163d Attack Wing developed the course known as Phoenix EMBER in response to support that evolution and enhance the fundamental skills emergency management Airmen need to operate in deployed environments.

“Emergency management used to be very focused on extensive response processes and doing things the way that was the standard historically. Readiness was just responsive, reactive and very hazmat focused,” said Staff Sgt. Kiara Newland, 163d RTS cadre assigned to the 163d Emergency Management Flight, California Air National Guard. “Now we’re moving toward being more tactical and integrating standard operating procedures with more emphasis on interoperability, modernization, and actually adapting the processes we operate in instead of just maintaining historical procedures.”

During the course, Airmen learned to employ their technical skills and perform emergency management duties in an expeditionary environment. Training scenarios required Airmen to navigate to designated locations, identify potential hazards and targets, and perform decontamination operations as part of small, lightweight teams.

Many units do not have the time or resources to provide training on this scale. As a result, the 163d RTS and other training sites play a critical role in producing Mission Ready Airmen and serving as force multipliers.

This is the case for Senior Airman Tasia Dykstra-Cochrun, 185th Civil Engineer Squadron, Iowa Air National Guard.

“I come from a National Guard base and we don't have the capabilities to make the training courses or exercises to the extent they are giving to us here,” said Dykstra-Cochrun. “So, it's really helpful to participate in an exercise that mimics real-world conditions.”

Airmen like Dykstra-Cochrun depend on the RTS because it supports a number of civil engineer readiness and contingency-training requirements through Phoenix EMBER, the Rapid Damage Repair course, bivouac training and other programs.

Emergency management subject matter experts from the 163d RTS, headed by Master Sgt. Daniel Johnston, 163d Emergency Management Flight, California Air National Guard, developed Phoenix EMBER over six years with an emphasis on expeditionary readiness and alignment with emerging career field functions.

“We take pride in knowing this course and other courses taught here at the RTS are preparing Airmen to provide an effective response when called upon and affect change across the force as our career field continues to evolve,” said Johnston.

Through RTS's role as a force-wide training hub, more than 1,000 civil engineer Airmen receive training annually to support Air Force and Space Force installations. Bringing realistic, mission-focused training to Airmen from across the force ensuring civil engineer Airmen ready to respond to evolving threats and support future operations.

articles.title: I am The 908th: Tech. Sgt. Asyndace Turner
articles.body:
Tech. Sgt. Asyndace Turner, 908th Operations Support Squadron Aircrew Flight Equipment assistant noncommissioned officer in charge of quality assurance, oversees program management and compliance within Aircrew Flight Equipment.

Turner was recently recognized as the 908th Flying Training Wing Noncommissioned Officer of the Quarter for the 4th Quarter of 2025.

“It was a complete surprise,” said Turner. “I was really shocked when I found out because, to me, I was just doing my job.”

Turner became the first Aircrew Flight Equipment instructor to assist Survival, Evasion, Resistance and Escape specialists with water survival training. She then trained eight additional instructors, expanding the program’s capacity and helping equip 120 aircrew members with critical survival skills.

Her efforts also contributed to a 100% readiness rate for protective equipment, helping the unit reach optimal preparedness for fiscal year 2027 deployments a year ahead of schedule.

Turner serves as an Air Reserve Technician, a dual-status position that combines full-time federal civilian employment with military service in the Air Force Reserve. ARTs maintain simultaneous membership in the Reserve while performing their civilian duties in support of the Air Force mission.

For Turner, what became a potential Air Force career initially began as an opportunity to pursue her education.

As a first-generation college student, Turner joined the Air Force with the goal of taking advantage of its educational opportunities while working toward her aspiration of eventually becoming a doctor. As her career progressed, however, her reasons for serving evolved.

“What I didn’t anticipate was how much I would grow to appreciate the Air Force itself,” said Turner. “Over time, I fell in love with the structure, values, opportunities, and sense of purpose that come with serving. What initially started as a way to accomplish my educational goals ultimately became something I could see myself making a career out of.”

That growth has also translated into greater leadership responsibilities within AFE.

Transitioning into the assistant NCOIC of Quality Assurance role allowed Turner to move beyond technical proficiency and take greater responsibility for shop compliance and Airman development.

When the 908th FTW transitioned to the MH-139A Grey Wolf helicopter, Turner identified an opportunity to improve training and continuity within the shop.

“I identified knowledge gaps when transitioning to the MH-139A helicopter,” said Turner. “To fix this, I implemented a quarterly rotation plan that not only reduced bottlenecks, but improved confidence in the mission. This initiative directly reinforced inspection standards, streamlined training, and ensured seamless continuity between full-timers and TRs.”

Outside of her military responsibilities, Turner enjoys traveling, fitness, attending concerts, spending time with friends and family, reading, and trying new recipes.

Her passion for travel began with an opportunity provided through her Air Force service. Her first international trip took her to Germany, an experience that sparked an interest in new places and cultures. She has also recently developed an interest in vlogging and hopes to document some of those experiences.

“Being a part of the Air Force means being a part of something greater than myself,” said Turner. “It has challenged me to grow personally and professionally, introduced me to people and experiences I may never have encountered otherwise, and given me opportunities that have shaped the person I am today.”

Looking to the future, Turner remains committed to building a lasting career in the Air Force, with a strong focus on developing herself both as an Airman and as a leader. She attributes much of her personal and professional growth to the diverse opportunities and experiences the Air Force has offered her.

“To me, serving also means continuously striving to become better—not only for myself, but for the people I work alongside and the mission we support,” said Turner. “I hope to continue making the Air Force a career, growing as an Airman and leader, and eventually earning a commission so I can serve and make an impact at an even higher level.”

Outside of her military responsibilities, Turner enjoys traveling, fitness, attending concerts, spending time with friends and family, reading, and trying new recipes.

Her passion for travel began with an opportunity provided through her Air Force service. Her first international trip took her to Germany, an experience that sparked an interest in new places and cultures. She has also recently developed an interest in vlogging and hopes to document some of those experiences.

“Being a part of the Air Force means being a part of something greater than myself,” said Turner. “It has challenged me to grow personally and professionally, introduced me to people and experiences I may never have encountered otherwise, and given me opportunities that have shaped the person I am today.”

Looking to the future, Turner remains committed to building a lasting career in the Air Force, with a strong focus on developing herself both as an Airman and as a leader. She attributes much of her personal and professional growth to the diverse opportunities and experiences the Air Force has offered her.

“To me, serving also means continuously striving to become better—not only for myself, but for the people I work alongside and the mission we support,” said Turner. “I hope to continue making the Air Force a career, growing as an Airman and leader, and eventually earning a commission so I can serve and make an impact at an even higher level.”

articles.title: Wyoming Air National Guard to host Discovery Day 2026: A Salute to STEAM
articles.body:
CHEYENNE, Wyo. Sept. 16, 2026 — The Wyoming Air National Guard will host Discovery Day 2026: A Salute to STEAM, a free hands-on science, technology, engineering, art and math event for school-age students, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sept. 24 at 217 Dell Range Blvd. in Cheyenne.

Attendance is arranged through schools and educators. The event is not open to the general public as a walk-in event, and students may not attend without a registered educator.

Discovery Day is an annual event designed to inspire youth, spark creativity, encourage innovation and show the possibilities awaiting the rising generation.

Students will enter a large aircraft hangar and explore dozens of exhibits demonstrating how STEAM and career and technical education fields are applied in the workforce. Larger displays, including aircraft and ground vehicles, will be staged outside the hangar. Planned activities include drones, simulators, virtual reality, robotics, live electrical demonstrations, computer programming, artificial intelligence, aviation and static aircraft displays.

More than 25 exhibitors are scheduled to take part, among them Laramie County Community College, the University of Wyoming, Eastern Wyoming College, Aims Community College, Spartan College, United Airlines, the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the Wyoming Army National Guard and the Wyoming Air National Guard, along with local businesses, medical providers, construction firms and artists.

Lunch will be provided free of charge to all participants and served from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Pizza, cookies, water and Gatorade will be available. Attendees with special dietary needs should plan to bring a lunch.

Educators must register their groups in advance so organizers can plan logistics and support each group's needs. Registration is available at https://forms.osi.apps.mil/r/CKiUG0y9rA.

Adults should bring a school-issued identification card, which grants entry to the installation without additional screening. Students 17 and younger are granted access provided they arrive on the bus with their group.

Homeschool students are welcome, but base access must be arranged in advance. Homeschool parents and teachers must contact the event point of contact to be added to the Entry Authority List, which is required for access to the installation. Walk-up access is not guaranteed on the day of the event; however, the access validation process takes approximately 15 minutes.

For questions about registration or the Entry Authority List, contact Staff Sgt. Ophelia Danso at ophelia.danso@us.af.mil or (307) 773-6724. Additional event information is available at (406)-546-5116.

Media wishing to cover Discovery Day should contact Wyoming Air National Guard Public Affairs via email 153.AW.Public.Affairs.Org@us.af.mil or (307) 772-6424 no later than September 22 to arrange escort and base access. Reminder, drones are prohibited.

articles.title: Bases unite through soccer to honor fallen, remember 9/11
articles.body:
CREECH AIR FORCE BASE, Nev. — Eight military soccer teams from Air Force and Space Force installations across the country came together in the Las Vegas area Sept. 11-13 for the inaugural 9/11 memorial soccer tournament, bringing service members together through competition and remembrance.

The tournament opened with a memorial ceremony honoring the lives lost during the attacks and recognizing the sacrifices made by military members and first responders in the years since.

“There was a huge effort from the team, and from Vegas as a whole, to make this event happen,” said 1st Lt. Patric Naranjo, 17th Attack Squadron MQ-9 pilot. “We made sure to have a wreath for those lost and included a moment of silence to emphasize how important this memorial ceremony is for us. Everybody plays a role to make sure an attack like that never happens again. So the ceremony is a reminder to instill that role.”

After the ceremony, participants gathered for the national anthem and remarks from a chaplain, giving players, coaches and family members a chance to reflect on the day’s significance before the competition began.

“Sept. 11 means something a little different for me because I was born and raised in Ghana, Africa,” said Master Sgt. Edward Adade, Nellis team coach. “After coming to the States, I actually joined the military to serve in support of what happened during the attacks, and I was able to deploy to Afghanistan to support that mission.”

Teams representing Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota; Vandenberg Space Force Base, California; Luke Air Force Base, Arizona; Hill Air Force Base, Utah; Joint Base San Antonio, Texas; Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico; Edwards Air Force Base, California; and Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, participated in the three-day tournament.

While the teams competed for a championship on the field, the tournament also gave service members from geographically separated installations a chance to build relationships and strengthen connections within the Air Force and Space Force community.

The tournament concluded with a championship match between the Nellis and JBSA teams. After three days of competition, the JBSA team claimed the tournament championship.

Beyond the final score, the tournament provided a shared opportunity to honor those who were lost and recognize those who answered the call to serve following the Sept. 11 attacks.

“We wanted to do something that hasn’t been done before to commemorate 9/11,” said Tech. Sgt. Joseph Adu, founder of the tournament’s organizational team. “There is no tournament on base such as this, and we wanted to give other bases the chance to participate as well.”
