articles.title: Eyes on the Airfield: AFIT sUAS Research Aims to Accelerate Combat Recovery
articles.body:
The Air Force Institute of Technology is confronting a high-stakes reality: Airmen Engineers operate in harm’s way working to recover damaged airfields. They confront this task often without a clear picture of the hazards present, creating higher operational risks and slowing the Air Force's ability to regenerate combat power.The Air ForceCivil Engineer community has spent more than a decade building toward a solution, and AFIT researchers are now working to close the gaps that remain with rigorous academic and technical research.

Unexploded ordnance, possible chemical or biological contamination, cratered pavement and debris are all hazards that Airmen Engineers must be prepared for while recovering airfields after an attack. For that reason, AFIT researchers are looking beyond traditional post-attack assessment methods to speed up recovery and safeguard Airmen.

Small unmanned aircraft systems may be part of the answer AFIT is working toward. A team of Civil Engineer graduate students, backed by faculty in developmental and digital systems engineering, is building on more than a decade of Civil Engineer investment in sUAS-based airfield reconnaissance. This cohort has added rigorous graduate-level research and, notably, a fixed-wing component alongside multirotor systems.

“This effort supports the Air Force’s need to rapidly open, operate, and recover airbases in contested environments,” said Capt. Ross C. Jurek, a Graduate Engineering Management student at AFIT leading much of the research. sUAS, he said, can help Airmen quickly map unfamiliar locations, assess runways and routes, identify hazards, and build situational awareness before committing personnel and equipment. This is a direct enhancement of the Integrated Base Response and Recovery and Rapid Airfield Damage Repair capabilities that underpin the Air Force’s approach to post-attack recovery.

Today, situational awareness of airfield hazards is largely generated from eyes-on assessment and communicated over the radio. An Airman on the ground describes what they see, and command and control pieces together a complete picture from a string of verbal reports. It works but can oftentimes be slow or incomplete.

“The biggest impact is safer Airmen and faster, higher-quality information,”Jurek said. “A picture really is worth a thousand words.”

AFIT’s research splits the challenge into two distinct yet complementary pieces. A multirotor aircraft, which is the focus of Jurek’s graduate research, can launch from almost anywhere, hover, change angle, and pick its way through the confined, unpredictable routes that Damage Assessment and Response Teams would otherwise have to physically enter first.

A fixed-wing aircraft, the subject of a parallel developmental engineering project Jurek is running with Capts. Peter Stobinski, Nicholas Rife, and Spencer Peters, trades that maneuverability for endurance and reach, sweeping runways, taxiways, and parking aprons for craters, spalls, and debris across much larger operating areas.

Each capability works in concert with one another to provide the Airmen with relevant hazard information at the speed and level of detail required. Together, they could serve as a layered reconnaissance capability with one platform providing broad-area coverage while the other performs detailed inspection in confined or hazardous areas, ultimately enhancing leadership’s decision space.

“The goal is to put the sensor into the uncertain environment first and get the best possible information to the decision-maker as quickly as possible,” Jurek said.

“Efforts such as this enable Agile Combat Employment by accounting for and exploring solutions to an inevitable circumstance in a combat environment,” said Capt. Nicholas Rife, a Systems Engineering student on the fixed-wing team. The project, he said, is meant “to leverage technical solutions that can be both effective and expedient while putting greater distance between the Civil Engineer Airman and the threat at hand.”

Jurek’s thesis, advised by Lt. Col. Daniel Weeks, is built to test that premise rather than assume it. It measures sUAS-supporter reconnaissance against conventional DART routes on three criteria—speed, accuracy, and safety—and evaluates the whole process, not just the aircraft: mission planning, flight execution, camera coverage, imagery collection, and the time it takes an analyst to turn footage into a usable hazard picture. If an aerial first-look cannot get accurate information to Civil Engineer leaders faster than the current DART methods, the case for fielding it falls apart.

AFIT treats the drone as one piece of a larger system rather than a standalone asset. The coursework and thesis process pushes students to trace an operational problem from concept, through requirements, into design and testing, and on toward fielding, accounting for the sensor, communications link, software, training pipeline, approvals, and the operator alongside the aircraft itself.

“Speed, precision, and usability are key to this effort,” Rife said. “By approaching this effort from a digital-engineering perspective, we can systematically root out technological anomalies to develop a reliable and usable system that can deploy at the speed of relevance.”

The ongoing research is helping AFIT build both operational experience and technical understanding as the Air Force continues evaluating how sUAS may support future operations. The objective behind the effort remains clear: give commanders a decisive information advantage over a damaged airfield, reduce the time it takes to get combat aircraft back in the air, and help Airmen Engineers restore combat capability more safely and effectively in contested environments. In short, the goal is to outpace the threat.

articles.title: 673d Medical Group offers new 24-hour prescription refill option
articles.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – The 673d Medical Group at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson now has a ScriptCenter Kiosk, providing users contactless access to refill prescriptions. While accessible to all, the automated kiosk will be of particular benefit to those working night and swing shifts, offering a modern and secure way for users to collect their prescriptions on their schedule.

“The ScriptCenter Kiosk advances the JBER Ready Airman and Soldier mission by providing modern pharmaceutical capability and after-hours prescription access that is conducive to their work schedules,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Brian Johnson, commander of the 673d Medical Support Squadron.

The kiosk, located in the Emergency Department waiting area, houses 44 non-refrigerated lockers. Users can place refill orders in the Military Health System GENESIS Patient Portal. If requests are made for refridgerated medication they will be routed to a standard pharmacy, and the individual will be notified when it is available.

The ScriptCenter has been designed to make refilling prescriptions easy. In the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal under the Rx refill tab, users can select the ScriptCenter under the ‘choose a pharmacy’ option. There will be an initial sign-up process when first using the kiosk. Users will set up a four-digit PIN for secure access. When picking up an order it is recommended to bring military ID and the prescription number. The lockers are accessible to both active-duty members and their dependents with valid ID.

Airman 1st Class Rossukon Gonphila, pharmacy technician assigned to the 673d MDSS, has been leading the program at JBER. Gonphila highlighted the benefit of the system helping those who have difficulty accessing pharmacy services during business hours.

“Some operations have personnel working night shifts, or shifts where they can’t pick up during normal hours,” said Gonphila. “They have the opportunity to pick up at the ScriptCenter even after we are closed.”

articles.title: Future Conflict Minor
articles.body:
Cadet 1st Class Hunter Levett and fellow cadets participate in a Future Conflict Minor class at the U.S. Air Force Academy, Colo., Sept. 14, 2026. The interdisciplinary program develops critical-thinking skills through the study of strategic behavior, emerging technologies and complex challenges. (U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley) By SSgt Michael Ward U.S. Air Force Academy Strategic Communications U.S. AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo. –Developing officers who can think critically, challenge assumptions and make decisions in complex environments is part of the U.S. Air Force Academy’s mission to prepare cadets for future service. One way the Academy develops those skills is through the Future Conflict Minor, an interdisciplinary pathway open to cadets in any major who want to explore where conflict is headed and how to prepare for it. Dr. Kerry Chavez, assistant professor with the Institute for Future Conflict and chair of the Future Conflict Minor working group, teaches two courses in the minor: Adversary Doctrine and Disruptive Tech and Future Conflict. Her courses challenge cadets to examine strategic behavior, emerging technologies and the factors that shape how nations approach conflict. “Predicting and preparing for the future is hard. We aim to equip students with substantive knowledge, but more of the intellectual toolkit to think through complex, dynamic challenges from start to solution,” Chavez said. Cadet 1st Class Hunter Levett participates in a Future Conflict Minor class at the U.S. Air Force Academy, Colo., Sept. 14, 2026. The course challenges cadets to examine emerging technologies and consider how different nations employ them in conflict. (U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley)

For Cadet 1st Class Hunter Levett, the Future Conflict minor has changed how he evaluates emerging technology and its role in warfare. “These courses have changed the way I view the development of new technologies and the ways that different nations employ them,” Levett said. A discussion on quantum technology, for example, expanded how Levett considers the potential applications of emerging technologies.. “The discussion on quantum technology changed the way I view the possibilities of computing, data gathering and the compiling of intelligence,” Levett said. The coursework also taught Levett to look beyond the technology itself when evaluating its potential impact on warfare and successfully applying it to gain an advantage. “These courses taught me that technology itself is not an innovation nor does it immediately give a nation an edge in warfare,” Levett said. Cadet 1st Class Ruan Brito, an international cadet from Brazil, and Cadet 2nd Class Emily Chang participate in a discussion during a Future Conflict Minor class at the U.S. Air Force Academy, Colo., Sept. 14, 2026. The program teaches cadets to examine problems from multiple perspectives and consider possible outcomes before reaching a conclusion. (U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley)

Understanding emerging technologies is one part of preparing for future conflict. Cadets must also learn to apply that knowledge when facing uncertainty, competing perspectives and problems without a single correct answer. For Cadet 2nd Class Emily Chang, the Future Conflict minor has changed how she approaches problems and prepares to lead. “The Future Conflict Minor has changed my way of thinking by teaching me to look at a problem from multiple perspectives and consider different possible outcomes before coming to a conclusion,” Chang said. Chang sees those lessons extending beyond the classroom to how she will lead after commissioning. “Learning to work through problems without a clear answer will affect the way I lead as an officer by making me more confident and adaptable in uncertain situations,” Chang said. “I’ve learned that there won’t always be one right answer, so I need to use the information I have, trust my judgment and be willing to adjust when things change.” Dr. Kerry Chavez leads a discussion during a Future Conflict Minor class at the U.S. Air Force Academy, Colo., Sept. 14, 2026. Chavez teaches cadets to think critically about future conflict and develop the skills needed to operate in uncertain environments. (U.S. Air Force photo by Trevor Cokley)

Cadets in the Future Conflict Minor study adversary doctrine, strategic competition and use fiction to explore potential conflict futures. They apply what they learn through research, analysis and a classified capstone focused on real-world Department of Defense problems. The coursework develops analytical habits cadets can carry beyond the classroom and into their future careers. “Much of what cadets will face after commissioning is nascent, nebulous or entirely novel,” Chavez said. “The minor helps build the intellectual reflexes to operate without fixed answers or complete information.”

Chavez said the minor ultimately prepares cadets to confront challenges that cannot be fully anticipated in the classroom. “They aren’t necessarily teaching cadets what the future security environment will look like,” Chavez said. “It’s to give them the ability and confidence to face it effectively.” View additional photos on https://www.flickr.com/photos/af_academy/albums/72177720335631286.

articles.title: COMAMC emphasizes air mobility’s role in ‘Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win’ at AFA 2026
articles.body:
Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, commander of Air Mobility Command, joined fellow commanders and senior leaders to address service members, defense industry partners and journalists during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference, Sept. 16.

Tulley joined Gen. S. L. Davis, commander of Air Force Global Strike Command, Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry, commander of Air Force Materiel Command and Maj. Gen. Jon Eberlan, Director of Logistics, Engineering and Force Protection, Headquarters Air Combat Command, for a panel discussion focused on the Chief of Staff of the Air Force's operational imperative to fly and fix aircraft to deter adversaries and, if deterrence fails, to fight and win decisively in contested theaters.

Addressing the current tempo of operations, Tulley highlighted that Air Mobility Command has roughly 300 aircraft deployed across several geographic combatant commands, supported by approximately 10,000 Airmen operating at an intense tempo. He stressed that strategic air refueling is only a fraction of the total support required to sustain the Joint Force. AMC also delivers the supplies, the munitions, the sustainment and the base operating support that combatant commanders count on.

"Air refueling is just part of the story," Tulley said. "What strikes me is the lessons that they're bringing back. We've got a generation of Airmen who are going to come back home with combat experience that will be priceless for [countering] our pacing threat."

When asked about managing readiness with a largely fixed inventory of aircraft, Tulley challenged legacy, binary models of preparedness, advocating for systems that measure combat capability in a protracted fight.

"When we think about readiness in Air Mobility Command, we really think about answering four questions: readiness of what, for what, for when, and at what cost. But when we look at the lessons in Ukraine, we also have to ask ourselves: for how long?" Tulley stated. "Readiness in contact is the way we're approaching this."

To illustrate the joint teamwork required to generate readiness in contact, Tulley noted that AFMC pushed forward depot-level capabilities to Royal Air Force Mildenhall, United Kingdom, where maintenance teams have successfully swapped 30 KC-135 Stratotanker boom assemblies in-theater rather than flying the aircraft back to the United States for repairs.

Turning to the challenges of concurrent global demand and operating across multiple theaters, Tulley explained that AMC functions as the global air component to U.S. Transportation Command, balancing requirements across 11 combatant commands.

"For us, it's really about discerning the requirements across those combatant commands to include TRANSCOM's own, and then their priorities," Tulley explained. "What we really need, and what we're moving towards, is a system that lets us see all 11 combatant commands."

Addressing the pilot pipeline and training constraints, Tulley emphasized that the command is looking at the entire enterprise to ensure experienced aircrews are in operational squadrons.

"At the end of the day, we really need experience in the squadrons," Tulley said, noting that he recently convened a team to examine how the command can simplify its training requirements. "How much time do we spend in training now? What are our requirements for all of our mission sets. How can we simplify that? Always assure we have the basic level of readiness to keep the global transportation system operating, but then tailor the training we need for that high-end fight."

To highlight the reality of operating and fixing aircraft while under fire, Tulley recounted a recent real-world mission where a KC-135 aircrew and maintenance team sheltered during a ballistic missile attack, then immediately emerged to contain a major fuel leak, patch shrapnel holes and repair the aircraft so it could complete a transoceanic flight home for depot restoration. Tulley stressed that readiness is a vital, continuous process for the command.

"Pretty simple for us: train like you fight, train like you will fight in a peer fight," Tulley said. "Training like you fight has got to stress our Airmen. It’s got to train them to be ready for those stresses, and then do it again and again and again."

Tulley concluded by discussing the evolution of contested logistics, highlighting that AMC has adapted to track detailed replacement parts for aircraft in contested theaters, alongside combat munitions shipments.

"One of the things I'd say about logistics and supply lines are that we are good, but we're getting better," Tulley stated. "If you can get to the granularity and the precision to say, 'Okay, I need these [Mission Impaired Capability Awaiting Parts] delivered with those munitions,' you're increasing combat capability. You're turning aircraft back into the fight faster."

As AMC continues to operate at a sustained global tempo, Tulley emphasized that the command’s advantage rests on its ability to generate, sustain and regenerate combat capability under contested conditions. By integrating maintenance, logistics, training and operational planning across the mobility enterprise, AMC is working to ensure its Airmen and aircraft can support the Joint Force wherever and whenever they are needed.

articles.title: The 'Magic Middle': AETC Chief Learning Officer Champions Mission Command, Culture of Candor
articles.body:
JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-RANDOLPH, Texas -- When Dr. Wendy Walsh stepped up to address leaders during Air Education and Training Command’s Gathering of the Torch leadership conference Sept. 10, she did not lead with technological roadmaps or administrative directives. Instead, she offered a candid admission of human fallibility and a challenge to rethink the cultural core of military education.

"One of my least favorite phrases in the world is 'fake it till you make it.' Early on, someone told me that was just how things operated under intense operational tempos. But our Airmen are placed in high-stakes environments where they have little time to adapt," said Walsh. "If we want leaders who can make sound, decentralized decisions in combat, we must create an environment where admitting what you don't know is the first step toward genuine competence."

To bridge the gap between classroom theory and real-world execution, Walsh pointed to the foundational principles of Mission Command, emphasizing that trust and decentralized execution begin long before an Airman enters a contested theater. She highlighted the framework known as the "five Cs": character, competence, cohesion, capability, and capacity. By grounding everyday instruction in character and competence, units naturally generate the operational cohesion required to solve ambiguous, complex challenges under pressure.

Cultivating that mindset across an enterprise of thousands requires intentional cultural architecture. Walsh introduced leaders to "gracious space," an intentional framework designed to establish genuine presence, evaluate working environments, welcome contrary viewpoints, and encourage public learning. For frontline leaders, this translates into discarding punitive responses when Airmen voice operational friction and replacing them with rigorous, team-wide problem-solving.

During a recent enterprise-wide continuous process improvement assembly that convened more than 70 leaders and instructors, participants tackled what has historically been labeled the "frozen middle" the bureaucratic layer between strategic intent and flightline execution. Through cross-functional problem-solving, attendees reframed that narrative entirely, recognizing that middle-tier leaders are not an obstacle to progress, but rather the "magic middle" that turns high-level strategy into everyday capability.

Throughout the session, attendees mapped how intent flows through squadrons, flights, and classrooms, culminating in an actionable accountability pledge: You're it. Rather than waiting for higher headquarters directives to address broken signals or ineffective practices, educators and commanders were charged with owning their sphere of influence immediately.

"You don't have to wait for someone else to grant permission to fix what is broken," Walsh stressed. "Whether you are a wing commander, an enlisted military training instructor or a civilian educator, you own an area of influence. Real readiness is built on character and accountability, ensuring every Airman is anchored in warrior identity and prepared to lead with competence and confidence in any environment."

articles.title: McConnell, Wichita turn up the heat on boil water advisory
articles.body:
MCCONNELL AIR FORCE BASE, Kan. – Easy access to readily available clean drinking water is a luxury 25 percent of the world, or one in four people, do not have. Airmen and residents of McConnell Air Force Base and the greater Wichita area experienced a loss of that luxury when a boil water advisory (BWA) was put into effect Sept. 16.

The BWA was the result of a power loss at the main water treatment plant and Hess Pump station, which led to a temporary drop citywide in water pressure. The facilities had switched to back-up generators after a storm-related power surge, but a malfunction caused two of them to fail and prevented two others from starting, cutting off power to the pumps for about 45 minutes.

“We’re still investigating the cause of the power failure to the generators,” said Gary Janzen, Wichita Public Works and Utilities director. “We’re committed to ensuring that we instill procedures that will prevent a multi-failure power outage. We want to do everything we can to safeguard not having this happen again.”

Thirty-four hours after the initial announcement, the Kansas Department of Health and Environment rescinded the order for Wichita after the results for 195 testing locations came back clear and free of contamination.

However, the boil order has not yet been lifted on McConnell. The 22nd Operational Medical Readiness Squadron Bioenvironmental Engineering collected water samples from eight locations around base and are still waiting for the results of those tests before lifting the advisory.

“The bottom line is that because the boil water advisory affected the entire water system of Wichita, and we are a consecutive system of that water system, we had to wait and sample until Wichita cleared their BWA,” said Maj. Brian Thompson, 22nd OMRS Bioenvironmental Engineering flight commander. “Then we sampled, and hopefully we clear ours once our samples get back.”

Bioenvironmental is testing the water samples for pH levels, chlorine residual, and bacteria. Because of the bacteriological test, they have to culture for a minimum of 24 hours before it can be determined safe or not.

Clean water is essential to the operations of multiple facilities on McConnell, many of which fall under the 22nd Force Support Squadron, such as the Child Development Center, dining facility, and fitness center. Once the BWA was announced, 22nd FSS personnel immediately took measures to mitigate risk by boiling water and purchasing water bottles.

The fountain drink machines were turned off and labeled as temporarily out of order at the Chisholm Trail Dining Facility and bowling alley, and all fresh produce is being cleaned using boiled water. A notice was provided to all parents of children at the CDC, School-Age Care, and Youth Center updating them on the protocols put in place regarding drinking water and hydration, food preparation and meal services, hand washing and hygiene, sanitation and diapering.

“Everyone was all hands on deck,” said Lt. Col. Latisha Cannon, 22nd FSS commander. “I think it’s important to be able to act quickly to make sure that our kiddos are safe and just the populous as well, because you need people to run the base. Making sure that we adhere to the standards and execute quickly, I think that’s what keeps us in line and mission ready.”

The BWA did not just affect Wichita proper and the base, but nine of the neighboring communities and three rural water districts. The other affected communities were Andover, Bel Aire, Benton, Derby, Kechi, Park City, Rose Hill, Valley Center, Maize South schools, and Sedgewick County Rural Water Districts 1-3.

“It’s vital for a community to have clean drinking water,” Thompson said. “We can’t do anything if we don’t have clean water. We saw contracting have issues purchasing bottled water, how fast those flew off the shelf, so it’s absolutely vital.”

The city of Wichita is constructing a new $573 million Northwest Water Treatment Facility to replace the current facility, which is more than 80 years old. The new facility is expected to open sometime between April and June 2027.

articles.title: ‘A Solemn Promise’: Painting features Air Force reservists supporting dignified transfer mission
articles.body:
A combat artist returned to Dover Air Force Base, Delaware, Sept. 12-14, 2026, to unveil a piece of art that was inspired by the base’s mission of returning the fallen.

Warren Neary, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel with the Air Force Reserve Command Office of Historical Services Combat Art and Outreach Section, hosted four showings of the 5-by-8-foot oil painting “A Solemn Promise,” which depicts a scene of 512th Memorial Affairs Squadron reservists participating in a dignified transfer in 2017.

A dignified transfer is the process by which, upon the return from the theater of operations to the United States, the remains of fallen military members are transferred from the aircraft to an awaitingvehicle. The remains are then transferred to the Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations facility at Dover AFB.The dignified transfer is not a ceremony; rather, it is a solemn movement of the transfer case by a carry team composed of military personnel from the fallen member's respective service.

The artist said he was grateful to have the opportunity to highlight the dignified transfer.

“The painting covers a very important topic of honoring our fallen, and it was a challenging and emotional subject,” he said. “It’s a vital mission that the Air Force Reserve supports.”

The 512th MAS is the only memorial affairs squadron in the Air Force that directly supports the Department of War’s mortuary operations and dignified transfers.

To honor this sacred mission, Neary channeled a lifetime of artistic training into documenting their work. He said he grew up painting and continued to hone his craft, earning an undergraduate and master’s degree in art. He visited Team Dover in 2017 and observed several dignified transfers. He said most media depict the dignified transfer from a side view, and he wanted to use the vantage point of straight-on to show faces and the emotion of the event. He said he spent hours on the flightline taking reference photos and testing different paints to ensure he captured the scene correctly. He estimated the painting required hundreds of hours to complete.

Neary traveled with his painting from Robins Air Force Base, Georgia, and had showings of the painting at an event in the city of Dover and on Dover AFB. He said he enjoyed seeing people’s reactions to the painting and getting to talk to them.

“Paint is a great format to highlight this mission, because it resonates with a variety of audiences,” he said. “With the lithographs, we’re able to send them home with a personalized piece of history.”

One of the attendees was a former 512th MAS reservist who is portrayed in the painting.

Nick Arndt served in the Air Force Reserve for eight and a half years before separating in 2022. He said he vividly remembers meeting the artist in 2017, and he said his year-long deployment to AFMAO was the highlight of his military career.

“It’s pretty humbling and profound being here today and seeing this,” he said. It’s nice to see a representation of the work I did in a beautiful, large painting that will be hanging somewhere forever.

Even though he has been separated from the military for four years, Arndt still had a lot of old friends to talk to at the show.

“The thing I miss the most is the great people I had an opportunity to work,” he said. “It’s nice to be back here and see some familiar faces.” David Jackson, the 512th Airlift Wing’s process manager, served as the onsite liaison, making it possible for the painting to be on display on and around Dover AFB. He said he was impressed by the painting.

“It’s an amazing awe-inspiring piece of art,” he said. “It’s a somber reminder of the sacrifices of our heroes.”

Jackson also worked closely with Neary to ensure the painting was securely stored in a manner that wouldn’t damage the work of art.

“A lot of people helped make this happen, volunteering their free time to help move the painting around, he said. “I was excited for everyone to have the chance to experience it.”

After four showings and hundreds of signed lithographs, Neary said he really enjoyed his trip to Delaware.

“The team here is awesome, and I really appreciated the opportunity to capture the mission here,” he said.

The next stop for “A Solemn Promise” is to be displayed at a Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency location at Joint Base Pearl-Hickam, Hawaii. As a part of the Air Force Art Collection, the painting could be displayed in any number of places in the future.

articles.title: Final A-10 units inactivate at Davis-Monthan
articles.body:
DAVIS-MONTHAN AIR FORCE BASE, Ariz. -- The 355th Operations Group, 357th Fighter Squadron, 357th Fighter Generation Squadron and the 355th Training Squadron were inactivated during a ceremony at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Arizona, Sept. 18, 2026, marking the official end of the A-10 legacy at DM.

U.S. Air Force Col. Jose Cabrera, 355th Wing commander, presided over the historic ceremony. Airmen, families, retired A-10 pilots, local civic leaders and community members attended the event to recognize each A-10 unit’s service and contributions.

Upon activation on May 1, 1992, the 355 OG was tasked with control of the flying units assigned to the 355th Wing. From 1992-2026, the group provided the capabilities of the A-10 Thunderbolt II for the missions of close air support, forward air control and combat search and rescue. The group also deployed personnel to support warfighters across the globe and oversaw all formal A-10 pilot initial qualification and requalification training.

“For decades, every single active-duty pilot, who flew into harm’s way, was built right there on this flightline,” said Cabrera. “For nearly 50 years, the A-10 Thunderbolt has occupied a sacred place in American air power. It was never just an airplane. It was a promise. Davis-Monthan was part of that promise.”

To signify the inactivation of each A-10 unit, the respective guidons were rolled and cased by their last commander and Cabrera.

“We say the word ‘attack’,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Rodney Dwyer, final commander of the 355 OG and 355 TRS. “We have a great amount of pride when we say that word because it’s not just the challenge or response. It’s a distinct mentality – that aggressive state of mind that means using the opportunity when conditions are chaotic.”

The audience responded aloud with a roaring “attack” to honor each commander that relinquished their duties moments before casing their former guidon.

Attendees also heard remarks from the pilot who flew the first A-10 aircraft into Davis-Monthan AFB, U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. (Retired) Glen “Wally” Moorhead.

“Nov. 7, 1975 was when I first flew the A-10 at DM,” explained Moorhead. “In 1974, I was very fortunate to be selected as the last and youngest member of the A-10 testing at Edwards [Air Force Base] and with a follow-on assignment I knew I would come to be the first A-10 pilot at DM.”

The ceremony focused on the history of the units and the members who put their lives on the line to support 18-year-old service members on the ground. It concluded with a group photo for all former 355 OG members and a ceremonious two-ship A-10 flyover.

“This has been an incredible job and opportunity, but it’s also been heavy,” U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Ryan Rutter, final commander of 357 FS. “I think about my time as a wingman, my job was to learn. As an instructor pilot, it was to teach. And now my charge [as a commander] is to leave.”

To preserve and present the 50-year legacy of the A-10 at DM, important historical documents and memorabilia from 355 OG, 357 FS, 357 FGS, and 355 TRS are being packed into containers to send to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson AFB.

articles.title: Building Better Leaders: CTANG S.T.A.F.F. Conference Develops the Next Generation of NCOs
articles.body:
CAMP NETT, Conn. — “You all got here because someone saw the potential in you. But the time for ‘potential’ is over. It’s time to look at what you might do. It’s now time to work at realizing whatever potential you think you might have.”

Those words from retired Brig. Gen. Marcus Jannitto brought a week of leadership development, professional growth and connection to a close as Air National Guard members completed the 2026 S.T.A.F.F. Conference at Camp Nett in Niantic, Connecticut.

Hosted by the 103d Airlift Wing Sept. 14-18, the five-day conference brought together 56 staff sergeants representing six states with a shared goal: developing, empowering and connecting the next generation of Air National Guard NCO leaders.

Throughout the week, participants heard from engaging military and civilian leaders, took part in hands-on workshops and team-building activities, and explored the responsibilities that come with becoming a frontline leader. Sessions challenged attendees to consider their individual leadership styles, strengthen communication skills and examine how NCOs influence the culture and climate of their organizations.

Speakers included Jannitto, who formerly served as the chief of staff and deputy adjutant general for the Rhode Island Air National Guard, and Nathan Wheeler, an 11-year Army veteran who served with the 10th Special Forces Group (Airborne) and now specializes in motivational speaking, leadership and financial empowerment. Airmen also heard from Dr. Michael Frost, a professor and organizational change agent with more than 20 years of experience in law enforcement. Each speaker offered impactful advice and hard-earned perspectives on leadership.

“I like that they pulled in speakers from outside the military,” said Staff Sgt. Griffen Smith, an MQ-9 sensor operator with the 174th Attack Wing in New York. “They did a great job engaging us, and it made it really different from almost every other military event I’ve gone to.”

Reflecting on the advice that had been most impactful throughout the week, Smith said that multiple speakers had emphasized the importance of connecting with the people you supervise.

“No matter how busy you may be,” Smith said, “it’s important to always look out for your people.” Staff Sgt. Kyle Marsh, a security forces specialist with the 157th Air Refueling Wing in New Hampshire, said one message from Brig. Gen. Thomas Olander, Connecticut Air National Guard chief of staff–air, particularly resonated with him: the immense impact NCOs have on the National Guard.

“We’re in charge,” Marsh said, recalling Olander’s message.

Participants also spent time at Stones Ranch on Wednesday, completing challenges on the Leadership Reaction Course. Each obstacle required small groups to pause, plan, adapt and lead. In one challenge, participants were given a single plank of wood, a piece of rope and instructions to get their entire team over a fence using only the limited materials provided. Working under time constraints and often alongside colleagues they had only recently met, participants had to communicate, problem-solve and put their leadership skills into practice to accomplish each task.

The week ended with a graduation ceremony attended by state leadership, during which participants were addressed by Col. Robert Krueger, commander of the 103d Airlift Wing; Chief Master Sgt. Rick Marks, command chief of the 103d Airlift Wing; and Maj. Gen. Francis Evon, adjutant general of the Connecticut National Guard. The focus throughout the final day shifted from what participants had learned at S.T.A.F.F. to what they would do with those lessons when they returned to their units.

“Now that you’ve entered the world of leadership, grab onto some of these things you’ve learned,” Jannitto said at the close of his remarks Sept. 18. “It’s much easier to talk about your potential. Anyone can do that. But will you squander it?”

articles.title: U.S., Polish Airmen launch Exercise Hussar Saber 26-4
articles.body:
POWIDZ, Poland – Hussar Saber 26-4, a bilateral training exercise between U.S. and Polish forces, began Sept. 14, 2026, and will focus on strengthening each nations’ mission readiness, interoperability and ability to rapidly deploy and sustain operations.

The two-week exercise includes service members and aircraft assigned to the 86th Airlift Wing and 435th Air Ground Operations Wing, at Ramstein Air Base, Germany; 52nd Fighter Wing, at Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany and Poland’s 33rd Air Base to conduct integrated training across Poland.

“Hussar Saber is a bilateral exercise conducted four times per year to facilitate integration and partner capabilities,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Brian K. Jarrell, 52d Operations Group Detachment 1 commander. “Integration between U.S. and Polish Air Forces sets the baseline for contingency operations and successful European deterrence on NATO's Eastern flank.”

The training includes tactical airlift and airdrop operations, low-level flights, night operations, and landings in austere conditions. The various scenarios are designed to replicate conditions they could encounter during Agile Combat Employment operations.

“Hussar Saber brings teams together to get after desired learning objectives that support U.S. Air Forces in Europe-Air Forces Africa priorities,” said U.S. Air Force Capt. Connor Ullom, 37th Airlift Squadron pilot and Hussar Saber 26-4 mission commander. “We simulate a deployed environment where a joint mission planning cell prepares our crews to execute complex missions to test our capabilities, tactics, techniques, and procedures.”

The exercise demonstrates the nations’ ability to operate together in support of collective deterrence and practice rapid deployment of personnel and equipment to meet demands of short-notice taskings.

articles.title: Mind over miles: Mental Grit Propels Champions at 2026 Air Force Marathon
articles.body:
WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio– Every mile of a race is a physical negotiation—a stark reminder that while the human body has limits, the mind can be trained to push past them.

More than 9,000 people across 50 states registered for the 2026 Air Force Marathon, testing their mental and physical endurance across several race categories Sept. 18-19. Races were held on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and grounds of the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force and Wright State University.

Leading the charge were full marathon champions U.S. Space Force 1st Lt. Nicholas McKenzie, Vandenburg Space Force Base, California with a time of 2:34:31 and Kayla Rice, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base employee, with a time of 2:56:39.

“I’m ecstatic – it’s a great day with super energy out on the course and beautiful weather,” McKenzie said. “This is my second time running the Air Force Marathon, and I’m super grateful for all the volunteers, the support, and all the other runners out here getting it done today.”

However, for McKenzie, the mental turning point came during the race’s most solemn stretch.

“Around mile 21, it definitely starts to get hard. But running and seeing the tributes to our fallen service members was emotional and heartwarming. It really helped me stay motivated to get to the end. Seeing that helps you realize the ultimate sacrifice they gave, and it motivated me to dig a little deeper.”

For Rice, crossing the finish line as the women’s champion marked the culmination of years of dedicated training right on her home base at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

“I feel incredible. This has been a goal I’ve been working toward for the past few years, and it’s great to finally achieve it,” Rice said. “This is my fourth time running it, so every year it’s been my goal to just get a little bit faster and eventually get where I am today. It was a big personal record for me, and getting to see all my friends, family, coworkers, and teammates out on the course was amazing.”

Sharing that spotlight of sheer determination were half-marathon champions Simon Heys, a civilian runner at 1:05:45 and 2nd Lt. Allyson Peterson, Ramstein Air Base, with a time of 1:19:10.

For Heys, pushing through the half-marathon course was a personal way to show gratitude for military service members.

“It was special,” Heys said. “I really wanted to come here and just run as hard as I could. I wanted to put the grind out there, like the men and women who fight for this country do every day.”

Peterson, competing in her first half marathon, relied on strategic pacing and late-race momentum to secure her victory.

“I’ve been looking forward to this race,” she said. “I had a great group of guys to chase coming down for the last like six miles. So, I was just focusing on closing that gap.”

Beyond individual determination on the course, Department of the Air Force leadership underscored how physical discipline and community support directly reinforce the strength and readiness of the joint force.

“If I have one message for you today, thank you for showing up to do hard things,” said Matthew L. Lohmeier, 29th Under Secretary of the Air Force. “Thank you for working together as a community, both to support the 30th Air Force Marathon and to make the Department of the Air Force and the entire joint force a better place to work, a more lethal, ready force. And thank you for taking care of yourselves to be a part of our ready force.”

As the cheers from the finish line festival filled the air and the champions took their places at the awards ceremony, the legacy of the 2026 race extended beyond the trophy stands. For the thousands who crossed the finish line, the race was more than an athletic showcase. It was a masterclass in mental readiness, proving that when the mission demands endurance, disciplined preparation will always carry us through.

articles.title: Ready to fly: 916th Security Forces Airmen complete wing’s first Fly Away Security Team training
articles.body:
SEYMOUR JOHNSON AIR FORCE BASE, N.C. — Sweat ran beneath helmets and body armor as 11 Airmen moved through a 916th Air Refueling Wing hangar, protecting a KC-46A Pegasus from simulated threats during the wing’s inaugural Fly Away Security Team (FAST) training course at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base, North Carolina, Sept. 7–12.

The six-day foundational course, managed by the 22nd Air Force, is designed to instill in Security Forces Airmen the confidence needed to meet the unique demands of protecting aircraft in unfamiliar environments. Training emphasizes communication, coordination and integration with operations and maintenance personnel, in addition to responding to threats.

“We don’t want to send Airmen downrange to a combat zone and have them encounter a mission they’ve never done before,” said Col. Charles Trovarello, 916th Mission Support Group commander and FAST instructor. “We teach them how to plan for this unique mission using the skills they already have, and the skills they’ve never seen before.”

For the Air Force Reservists moving through the hangar, the scenario-based training tested more than just their ability to react, something they had all been trained to do before. According to Trovarello, getting those repetitions in meant giving Airmen real-world experience in and around an aircraft, as well as teaching them how to operate as a team.

“I want them to see us as the team member who’s going to make sure the job gets done,” said Trovarello.

Training in the hangar followed classroom instruction, planning exercises and practical discussion. Trovarello led the course with four visiting instructors: Master Sgt. Sydney Whiteis, 934th Security Forces Squadron; Master Sgt. Taylor Adamson, 507th Security Forces Squadron; Tech. Sgt. Joi Gaffney, 932nd Security Forces Squadron; and Staff Sgt. Dylan Bowman, 932nd Security Forces Squadron.

“This course opens the door to more opportunities for our Airmen,” Whiteis said. “Once they become FAST-qualified, they qualify for missions because they’ve demonstrated throughout the course that they are capable.”

Throughout the week, instructors presented Airmen with changing mission requirements and required them to work backward through the details: where they were going, what

they were doing, who was in charge, and what personnel, equipment and resources they would need.

The planning process was followed by airfield and range assessments and force-on-force training events. Instructors wore protective gear and acted as opposing forces while students used training weapons to respond to simulated threats. Students were evaluated on their ability to appropriately apply escalation-of-force procedures and protect aircraft throughout each scenario.

The drills culminated in the course’s capstone event at Pope Army Airfield, where Airmen transitioned from the training environment to an operational KC-46A Pegasus flight.

“Each scenario is different,” said Tech. Sgt. Jacob Wilson, 916th Security Forces Squadron. “The instructors do a really good job of changing it up so no two scenarios are the same. A lot goes through your mind.”

For Wilson and other students who had not previously flown, the training provided an opportunity to see what a FAST mission could look like before encountering one in an operational environment.

“I’m a visual learner — I have to see it happen; I have to feel it happen,” Wilson said. “They’ve done an excellent job of demonstrating that for us, and I think that’s what will set us up for success during real-world missions.”

Trovarello began developing the idea for a localized, Reservist-centered FAST training course in 2019 while assigned to the 934th Security Forces Squadron, Minneapolis Air Reserve Station, Minnesota. After returning from a deployment and hearing stories from his Airmen who were at other locations, he knew he needed to better prepare his people for flyaway security missions. Previously, due to mission demands, many Airmen had little more training than a short class on FAST at pre-deployment or on the ground before departure.

Although the Airmen possessed the skills taught in Security Forces technical training, Trovarello identified a gap in preparing them for the planning, coordination and unfamiliar environments associated with flyaway missions.

Integration remains central to the program. Security Forces Airmen are expected to protect aircraft, Trovarello said, but they must also understand how to work alongside other Air Force specialties and how that work contributes to the larger mission.

articles.title: Final operational HH-60G Pave Hawk retires, closing a chapter in Air Force rescue history
articles.body:
MOFFETT AIR NATIONAL GUARD BASE, Calif. — For more than three decades, the HH-60G Pave Hawk served as a critical part of the Air Force’s combat search and rescue mission, carrying generations of rescue Airmen into some of the world’s most challenging environments to recover those in need.

From combat zones in Afghanistan and Iraq, to California communities devastated by disasters, the Pave Hawk stood ready to answer the call. The aircraft became synonymous with the Air Force rescue mission and its commitment to bringing people home.

That chapter closed on Sept. 10, as the California Air National Guard’s 129th Rescue Wing marked the retirement of the U.S. Air Force’s final operational HH-60G Pave Hawk with a divestment ceremony and final flight at Moffett Air National Guard Base, near Mountain View, California.

The ceremony commemorated more than the retirement of tail number 27045. It honored a legacy built by the pilots, special mission aviators, pararescuemen, maintainers and support personnel who transformed the Pave Hawk from a helicopter into a symbol of hope and survival. For those Airmen, the aircraft’s legacy is inseparable from the people who kept it flying and the lives its crews worked to save.

“Our motto is ‘these things we do that others may live’, which means that at any time, anywhere, any place, we’re going to send crews and helicopters into harm's way if necessary to save a life, because it matters,” said U.S. Air Force Senior Master Sgt. Sean Pellaton, flight engineer and senior enlisted leader of the 129th Rescue Squadron.

Since 1977, the 129th is credited with saving 1,190 lives, many of them with the Pave Hawk playing a critical role in the rescue. The aircraft supported many of the wing’s most critical missions, including operations following hurricanes Katrina, Ike, and Harvey.

Overseas, the Pave Hawk carried 129th crews during deployments in Afghanistan, contributing to more than 300 combat saves.

After training and combat losses in Afghanistan and Iraq impacted the rescue fleet, the Air Force converted six U.S. Army UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters to rescue, modified to become HH-60G Pave Hawks. Tail #27045, the last operational Pave Hawk, was one of them.

For air crews, accomplishing that mission required countless hours of training and trust built between crew members and the aircraft.

“When you’re flying the [Pave Hawk], you kind of become one with that machine,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Benjamin Buchta, HH-60 pilot and commander of the 129th Rescue Squadron. “The Golf feels like home when I sit in it.”

Before every launch was another team of Airmen whose work began long before wheels left the ground.

Maintainers spent long hours inspecting and repairing the Pave Hawk, working to sustain an aging aircraft, where readiness could directly affect whether someone made it home.

“You go through all this training and finally all this training comes to a point when you have to prove yourself that you performed training correctly,” said U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Brock Woodward, a flight engineer and prior maintainer assigned to the 129th Rescue Squadron.

For many of those Airmen, the HH-60G was the aircraft they learned their profession on, deployed with, and devoted their lives to help save others.

“Rescuing another human being is much more rewarding than any award and [decoration] that you could receive,” said Woodward.

The Pave Hawk’s retirement, however, does not mean the end of the mission it helped define. “It built the helicopter combat search and rescue community into what it is today,” said Buchta.

The Pave Hawk was the platform and cornerstone for many of the tactics the Air Force uses now, he said.

The HH-60W Jolly Green II carries the Air Force’s next generation of combat rescue capabilities, bringing new technology and increased capabilities to the personnel recovery mission.

The final flight of the HH-60G marked the end of an era that stretched across generations of rescue Airmen. Its legacy can be measured in missions flown and lives saved, but it also lives in the Airmen who crewed its cockpits, worked on its flight line and supported every launch.

They gave the Pave Hawk its purpose.

And while the last HH-60G has flown its final Air Force mission, the legacy those Airmen built will continue wherever rescue crews answer the call to bring someone home.

articles.title: 106th Rescue Wing Marks 25th Anniversary of Sept. 11 Attacks with Two Days of Remembrance
articles.body:
FRANCIS S. GABRESKI AIR NATIONAL GUARD BASE, WESTHAMPTON BEACH, N.Y. —The 106th Rescue Wing commemorated the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks with two days of remembrance events Sept. 11 and 13 at Francis S. Gabreski Air National Guard Base.

The events brought together current wing members and retired members who shared their experiences from that day, including a former wing commander, four pararescuemen and a C-130 navigator. A show of hands revealed that five uniformed members in attendance had not yet been born when the attacks occurred.

Retired Col. Michael F. Canders opened commemorations on Sept. 11 in the 106th Operations Group auditorium. He led the 102nd Rescue Squadron at the time of the attacks and spoke to Airmen about how that day fundamentally reshaped the wing.

Canders was a traditional Guardsman, drilling once a month, but became a full-time member as the 106th wing commander in December of that year.

“9/11 was really a demarcation point for the 106th,” Canders said. “We had this cataclysm that changed everything very rapidly. We were able to step up, step in, and quickly respond, and I can’t overstate that change for our readiness and for the, ‘That Others May Live,’ mission.”

Canders was at his civilian employer when the attacks occurred, and he learned of the attacks when an administrative assistant turned the television on.

He credited the wing’s previous Northern Watch and Southern Watch deployments, enforcing Iraqi no-fly zones throughout the 1990s, as essential preparation for the challenges that followed. Canders closed with a direct challenge to the Airmen:

“Our enemy really is complacency,” Canders said. “Your willingness to come out here, to train, and to be ready to go on a moment's notice is essential, and it makes a difference.”

Later that morning, current 106th Commander Col. Jeffrey D. Cannet moderated a Pararescue panel featuring four of the roughly 18 PJs who arrived at Ground Zero a few hours after the attacks: retired members Chief Master Sgt. Craig Johnson, Chief Master Sgt. Timothy Malloy, Senior Master Sgt. Jeffrey Baker, and Senior Master Sgt. Kevin Carrick.

"This wing was completely transformed by 9/11," Cannet said. "It was life before and life after. Everything we've done in the last 25 years started on that day, and it's important that we refresh our minds on those moments.”

The former PJs described being scattered across Long Island that morning. One was in his third day at the corrections academy. One was on patrol as a Suffolk County police officer. Others were on leave. Upon learning of the events that morning, PJs assembled at the base, loaded into vans, and headed toward New York City on empty highways.

With New York City locked down, Tech. Sgt. Ken Smith, a PJ and New York City police officer, arranged an NYPD helicopter to transport the PJs from Floyd Bennett Field, Brooklyn, to Ground Zero, according to Carrick.

”When we turned the corner and walked into that site, it was like walking on the moon," Carrick said. "The ground was gray talcum powder. Every time you took a step, it was like hoops of smoke."

The men described a debris field that continued to burn beneath their feet. Hundreds of firefighter air packs, known as Scott Packs, or Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus, lay scattered across the ruins, their alarms beeping from the absence of movement. Nearby medical triage stations stood fully staffed and ready to treat survivors, but they received almost no patients, according to Carrick. Still, the rescue effort continued. According to the mission report, a 106th member helped bring the last known survivor out of the rubble 26 hours after the towers collapsed.

For Senior Airman Karen Diaz, a logistics plans specialist who joined the wing in 2022, the panel held personal significance. She was 9 years old on Sept. 11, and lost two uncles in the collapse and she said the tragedy drove her desire to serve.

"I don't want my kids to have to experience what I experienced," she said. "I wanted to do my part for national security."

"It was humbling hearing their stories," Diaz added. "They left what they were doing on Long Island and, instead of staying safe, they went toward the disaster to do what they do best. They were ready, willing, and able at a moment's notice to go take care of others.”

On Sept. 13, Col. Neil Theisen, 106th deputy commander, introduced retired Lt. Col. Christopher Hardej, a former 102nd Rescue Squadron C-130 navigator who delivered a lessons-learned briefing centered on his personal account of escaping the World Trade Center’s North Tower.

On the morning of the attacks, Hardej was working as a New York State Department of Transportation employee on the 82nd floor when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the building some 10 floors above his workspace.

He recalled the morning sky being clear and perfect: “I remember thinking, ‘What a beautiful day to fly,’" Hardej said.

Minutes later, the building violently shook, he said. Looking outside, Hardej saw debris falling through the air. So much office paper fluttered down the, for a moment, it looked like a ticker-tape parade. Drawing on his military training, Hardej went down 82 flights of stairs, encountering severely burned victims and firefighters rushing upward and he led a group of people from his office to the underground concourse near Tower 2. It was then that the South Tower collapsed.

"I heard the air rush and ran for the wall," Hardej said. "I grabbed it, closed my eyes and thought, 'So this is what it feels like to die.'"

In total darkness, Hardej called out to coworkers and navigated the debris-filled underground complex from memory, leading the group to safety on the street.

Two months later, he deployed with the wing as scheduled.

"Nobody would have faulted me if I said I couldn't do it," Hardej said. "But no way were my guys going over there without me. By then, it was personal.”

The remembrances brought together past and present members of the wing to reflect on an event that continues to shape the wing 25 years later.

"You never know when it's going to be your turn," said Malloy, "You better be able to ride back on your training.”

The 106th Rescue Wing, based at Francis S. Gabreski Air National Guard Base in Westhampton Beach, New York, operates and maintains the HC-130J Combat King II search and rescue aircraft, and the HH-60W Jolly Green II search and rescue helicopter. The 106th Rescue Wing is home to a special warfare squadron with pararescuemen and combat rescue officers, specializing in rescue and recovery, and deploys for domestic and overseas operations.

articles.title: AEDC at 75: AEDC testing in late 1950s supports early space programs
articles.body: ARNOLD AIR FORCE BASE, Tenn. – Throughout the tail end of the same decade in which it was dedicated, test cells at what was then known as Arnold Engineering Development Center were frequently called upon to support the goal of sending an American into space. In the late 1950s, work began at AEDC, now known as Arnold Engineering Development Complex, that directly supported Project Mercury and later supported Project Gemini, the first two U.S. human spaceflight programs and the precursors to the Apollo program of the 1960s that would land an American on the moon before the close of that decade. The Soviet Union’s successful launch of the Sputnik 1 satellite in October 1957 spurred the Space Race between the Soviets and U.S., with each nation vying to better its Cold War rival in spaceflight achievement. Before the space-centric competition truly ramped up, an unprecedented feat was accomplished at AEDC. On March 27, 1957, escape velocity, the speed required to leave Earth’s gravity, was achieved for the first time during calibration and shakedown runs in the Hotshot II wind tunnel of what is now known as the von Kármán Gas Dynamics Facility, or VKF. This event predates the July 29, 1958, establishment of NASA. “The test run peak lasted about one-tenth of a second during which an airflow of approximately nine miles per second – 32,400 miles per hour – was achieved,” stated an AEDC news release about the Hotshot II issued in February 1958. “This is nearly twice the speed required to place a satellite in orbit. It is the first time escape velocity, seven miles per second, has ever been reached in a wind tunnel.” In June of the following year, the first in a series of tests of solid propellant rockets for the third stage of a vehicle being assembled for the newly created Advanced Research Projects Agency, established in response to the Sputnik launch, was fired in an Engine Test Facility test cell. This effort represented the first solid-propellant rocket motor test fired in the ETF. Tests were also conducted on rockets for an orbital launch system. AEDC engineers were especially busy with space-related testing throughout the final year of the 1950s. On Jan. 10, 1959, a scale model of the Titan rocket was tested in an AEDC wind tunnel. This marked the first liquid-propellant rocket fired in the wind tunnel. Titan rockets were eventually used as launch vehicles during the crewed Project Gemini space missions that occurred around the mid-1960s. “The Gemini Program had four objectives – to subject astronauts to long-duration flights, a requirement for projected later trips to the moon or deeper space; to develop effective methods of rendezvous and docking with other orbiting vehicles in space; to perfect methods of reentry and landing the spacecraft at a preselected landing point; and to gain additional information concerning the effects of weightlessness on the crew and record their physiological reactions during long-duration flights,” states Beyond the Speed of Sound, a book detailing the history of AEDC. In April 1959, the same wind tunnel utilized for the Titan rocket firing was used to investigate two escape configurations for Project Mercury, the first U.S. human spaceflight program initiated in 1958. This work was done to determine characteristics related to the stability and drag of the configurations. The first Project Mercury flight occurred in May 1961, and the program ran for about another two years afterward. “The objectives of the program, which made six manned flights from 1961 to 1963, were specific: to orbit a manned spacecraft around Earth; to investigate man’s ability to function in space; and to recover both man and spacecraft safely,” states Beyond the Speed of Sound in reference to Project Mercury. “Mercury was a cone-shaped, one-man capsule with a cylinder mounted on top and an escape tower fastened to the cylinder of the capsule. The Mercury program used two launch vehicles – a Redstone for the suborbital flight and an Atlas for the four orbital flights. Prior to the six manned flights, unmanned tests were made of the booster and the capsule, carrying a chimpanzee.” During the summer of 1959, numerous tests to assess static stability, heat transfer and pressure distribution were conducted on Project Mercury capsule models the VKF Hotshot 2 tunnel. The reliability for Mercury escape system to ignite at great distances above the Earth’s surface was verified at AEDC on Nov. 27, 1959, through successful firing tests at a simulated high altitude. This is the 23rd in a series of articles highlighting the history of Arnold Engineering Development Complex during its first 75 years. Additional articles will be published throughout 2026 to commemorate the anniversary of AEDC.

articles.title: Kirtland AFB demonstrates operational readiness, modernization efforts
articles.body:
KIRTLAND AIR FORCE BASE, N.M. -- Every day, the security, maintenance, and operational readiness underpinning the nation’s nuclear deterrence enterprise hinge on the discipline and ingenuity of the Airmen stationed at Kirtland Air Force Base. From safeguarding vital national security assets to developing cost-saving maintenance processes on the flightline and inside munitions facilities, Team Kirtland Airmen routinely transform high-stakes operational requirements into everyday mission success.

During an immersion tour Aug. 27–28, 2026, 20th Air Force leadership and their spouses witnessed firsthand how the installation’s mission-ready personnel drive capability forward across the strategic landscape.

“The strength of this installation comes down to its people,” said Maj. Gen. Colin Connor, 20th AF commander. “The work happening here and the investment in its future make it clear that Team Kirtland is committed to excellence and to strengthening the nuclear enterprise every day.”

That operational backbone begins at the perimeter, where the 377th Security Forces Squadron manages continuous security operations supporting more than 20,000 personnel and visitors passing onto the installation daily, alongside specialized defenders securing vital strategic facilities.

At the Kirtland Underground Munitions Maintenance and Storage Complex, Airmen like Staff Sgt. Robert Ecklor, a 377th Weapons Systems Security Squadron defender, stand watch over one of the Department of Defense’s most critical assets, ensuring uncompromised security and continuous deterrence readiness. Connecting these frontline capabilities requires focused leadership and unwavering support across all operational units.

“Kirtland’s missions are diverse, but they all tie back to enabling the nuclear enterprise and supporting our priorities,” said Col. Justin Secrest, 377th Air Base Wing and installation commander.

Beyond physical security, Team Kirtland’s maintainers are actively innovating to make operations safer and more efficient. At the 377th Maintenance Squadron, Airmen demonstrated an organic brass inspection and recycling initiative, where Staff Sgt. Riston Mais showcased the meticulous debris-vetting process for spent brass casings to ensure only clean, serviceable material re-enters the reclamation pipeline. The unit-led initiative has recouped nearly $100,000 in savings and earnings - funds returned directly to the installation to enhance operational readiness and mission support.

“Our maintainers are solving problems that matter,” emphasized Chief Master Sgt. Jeffery Sipos, 20th AF command chief master sergeant. “They’re not just maintaining capability - they’re improving it.”

Senior leaders engaged directly with Airmen, Non-Commissioned Officers, and Company Grade Officers over discussions highlighting installation priorities and walked ongoing dormitory renovation sites. These infrastructure and environmental modernizations directly target living conditions, ensuring Airmen have high-quality, modern quarters that foster personal and professional resilience.

Parallel to dormitory updates, leadership spouses focused on family-centric support structures, including spouse employment panels, medical readiness discussions at the Kirtland Medical Group, and Science, Technology, Engineering and Math outreach programs at Starbase New Mexico and Sandia Base Elementary School.

“Readiness is more than the mission itself; it’s also having the right support systems in place,” said Sara Connor, spouse of the 20th Air Force commander, emphasizing how family stability directly reinforces the operational readiness of the warfighter.

Whether inspecting munitions casings, patrolling critical areas, modernizing civil infrastructure, or mentoring the next generation through community STEM partnerships, the Airmen of the 377th Air Base Wing continue to prove that strategic deterrence is built from the ground up. As 20th AF continues modernizing its capabilities, the dedicated professionals across Team Kirtland remain the driving force ensuring the nation’s deterrence posture remains credible, safe, and ready around the clock.

articles.title: HIANG, Philippine Air Force strengthen air defense interoperability
articles.body:
Hawaii Air National Guard (HIANG) and Philippine Air Force (PAF) personnel strengthened air defense interoperability during a Ground Radar Air Defense Subject Matter Expert Exchange held Sept. 14–18, 2026, at multiple locations across the Philippines.

The exchange focused on ground radar operations, air battle management, intelligence integration and organizational support functions, with training designed to improve skills and how both forces integrate.

“The ground radar air defense subject matter expertise is critical because, in holding these exchanges, we ensure our interoperability and our tactics, techniques and procedures are all aligned,” said Senior Master Sgt. Jennie Hale, 169th Air Defense Squadron command and control battle management operations specialist. “In case we need to integrate and work with the Philippine Air Force, we have that alignment with their similar experts and operators.”

HIANG air defense experts worked alongside Philippine Air Force radar operators, air battle managers, weapons directors and surveillance operators throughout the exchange. Practical training and simulated air defense scenarios were conducted at Wallace Air Station, while engagements at Clark Air Base and the Philippine Air Defense Command Center at Villamor Air Base focused on tabletop discussions, coordination and cultivating relations.

The PAF identified several training priorities ahead of the engagement, allowing planners to tailor its team and customize the curriculum.

Training included mission planning and intelligence incorporation, air defense command concepts, radar safety, maintenance practices and organizational structure. Participants also examined how support functions integrate with operational air defense units to accomplish the broader air defense mission.

“This year’s engagement, we hope to build on the air battle manager and operations side of things,” Hale said. “But we also wanted to re-engage with our ground radar expertise, which is why we also brought two radar operators as subject matter experts.”

A highlight of the exchange was integrating intelligence inputs into simulated air defense scenarios, giving participants an opportunity to react to exercise inputs in a practical setting. The training culminated in several simulated air defense exercises, moving the exchange beyond discussion and into hands-on application.

On the radar side, Philippine personnel examined HIANG practices involving radar safety, maintenance and the integration of support and operational functions.

“I wanted to impart on my Philippine counterparts that integrity and a safety-first mindset are of utmost importance in radar maintenance,” said Senior Master Sgt. Eugene Mariano, 297th Combat Airfield Operations Squadron radar airfield weather systems superintendent. “You cannot operate properly if you cannot operate safely.”

Mariano has participated in the engagement with the Philippines since 2014. With his retirement approaching, this year’s exchange marked his final opportunity to take part in the long-running engagement and share more than a decade of experience with Philippine counterparts.

Mariano, who also works for the Federal Aviation Administration in a civilian capacity, brought an additional perspective on the importance of civilian-military coordination in air defense operations.

“I tried to impart the importance of lessening the gap and bridging bureaucracy, strategy and continuity by finalizing agreements with their civilian counterpart agencies,” Mariano said.

The subject matter expert exchange is part of a long-standing partnership between the Hawaii National Guard and the Armed Forces of the Philippines dating back to the early 2000s through the State Partnership Program. Managed by the National Guard Bureau, the program pairs state National Guard organizations with partner-nation militaries, security forces and disaster-response organizations to strengthen relationships, build capacity and improve interoperability.

The first engagements revolving around air defense occurred in 2013. Those early iterations focused largely on academic briefings and professional exchanges. More recent engagements expanded to include hands-on simulation, marking a shift from information sharing toward practical application.

“For most of the engagements we did mostly academics, briefings,” Hale said. “Starting in 2024, we translated that into hands-on training, and that’s when we started doing simulations with the Philippine Air Force. Now our subject matter expert exchange is no longer just informational. It’s in practice.”

The engagement also continues to strengthen professional relationships developed over several decades of cooperation. Hale said Hawaii’s large Filipino-American community provides an additional cultural connection for some participants, although the partnership extends beyond shared heritage.

articles.title: 2026 SNCO induction ceremony at Goodfellow AFB
articles.body:
GOODFELLOW AIR FORCE BASE, Texas – The 17th Training Wing held an induction ceremony to recognize the technical sergeants selected for promotion and the newest master sergeants, Sept. 22.

The ceremony is a traditional rite of passage that welcomes newly promoted master sergeants and SNCO selectees into the highest echelon of the enlisted force.

Inductees transition from technical experts to operational leaders, taking on the responsibility of guiding teams, synchronizing efforts across units, shaping the success of the mission and developing future generations of Airmen and Guardians

“Tonight we celebrate you and your achievement,” said U.S. Air Force Chief Master Sgt. Derek Neill, 17th TRW command chief. “New SNCOs, take a pause, reflect on where you’ve been, how you can get better, and then we need you back here, locked in and getting our Airmen ready to go to war because that’s what we do. We need you at the front, leading them ever into danger."
